courseMetadata.title: React Front End Stack: From Runtime to Delivery
courseMetadata.description: A practical, transfer-focused course for software and UI/UX professionals who are joining or contributing to a React codebase. It covers the JavaScript runtime beneath React, TypeScript modelling at data boundaries, the rendering and component model, CSS and motion, debugging unfamiliar code, state placement, server state and routing, forms and internationalization, performance and accessibility, testing, client security, delivery gates, and an orientation to server rendering. The goal is not familiarity with APIs but the judgement to place state correctly, diagnose a defect from a symptom, and ship a change that does not break other things.

prerequisites.description: Working knowledge of JavaScript syntax: functions, arrays, objects, destructuring, and template literals. You do not need to know the event loop or closures in depth; the course teaches those.
Basic HTML and CSS: elements, attributes, selectors, and the box model. Semantic HTML and modern CSS features are taught in the course.
Comfort using a terminal, a code editor, and Git for everyday tasks such as branching, committing, and opening a pull request.
Some exposure to React components and hooks. You should have seen useState and useEffect before, even if their behaviour still surprises you.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Reference equality is one idea wearing five costumes: structural sharing in plain JS, keys and re-render triggers in React, selector memoisation in Redux, useShallow in Zustand, and blast-radius diagnosis when profiling. Learners who meet these as five separate rules memorise five rules and transfer none. Interleaving them forces the shared mechanism to surface.

Every boundary in the application asks the same question: is this data trustworthy, and who enforces that? A fetch response, a URL parameter, a form submission, and an API request are all the same problem. Mixing them prevents learners from filing 'validate with Zod' under forms only, and sets up the security section's argument that the client validates for usability while the server validates for truth.

The CSS decision rule and the accessibility semantics rule are the same rule applied to different platform layers: prefer the built-in behaviour, because it is faster and more correct across input modes you did not consider. Interleaving makes the parallel explicit, and links compositor-friendly animation to the performance measurement discipline that justifies it.

Tier selection is only learnable by repeatedly deciding between tiers, not by reading the list once. These experiences each present a placement decision from a different angle: the rule itself, the URL tier, the server-cache tier, the scoped tier, and the per-request tier that appears only under server rendering. Module semantics belongs here because 'where does this instance live' is the same question at a different scale.

Debugging, profiling, and testing are the same epistemic loop: form a hypothesis, gather evidence that could disprove it, change one thing, verify. Learners typically treat them as three unrelated skills. Interleaving them teaches the loop rather than three tool sets, and connects error propagation to why some failures are invisible until you look for them.

Three of this course's sharpest points are that a performance decision can be a data-exposure decision, that an unhandled async state is a correctness defect rather than a polish issue, and that moving code to a server changes what a habit costs. These only land if learners meet them together, because each one alone reads as a niche caution.

Several decisions in this course are cheap now and expensive later: logical properties before any translation exists, meaning-based props before a redesign, behaviour-coupled tests before a refactor, and a written decision record before its authors leave. Grouping them teaches the shape of that judgement rather than four disconnected pieces of advice.

probeQuestions.prompt: A loader runs `for (const id of ids) { results.push(await fetchRow(id)); }` for 20 ids. Each request takes about 200 ms. Roughly how long does the loop take?
options: About 200 ms, because `await` lets the requests run at the same time
About 4 seconds, because each request waits for the previous one to finish
About 200 ms, because the browser automatically batches requests to the same host
It depends entirely on the server, and cannot be estimated from the client code

optionFeedback.feedback: This is the most common misreading of `await`. `await` gives control back to the event loop, but the next request is not even created until the previous one settles. To overlap them you must start them all, then await the aggregate with `Promise.all`.
Correct. The loop is strictly sequential: 20 requests at roughly 200 ms each. This pattern is the single most common cause of a screen that takes seconds to appear for no visible reason.
Browsers do limit and pipeline connections per host, but that affects requests already in flight. Here only one request exists at a time, so there is nothing to batch.
Server latency is a variable, but the structure of the client code determines whether that latency is paid once or twenty times. That is knowable from the code alone.

routingRules.action: Mark fe-js-runtime-model async subskill as provisionally known. Section 1's async experience may be collapsed to its retrieval items.
Require Section 1 in full. Flag mis-await-parallel for reinforcement in the Section 7 server-state experience, where the same mistake reappears as parallel query design.

probeQuestions.prompt: A list of editable rows uses `items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)`. A user deletes a row in the middle of the list while another row has half-typed text in it. What is most likely to happen?
options: Nothing unusual; React removes the correct row and preserves the other rows' text
React throws a warning but behaves correctly at runtime
The half-typed text can end up attached to a different item than the one it was typed into
All rows lose their local state, because the list re-rendered

optionFeedback.feedback: This is what index keys appear to do until a list reorders. Deleting a middle item shifts every later index down by one, so React matches old component instances to new data by position rather than by identity.
React only warns when keys are missing entirely. An index key is a valid key, so there is no warning; the corruption is silent, which is exactly what makes this defect survive for months.

Correct. A key is a claim about identity. When the claim is wrong, React reuses a component instance for different data, and that instance keeps its state. This is the most common data-corruption defect in React codebases.
A re-render does not discard state. State is discarded when a component unmounts, or when its key changes. Here the problem is the opposite: state is preserved when it should not be.

routingRules.action: Mark the keys subskill of fe-react-rendering-model as provisionally known, but keep the Section 5 diagnosis experience, where the same defect must be recognised from a symptom rather than from code.
Require Section 3 in full and prioritise the Section 5 symptom-to-cause table.

probeQuestions.prompt: What does `const user = await res.json() as User` guarantee at runtime?
options: That the response matches the `User` shape, because TypeScript checks the cast
Nothing. The cast is a compile-time claim, and the data is whatever the server returned
That missing fields will be `undefined` rather than causing an error
That the response is valid JSON, but not that its fields are correct

optionFeedback.feedback: A type assertion tells the compiler to stop checking, rather than asking it to verify. TypeScript erases entirely at build time, so no assertion can inspect a runtime value.

Correct. The cast silences the compiler and moves the failure downstream, where it appears as `Cannot read properties of undefined` several components away from its cause. Validate at the boundary and derive the type from the validator instead.
Missing fields will indeed be `undefined`, but the type says they are present, so nothing forces you to handle that. The type system is now actively misleading you.
`res.json()` does guarantee parseable JSON, and it rejects otherwise. But that guarantee comes from `json()`, not from the cast, and it says nothing about the shape.

routingRules.action: Unlock the advanced Section 2 material on branded types and `satisfies`, and treat the boundary-validation experience as review.
Require Section 2 in full. Reinforce in Section 7, where URL parameters are shown to be the same untrusted input.

probeQuestions.prompt: You are modelling a lab result that is pending, running, complete, or failed. Which approach makes it impossible to write code that reads a result value from a failed test?
options: An interface with `status: string` and optional `value`, `error`, and `isLoading` fields
A discriminated union of four variants, each carrying only the fields that state actually has
An interface with all fields required, using sentinel values such as `-1` for a missing result
An interface with `status` typed as an enum, and all other fields optional

optionFeedback.feedback: Optional fields describe which fields may be absent, not which combinations are legal. This shape permits a result that is simultaneously loading, failed, and complete.

Correct. Once the variants are separate, narrowing on the tag gives you exactly the fields that state has, and a `never` assignment in the default branch turns any new state into a compile error everywhere it must be handled.
Sentinel values move the problem rather than removing it: now every reader must know that `-1` means absent, and forgetting that check produces a wrong number rather than a type error.
An enum constrains the tag, which is an improvement, but the other fields remain independently optional, so the impossible combinations are still writable.

routingRules.action: Treat discriminated unions as known; emphasise the exhaustiveness check and branded types instead.

probeQuestions.prompt: A search filter on one screen is currently held in a global store. Users complain that they cannot send a colleague a link to a filtered view, and that refreshing loses the filter. Where does the filter belong?
options: In the global store, with an added effect that saves it to local storage
In the URL as a query parameter, so it is shareable, survives refresh, and works with the back button
In component state, since only one screen uses it
In the server cache, so it stays consistent across sessions

optionFeedback.feedback: Local storage fixes the refresh complaint and neither of the others. The view still cannot be shared, and the back button still does not restore the previous filter.

Correct. The URL is the only tier that is shareable, survives a refresh, and participates in navigation history. The general rule: if a user would reasonably send this view to someone, it belongs in the URL.
Component state is the right default for most things, but it fails all three complaints here. The deciding question is shareability, not audience size.
The server cache holds data the server owns. A filter is a description of what the user is looking at, not data the backend is authoritative for.

routingRules.action: Collapse the Section 6 tier-introduction experience to its retrieval items; keep the five-questions decision experience, which requires applying the rule to ambiguous cases.
Require Sections 6 and 7 in full.

probeQuestions.prompt: An application hides a Delete button for users without delete permission, using `{canDelete && <DeleteButton />}`. The API has no permission check on the delete endpoint. How secure is this?
options: Secure enough, because a user without the button has no way to trigger the request
Not secure. Anyone can call the endpoint directly, so the server must check permission independently
Secure if the bundle is minified, since the endpoint URL is not human-readable
Secure if the check also happens in a route guard before the page loads

optionFeedback.feedback: Everything the browser holds, the user holds. The endpoint is visible in network traffic and can be called with `curl`. Hidden UI improves the interface; it enforces nothing.

Correct. The client check exists so users are not shown actions that would fail. The server is the only authority. A correct implementation also handles a 403 response as a normal outcome, because permissions change while long-lived tabs stay open.
Minification changes names, not behaviour, and the request is visible in the network panel regardless. Obscurity is not a control.
A route guard is still client-side code. It is the same misconception one layer up: it improves the experience and enforces nothing.

routingRules.action: Treat the enforcement principle as known; direct attention in Section 10 to the less familiar exposures: bundle secrets, telemetry payloads, and CSV formula injection.
Require Section 10 in full, and flag mis-hidden-ui-enforces for reinforcement at the Section 7 route-guard experience.

probeQuestions.prompt: A card should show a shadow and reveal a detail line when the user hovers over it. A developer implements this with `useState` plus `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave`. Beyond the extra renders, what is the most significant problem?
options: The state is not memoized, so the parent re-renders as well
`onMouseEnter` never fires for keyboard users, so the revealed content is unreachable without a mouse
Mouse events do not work on touch devices, so mobile users see the shadow permanently
There is no significant problem; this is the idiomatic React approach

optionFeedback.feedback: The extra renders are real but were excluded by the question. Memoisation would not address the deeper defect here.

Correct. `:hover` combined with `:focus-within` covers pointer and keyboard users in two lines of CSS. The JavaScript version silently hides content from anyone navigating by keyboard, and accessibility audits routinely miss it because the content exists in the DOM.
Touch behaviour is genuinely awkward for hover interactions, but browsers do synthesise some mouse events on tap. The reliable and complete failure is the keyboard one.
It is common, which is not the same as correct. The platform already expresses this behaviour, faster and across more input modes.

routingRules.action: Unlock the advanced Section 4 material on container queries, cascade layers, and FLIP; treat the decision-rule experience as review.

probeQuestions.prompt: A table of 200,000 rows is made usable by virtualizing it, so only the visible rows exist in the DOM. Which of the following is now broken and needs deliberate work to restore?
options: Nothing; virtualization is transparent to users once the library is configured
Only scrolling performance on low-powered devices
Screen reader row position, keyboard navigation beyond the visible window, find-in-page, and printing
Only sorting, which must now happen on the server

optionFeedback.feedback: This is the assumption that produces a fast table nobody can use. Each broken behaviour has a specific fix, but none of them is automatic.
Scrolling performance is what virtualization improves, not what it breaks.

Correct. Because the DOM no longer contains the dataset, it no longer tells the truth about it. `aria-rowcount` and `aria-rowindex` restore position, a roving tabindex plus scroll-to-index restores navigation, in-app search replaces Ctrl+F, and export must be handled on the server.
Sorting can remain on the client if the dataset is already in memory. Whether it should is a separate question about data exposure, not a consequence of virtualization.

routingRules.action: Treat the virtualization trade-off as known; focus Section 9 on the profiling method and the data-exposure argument instead.
Require Section 9 in full, with the accessibility experiences marked as non-skippable.

probeQuestions.prompt: A team has 2,300 tests and 91% line coverage, but has not completed a refactor in seven months because every attempt breaks hundreds of tests. The tests assert on CSS class names and internal component state. What is the root problem?
options: Insufficient test coverage; more tests would catch the breakages earlier
The tests are coupled to construction rather than to behaviour, so implementation changes produce false failures
Too many end-to-end tests, which are inherently fragile
The refactors themselves are too large and should be broken into smaller commits

optionFeedback.feedback: More tests of the same kind make the problem worse. Coverage measures which lines executed, not whether the assertions describe anything a user cares about.

Correct. A test should fail when behaviour changes and pass when only implementation changes. A suite that fails on a class rename teaches the team to stop refactoring, so a suite bought to enable change ends up preventing it.
End-to-end tests are slow and can be flaky, but they generally assert on behaviour, so a class rename would not break them. The described symptom points the other way.
Smaller commits are good practice and would reduce the pain per attempt. They would not change the fact that renaming a class breaks tests that assert nothing about behaviour.

routingRules.action: Treat the contract-versus-construction rule as known; emphasise network-boundary mocking and configuration coverage in Section 10.

probeQuestions.prompt: You join a team today. A user reports that the delivery estimate on one screen is sometimes wrong. You have never seen this codebase. Describe your first three actions, in order, and say why each one comes before the next.
scoringCriteria: Reproducing the defect reliably appears before any code is read or changed, with the reasoning that an unreproducible defect cannot be verified as fixed.
The response works backwards from what is on screen — locating the visible value, then its props, then its owner, then its data source — rather than reading the codebase from an entry file.
The actual network response is inspected before assuming the defect is in the frontend.
The word 'sometimes' is treated as an unidentified condition to be narrowed, not as randomness.
A hypothesis is stated before files are opened, and only one thing is changed at a time.

routingRules.condition: self-rated Strong AND all criteria addressed
routingRules.action: Section 5 may be delivered as its diagnosis activity only, skipping the tracing and tooling content blocks.

routingRules.condition: self-rated Weak OR reproduction step absent
routingRules.action: Require Section 5 in full; it is the highest-leverage section for this learner.

probeQuestions.prompt: In a query library, a list already has cached data on screen and a background refresh begins. Which flag is true, and what should the UI show?
options: `isLoading` is true; show a skeleton in place of the list
`isFetching` is true; keep the existing rows visible and show a small activity indicator
Both are true; the choice of indicator is a matter of taste
Neither is true, because the data is already cached

optionFeedback.feedback: `isLoading` is true only when there is no cached data yet. Showing a skeleton on every background refresh makes the screen flash back to empty, which users read as the application breaking.

Correct. `isLoading` means there is nothing to show yet; `isFetching` means a request is in flight, including a refresh over existing data. Keeping content visible during a refresh is one of the cheapest available improvements to perceived speed.
They mean different things and are not both true here. Treating the distinction as taste is what produces the flashing-skeleton defect.
A request really is in flight, so `isFetching` is true. Cached data affects `isLoading`, not `isFetching`.

routingRules.action: Treat the two-flag distinction as known; focus Section 7 on tag invalidation and the four async states.

probeQuestions.prompt: A file contains `export const store = createStore()` at the top level. This has worked correctly in the browser for two years. The team now adds server-side rendering. Explain what changes, and why the same code is safe in one environment and a security defect in the other.
scoringCriteria: States that a module is evaluated once per JavaScript context, so module scope is a singleton for that context's lifetime.
Identifies that in a browser each user has their own context, so the singleton is per-user by construction.
Identifies that a server process handles many requests, so the same instance is shared across concurrent users.
Names the consequence as one user's data appearing in another user's response, rather than as a performance or correctness annoyance.
States the fix as creating the store per request, and ideally notes that the defect is load-dependent and therefore likely to survive low-traffic testing.

routingRules.condition: self-rated Strong AND cross-user consequence named
routingRules.action: Section 11 may be delivered in condensed form, keeping the hydration and 'use client' boundary material.
Require the Section 1 module-semantics experience before Section 6, since the store-creation rule there depends on it.

competencies.title: The JavaScript runtime beneath React
competencies.description: Reason about the single thread, the microtask and macrotask queues, what `await` does and does not do, and how reference equality drives change detection across React, Redux, and memoization.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict the execution order of synchronous code, promise continuations, and timers, and explain why an async function body runs to its first `await` before yielding.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly orders a mixed example and justifies the ordering by naming the queue each item enters, not by pattern-matching to a memorised output.

desiredOutcomes.description: Distinguish sequential from concurrent asynchronous work, and restructure accidentally sequential code without changing its error handling.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Converts a sequential loop to concurrent execution, states the timing difference, and identifies at least one case where sequential execution is the correct choice.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain why a mutated object does not trigger a re-render, and apply structural sharing to update nested state.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names reference comparison as the mechanism and produces a correct immutable update that copies only the changed path.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Using async/await makes my requests run at the same time.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: `await` suspends the current function and returns control to the event loop. The next expression is not evaluated until the awaited promise settles, so the following request is not even created yet. Concurrency comes from starting the work, not from how you wait for it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner instrument both forms with timestamps at request start and finish, so the gap between starts is visible rather than inferred. Then require them to name one situation where sequential execution is correct — a dependent request, or deliberate rate limiting — so the lesson is 'not by accident' rather than 'always use Promise.all'.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Changing an object in place is fine as long as I call the setter afterwards.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: React compares by reference using `Object.is`. Mutating an object changes its contents but not its identity, so the comparison reports no change and the render is skipped. Passing the same reference to a setter does not help, because the reference is what is compared.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show the same update twice side by side, logging the result of `Object.is(prev, next)` in both. Then have the learner update a value two levels deep, which forces them to copy the path rather than the leaf, and connect this to why the copy is cheap: every unchanged branch is reused.

competencies.title: Module evaluation and instance lifetime
competencies.description: Explain that an ES module is evaluated once per JavaScript context, and predict the consequences for shared caches, stores, and side effects in browser and server environments.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict whether a value declared at module level is shared, and by whom, in a browser tab and in a server process.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly identifies the sharing scope in both environments and names the consequence in security terms, not only correctness terms.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify side effects at module scope and explain when they run.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Recognises that module-level effects run on import regardless of whether the export is used, and proposes moving them into an explicitly called initialiser.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A store or cache created at module level belongs to whoever is using the app, so it is naturally per-user.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It is per-context, not per-user. In a browser those happen to coincide, because each user has their own tab. A server process handles many users' requests in one context, so the same instance is shared, and one user's data can be read into another user's response.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run two concurrent simulated requests against a module-level store with different user identities and observe the leak directly, then repeat with per-request creation. The demonstration matters more than the explanation, because the defect is load-dependent and therefore easy to disbelieve.

competencies.title: Error propagation across sync, async, and React boundaries
competencies.description: Predict where an error will surface, choose the correct handling mechanism for synchronous, promise-based, event-handler, and render-time failures, and recognise the failure modes that produce silent wrong answers.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain why `try`/`catch` requires an `await`, and why `fetch` does not reject on a 500 response.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifies both behaviours and writes a fetch wrapper that checks `response.ok` and throws a typed error.

desiredOutcomes.description: State what an error boundary catches and what it does not, and choose the correct mechanism for each uncaught case.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names event handlers, timers, and async code as outside a boundary's reach, and supplies the correct handling for each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An error boundary catches the errors in my components, so I do not need try/catch inside them.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Error boundaries catch errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. They do not catch errors in event handlers, in `setTimeout`, or in async code, because those do not run inside React's render call stack.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner throw from three places inside a component wrapped in a boundary — render, a click handler, and a timeout — and observe which one the boundary catches. Then have them write the correct handling for the two it misses, including a global `unhandledrejection` listener so that missed rejections become visible.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the server returns an error status, my fetch call will throw and my catch block will run.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: `fetch` rejects only when the network request itself fails. A 404 or a 500 is a successful HTTP exchange from the browser's point of view, so the promise resolves and your error handling never runs. The error body is then parsed as if it were data.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call an endpoint that returns 500 with a JSON error body and observe the success path executing with nonsense data. Then require an `ok` check that throws a typed error, and connect this to the boundary-validation habit taught for data shape: both are checks at the same edge.

competencies.title: Modelling data and validating at boundaries
competencies.description: Model domain states so invalid combinations cannot be written, validate external data where it enters the application, and use branded types and `satisfies` to close the gaps that plain structural typing leaves open.

desiredOutcomes.description: Convert an optional-field model into a discriminated union with an exhaustiveness check.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Produces variants that carry only their own fields, adds a `never` assignment, and can state how many compile errors a new variant would produce and why that is the benefit.

desiredOutcomes.description: Validate external data at the boundary and derive the type from the validator.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Places validation at the network edge, uses `z.infer` rather than a parallel interface, and explains why the failure location matters for diagnosis.

desiredOutcomes.description: Apply branded types to identifiers that share a primitive type.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Brands two identifiers, demonstrates the compile error on a swapped argument, and creates branded values at the validation boundary rather than by scattered casts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Casting the response with `as` gives me type safety at the network boundary.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A type assertion instructs the compiler to stop checking. It performs no runtime work and TypeScript erases entirely at build time, so nothing inspects the actual value. The claim is simply believed, and the failure appears far from its cause.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner cast a response whose shape they then change on the server, and trace how far the wrong data travels before anything fails. Then replace the cast with a schema parse and observe the failure move to the boundary with a message naming the offending field.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Optional fields are how you model something that is sometimes present.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Optional fields describe which fields may be absent individually. They cannot express which combinations are legal, so a shape with optional `value`, `error`, and `isLoading` permits states that make no sense, and every consumer must defend against combinations that should be impossible.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask the learner to enumerate the combinations their optional-field interface permits, then compare that count to the number of real states. The gap is the defect surface. Then have them rewrite as a union and repeat the count.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Using `any` here is pragmatic; I will tighten it later.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: `any` disables checking for every expression it touches, and it propagates silently through call chains, so the damage is not local to the annotation. `unknown` provides the same escape from over-specification while still forcing a check before use.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner replace one `any` with `unknown` and observe how many downstream sites the compiler now flags. Those sites were already unsafe; the annotation was hiding them.

competencies.title: React's rendering, reconciliation, and effect model
competencies.description: Distinguish render from commit, identify what triggers a re-render, use keys as identity claims, and treat effects as synchronization with an explicit undo.

desiredOutcomes.description: Name the four re-render triggers and distinguish a re-render from a DOM update.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Lists all four triggers and explains why a re-render producing identical output costs nothing at commit.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict the consequence of an incorrect key and use a key change deliberately to reset state.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Describes state attaching to the wrong item on reorder, explains why static test data hides it, and applies key-as-reset in place of a clearing effect.

desiredOutcomes.description: Decide whether a given piece of work belongs in an effect, in render, or in an event handler.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Applies the synchronization test, writes a correct cleanup, and correctly rejects derived-state and event-response uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Index keys are fine as long as I am not sorting the list.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Insertion, deletion, and filtering all shift indices, so the key no longer identifies the same item. React then reuses a component instance for different data and preserves its state, which corrupts local state silently. Only append-only, never-filtered lists are safe, and that constraint rarely survives a product cycle.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner delete a middle row while another row holds unsaved input, and watch the input attach to the wrong record. Then require them to add exactly one interaction — a mid-list deletion — to a test suite built on static data, so they learn which test would have caught it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: useEffect is where you put code that should run after the component mounts.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That description explains the timing but not the purpose, and it leads to effects that derive state from props, respond to events, or subscribe without cleaning up. An effect keeps an external system in sync with React state and undoes that when it no longer applies; the cleanup is not optional bookkeeping but half the definition.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Apply the cleanup test to each effect in the learner's own code: if they cannot write a cleanup that reverses exactly what the effect did, the work probably belongs in render or in a handler. Then have them run under Strict Mode, where double invocation exposes the missing cleanups.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Every re-render updates the DOM, so re-renders are what make my app slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Rendering produces a description of the UI; only the commit touches the DOM, and only where the description differs. Rendering is comparatively cheap. Treating all re-renders as costs leads to memoization applied everywhere, which adds comparisons and obscures the real bottleneck.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner profile a component that re-renders frequently with identical output, and read the commit duration separately from the render duration. Connect this to the classification step in the performance section, where the distinction decides which fix applies.

competencies.title: Component API design
competencies.description: Design props that express meaning rather than appearance, prefer composition to configuration, and use custom hooks and headless patterns as the units of reuse.

desiredOutcomes.description: Refactor appearance props into meaning props and explain the maintenance consequence.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Replaces a colour or variant prop with a domain-meaningful one and states what a theme change costs under each design.

desiredOutcomes.description: Convert an accumulation of boolean props into a composed API.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Produces a children-based or compound API, and counts the props removed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The more props a component takes, the more reusable it is.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Each additional boolean prop multiplies the states the component must support and pushes decisions onto every caller. Past a small number, the component becomes a small framework that is harder to use correctly than writing the markup directly. Composition moves the variation to the call site without expanding the API surface.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner count the combinations their prop set permits and identify how many are actually used and tested. Then convert the component to accept children and recount. The reduction is the argument.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A component that needs a different layout in a sidebar should take a variant prop.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That prop encodes an appearance decision in the component's API, so every caller must know which variant suits the space they are placing it in. It also breaks the moment someone places the component somewhere new, and the resulting bugs look unrelated to each other. A container query moves the decision inside the component.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner place a variant-driven card in a narrow sidebar on a wide viewport and observe the failure. Then replace the prop with a container query and verify the same component in three contexts without any caller knowledge.

competencies.title: Styling system structure
competencies.description: Structure styles with cascade layers, design tokens as custom properties, and logical properties, so that overrides are predictable and later internationalization is inexpensive.

desiredOutcomes.description: Resolve a specificity conflict using cascade layers rather than `!important`.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Declares a layer order, removes the `!important`, and explains why layer order beats specificity.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement theming with custom properties and demonstrate that switching causes no React renders.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Themes via a root data attribute and confirms zero renders with the profiler.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When a style will not apply, the fix is a more specific selector or !important.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Escalating specificity wins the current conflict and makes the next one harder, because the ceiling rises permanently and `!important` can only be beaten by another `!important`. Cascade layers express the intended precedence directly, so a low-specificity utility can override a high-specificity component rule.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner find an existing `!important` in their codebase, declare a layer order, and remove it. Then ask what would happen to the next override under each approach.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I will switch to logical properties if we ever need right-to-left support.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Logical properties are identical to physical ones in a left-to-right language, so adopting them early costs nothing. Retrofitting them is not a find-and-replace: every directional declaration must be individually judged for whether it should mirror, and the failures are visual rather than compile-time, so verification is manual across every screen.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner set `dir="rtl"` on an existing component built with physical properties and count the defects, then convert to logical properties and count what that alone fixed. The proportion is usually persuasive.

competencies.title: Choosing the platform over JavaScript
competencies.description: Decide whether a behaviour belongs in CSS or in JavaScript, using the test of what information the browser does not already have, and recognise that platform implementations are frequently more correct across input modes.

desiredOutcomes.description: Apply the decision rule to a mixed set of behaviours and justify each assignment.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly assigns hover, layout response, sticky positioning, data-driven sizing, and gesture handling, and names a cost beyond performance for at least two JavaScript reimplementations.

desiredOutcomes.description: Replace a viewport-driven layout decision with a container query.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Removes the prop, and verifies the component in a grid, a narrow sidebar, and a modal without caller changes.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: JavaScript can do everything CSS can, so using state for interaction styling is the general solution.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Capability is not suitability. The platform version runs in the browser's own engine rather than on your main thread, works before hydration, survives a failed bundle, and handles input modes you did not consider — `onMouseEnter` never fires for a keyboard user, so the JavaScript version silently hides content from them.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build the hover card both ways, profile a pointer traverse across forty cards under CPU throttling, and then unplug the mouse and tab through both. The performance number and the missing keyboard reveal make two independent arguments, and the second is usually the one that changes behaviour.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Media queries are how a component responds to the space it has.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A media query asks about the viewport, but a component's constraint is its container. The same card in a 300 px sidebar on a 1440 px screen receives the wide-viewport branch and overflows. The resulting defects appear in unrelated tickets because nothing points at the shared cause.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner reproduce the sidebar failure deliberately, then fix it with a container query and confirm that several separately-reported layout tickets close together. That co-occurrence is the diagnostic signature of an architectural fault.

competencies.title: Motion that communicates
competencies.description: Use animation to explain change rather than to decorate, choose the cheapest tool that expresses the motion, animate compositor-friendly properties, and honour reduced-motion preferences without removing feedback.

desiredOutcomes.description: Assign a set of motion requirements to transitions, keyframes, the Web Animations API, or a library, with justification.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reserves the library for exit animation, gestures, or springs, and justifies it by React's unmounting behaviour rather than by animation in general.

desiredOutcomes.description: Produce a reduced-motion response that removes travel while preserving the state-change signal.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Documents per animation what was removed and what was kept, with a reason for each retention.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Animation is polish, so it is a nice-to-have that can be added at the end.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Motion carries information: where an element came from, where it went, and whether it is the same object. Motion that answers none of those questions delays interaction for no benefit, and for users with vestibular sensitivity it causes physical symptoms. Treating it as decoration produces both useless motion and missing motion.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For each animation in the learner's interface, require a one-sentence statement of what it tells the user. Anything without an answer is removed. This converts a taste discussion into a content question.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Supporting prefers-reduced-motion means turning animation off.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Removing all feedback leaves users unable to tell what changed or where it went, which makes the interface harder to use for exactly the group you were trying to help. The harmful component is travel — parallax, large translations, and repetition — not the fact that something changed.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner ship the blunt global reset first, to stop harm, then revisit each animation and record what was removed and what was kept. The two-stage response is itself the lesson: stop the harm immediately, then restore the communication.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding will-change to animated elements makes animation faster.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: `will-change` promotes an element to its own compositing layer, which costs memory. Applied broadly it can reduce performance, and modern browsers already promote automatically for transform and opacity transitions, so the hint is usually redundant.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner measure memory and frame rate with `will-change` applied to every card, then with it removed. Then discuss the legitimate narrow use: applied just before a known-expensive animation and removed after.

competencies.title: Systematic diagnosis
competencies.description: Move from a reported symptom to a verified cause using reproduction, isolation, bisection, a single stated hypothesis, and one change at a time.

desiredOutcomes.description: Apply the diagnostic sequence to an unfamiliar defect and explain the mechanism of the fix.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reproduces before reading code, states one hypothesis before opening files, changes one thing, and explains the mechanism rather than describing the edit.

desiredOutcomes.description: Map a React symptom to its likely mechanism from the five common causes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly identifies at least four of five symptom-to-cause mappings and names the tool that would confirm each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The fastest way to fix a bug is to try things until the symptom goes away.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without a reproduction you cannot distinguish a fix from a coincidence, and without one change at a time you cannot attribute the improvement. Untested edits accumulate, so a one-line defect becomes an unreviewable diff, and the masked cause resurfaces later in a different form.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require a written hypothesis before any file is opened, and require reverting a failed attempt before trying the next. Then show a file containing three overlapping previous 'fixes' for one cause, and ask which of them can now safely be removed — the answer is nobody knows, which is the cost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the symptom is gone, the bug is fixed.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A loading flag placed over a stale value hides the wrong data rather than correcting it, so the defect reappears wherever the same mechanism operates. If you cannot state why the change works, you have probably moved the problem.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require a one-sentence mechanism explanation before a ticket is closed, and treat inability to write one as the ticket not being finished. Then have the learner search the codebase for other uses of the same mechanism.

competencies.title: Orienting in unfamiliar code
competencies.description: Locate the relevant code in a codebase you did not write by tracing a value backwards from the rendered output to its data source, and read a stack trace to find the first frame that matters.

desiredOutcomes.description: Trace a displayed value back through props, ownership, and the network response.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names the ordered steps, ends at the actual network response rather than at the code describing it, and identifies what the trace revealed about the architecture.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify the first first-party frame in a stack trace and state what it tells you.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Skips framework frames, reads the message literally, and notes the need for source maps in production.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: To work in a new codebase you first read it, starting from the entry file and following the imports.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That approach has no end point and produces recall without orientation. Following one specific value backwards from the screen terminates, and in a single pass it teaches the routing convention, the data layer, the state library, and the folder rule — the things you actually need to make a change.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner twenty minutes and one value to trace end to end in an unfamiliar repository, then ask them to describe the architecture from memory. Compare against a learner who spent the same time reading files.

competencies.title: Changing code safely and reviewing changes
competencies.description: Make the smallest change that fixes the defect, separate fixes from refactors, respect local convention, check what depends on shared code, and review others' changes against the places defects concentrate.

desiredOutcomes.description: Separate a defect fix from an accompanying refactor and justify the separation.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: States the reviewability and revert arguments, not merely that it is tidier.

desiredOutcomes.description: Review a change against the concentration points for React defects.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Checks scope against the ticket, state placement, keys, dependency arrays, cleanups, error and empty paths, keyboard operability, and test coupling.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Since I am already in this file, I should clean it up in the same commit as the fix.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The reviewer can no longer see which lines are the correction, so the fix is effectively unreviewed. And if the refactor causes a regression, reverting it also removes the fix, which forces a choice between two defects.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner produce a mixed commit and a split pair for the same work, and review both as a reviewer would. Then ask which one they could revert safely at 6pm on a Friday.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A large pull request is fine as long as the changes are related.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Review quality falls sharply with size. A very large diff receives approval rather than inspection, so the review provides no defect-finding value while still consuming everyone's time and creating a false record of scrutiny.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner review a 2,000-line diff under a time limit, list what they actually verified, then review a 200-line diff and repeat. The difference in the two lists is the argument.

competencies.title: State placement
competencies.description: Assign each piece of state to exactly one tier — server cache, URL, global client, scoped store, injected context, or local — using ownership, lifetime, audience, shareability, and blast radius.

desiredOutcomes.description: Assign a mixed set of state to tiers with a written justification per item.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Applies the five questions explicitly, and identifies at least one item where two tiers are defensible, arguing for one.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose misplaced state from its symptoms in both directions.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Distinguishes too-low symptoms such as repeated lifting and diverging sibling copies from too-high symptoms such as unrelated re-renders and manual clearing.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Putting state in the global store is the safe default, since anything can read it if we need it later.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It widens the blast radius so unrelated components re-render, it accumulates single-screen concerns that nobody is willing to delete because the dependencies are unclear, and it requires remembering to clear state when a feature unmounts. Optionality is bought with permanent coupling.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner audit an existing global store and mark each entry with the number of distinct screens that read it. Entries with one reader are the evidence. Then move one and record the diff size and what improved.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The URL should reflect state that is kept in a store, so the store stays the source of truth.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Two copies of the same fact will disagree, most visibly after a back navigation, when history changes the URL without notifying the store. The URL must be the source of truth and the store must derive from it, or one of them must not exist.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build the mirrored version and press the back button, then rebuild with the URL as the single source. The failure is immediate and needs no explanation.

competencies.title: Redux Toolkit patterns
competencies.description: Work in a Redux codebase: pure reducers, Immer drafts, actions shaped as events, memoized selectors and their cache limits, and normalised entity storage.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write an event-shaped action and explain what it communicates that a setter does not.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names multi-slice response and readability as a record of user activity, and produces a reducer that stays pure.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose and fix a memoized selector that never hits its cache.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifies the single-result cache, demonstrates the recomputation, and applies a per-instance factory or memoization options.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An action is how you set a value in the store, so naming it after the value is clearest.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A setter records the decision the call site already made, so the reasoning lives in the component and cannot be shared. An event names what happened, which lets several slices respond independently and makes the action log readable as a record of user activity rather than a list of assignments.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write both forms for the same interaction, then introduce a second slice that must also react. The setter version requires a second dispatch from the component; the event version requires no component change at all.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: createSelector memoizes per argument set, so one shared selector is fine everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The default cache holds one result. Components calling the same selector with different arguments alternate, so every call misses, recomputes, and returns a new reference — which then defeats downstream memoization as well. The selector appears to work while providing no benefit.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner log recomputations from two components with different arguments, then fix with a per-instance factory and log again. The count difference is the lesson.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Immer lets me mutate state, so the old immutability rules no longer apply.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: You are mutating a draft Proxy, not the state. Returning a value while also mutating the draft is an error, and holding a reference to the draft beyond the reducer produces a revoked-proxy crash. The immutability contract is unchanged; only the syntax is different.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner deliberately keep a draft reference outside a reducer and observe the crash, then explain what Immer produced at the moment the reducer returned.

competencies.title: Scoped and lightweight stores
competencies.description: Use a selector-based lightweight store correctly, including shallow comparison for multi-value selections and per-instance store creation carried by context.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a component re-rendering on every store change and fix the selector.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifies reference comparison of a freshly created object as the cause and applies shallow comparison.

desiredOutcomes.description: Create a store per feature instance and pass the handle through context without causing consumer re-renders.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Creates the store once per instance and explains why carrying a stable handle in context is a correct use of context.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Selecting several values at once by returning an object is just a convenience.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The default comparison is by reference, and an object literal is a new reference on every call. So the store concludes that the selection changed on every update, and the component re-renders for changes it does not care about — the exact problem selectors exist to prevent.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner count renders with an object-returning selector while mutating an unrelated part of the store, then add shallow comparison and count again.

competencies.title: Server state and caching
competencies.description: Treat server data as a cache of something you do not own: reason about cache keys, distinguish loading from fetching, diagnose invalidation failures systematically, and choose optimistic or pessimistic updates by consequence.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a failure to refresh after a mutation using the four ordered checks.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Runs provides, invalidates, IDs match, and subscribed in order, and identifies which check found the fault.

desiredOutcomes.description: Decide optimistic or pessimistic for a given action and design the rollback.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Argues from the consequence of being wrong and makes the rollback visible to the user.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Server responses should be copied into the client store so components have one place to read from.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That creates two sources of truth for data the server owns. The copy has no invalidation story, so it drifts, and the resulting defects appear as data that is correct on one screen and stale on another with no obvious pattern.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner trace one field that exists in both the cache and the store, and find the code responsible for keeping them equal. Usually there is none. Then delete the copy and read from the cache directly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: isLoading tells me whether a request is in progress.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: `isLoading` is true only when there is no cached data yet. Using it for background refreshes replaces visible content with a skeleton every time data refreshes, which users experience as the screen breaking, and which also destroys scroll position and focus.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner trigger a background refetch with both flags logged, then implement the skeleton-versus-indicator split and observe the difference in perceived stability.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Optimistic updates are better because the interface feels faster.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Speed is not the only variable. Showing success for an action that failed can produce real-world consequences — an unwatered field, an unissued refund — and a silent rollback compounds it by removing the user's chance to notice. The decision is about the cost of being wrong.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner classify five actions by what happens if the optimistic display is wrong, then implement one of each kind, ensuring the rollback is visible in the optimistic case.

competencies.title: Designing for all async states
competencies.description: Design loading, empty, error, and partial states as first-class requirements, including out-of-order responses and skeletons that do not shift layout.

desiredOutcomes.description: Specify all four states for a data-driven view, including what the empty and error states offer the user.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Empty and error states each provide a next action; partial state is designed rather than omitted.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Loading and error states are polish; the important work is making the successful path correct.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The failure states are where users spend their worst moments, and the partial state — some data present, some failed — produces a page that looks correct while a value is silently wrong. That is harder to notice and harder to report than an outright failure, so it survives longest.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner force each of the four states deliberately, including partial failure of one parallel request, and write the user-facing copy for each. Requiring the copy exposes empty states that offer no next action.

competencies.title: Routing and URL as state
competencies.description: Treat routes as simultaneous boundaries for URL state, code splitting, data loading, errors, and layout, and apply the rules governing what belongs in a URL and how it is validated.

desiredOutcomes.description: Move shareable view state into the URL, validated as external input.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Distinguishes path from query parameters, uses replace for continuous changes, and degrades safely on a hand-edited URL.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A route guard that blocks the admin page keeps unauthorised users out of admin functionality.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A guard is client code deciding what to render. The underlying endpoints remain callable directly, so the guard prevents an unpleasant experience rather than an unauthorised action. Every guarded route needs an independent server-side check.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call a guarded route's endpoint with `curl` while signed in as an unauthorised user, document the successful response, and only then write the server-side check. The documented response is what makes the principle stick.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The URL identifies the page; view state like filters and tabs belongs in memory.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That view state determines what the user is actually looking at, so keeping it in memory means it cannot be bookmarked, shared, restored after a refresh, or navigated with the back button. Those losses are usually reported as several unrelated complaints, which hides the single cause.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner collect the complaints a memory-held filter produces — unshareable, lost on refresh, broken back button — and confirm that one change resolves all three.

competencies.title: Form lifecycle and validation
competencies.description: Build forms that scale: uncontrolled inputs with subscriptions, one schema serving as validator and type, correct validation timing, dirty tracking, server error mapping, and accessible error presentation.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement a form whose schema is both validator and type, including a cross-field rule attached to the correct field.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses `path` on the refinement, emits message keys rather than English strings, and maps a 422 response onto the named field.

desiredOutcomes.description: Handle the four submission states and dirty tracking correctly.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Disables during submission, resets with saved values afterwards, and avoids recreating default values each render.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Controlled inputs are the correct React default for forms.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Controlled inputs re-render the form on every keystroke, which is invisible on a small form and clearly laggy on a large one. An uncontrolled approach with per-field subscriptions keeps values in the DOM and re-renders only the fields that display them.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner profile keystroke renders on an eight-field form in both implementations, then extrapolate to forty fields. The measurement, not the principle, is what changes practice.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A cross-field validation rule will show its error next to the relevant field automatically.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without an explicit `path`, the error attaches to the form root. The rule fires, the submit is blocked, and the user sees nothing anywhere — which they experience as a broken button rather than as a validation failure.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build the rule without `path` first and try to submit, so they experience the dead button, then add `path` and observe the message appear. The order matters: the failure must be felt.

competencies.title: Internationalization beyond strings
competencies.description: Handle locale-dependent formatting, parsing, collation, pluralization, text expansion, and mirroring, and recognise which decisions are free now and expensive later.

desiredOutcomes.description: Format and parse numbers, dates, and lists correctly for several locales using built-in APIs.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the locale explicitly, constructs formatters once, uses locale-aware collation for sorting, and parses locale-formatted numeric input correctly.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify the structural decisions that make later localization cheap.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names logical properties, message keys in schemas, ICU messages, and locale in the URL, and explains why each is free to adopt early.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Internationalization means extracting the strings and sending them to translators.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Strings are the cheapest part. The expensive parts are layout that assumed English length, physical CSS directions that will not mirror, hand-rolled formatting, grammar categories that do not exist in English, locale-dependent collation, and numeric parsing — several of which produce silently wrong values rather than visibly wrong text.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run a pseudo-locale pass before any translation is commissioned; it surfaces truncation and unextracted strings together. Then have the learner audit one numeric input and one sorted list, which are where the silent defects live.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A count check like `count === 1 ? 'day' : 'days'` can be translated by a good translator.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Arabic has six plural categories and Polish four. The branches do not exist in your code for a translator to fill, so no amount of translation effort fixes it. The message structure, not the vocabulary, is wrong.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show the learner the CLDR plural rules for Arabic, then have them convert one ternary to an ICU message and verify the categories resolve. Connect this to the fragment-concatenation problem, which fails for the same structural reason.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: parseFloat is a reasonable way to read a number the user typed.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: German and many other locales use a full stop as the thousands separator, so `parseFloat('1.234,56')` returns `1.234` — an error by a factor of a thousand, with a plausible-looking result that passes review and survives for months.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner enter a German-formatted amount into their own form and observe the stored value, then implement locale-aware parsing. The plausibility of the wrong number is the point.

competencies.title: Rendering large datasets
competencies.description: Choose between client pagination, server pagination, and virtualization on the basis of both scale and data exposure, and restore what virtualization breaks.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select a list strategy and justify it in terms of scale and entitlement.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Argues from what the browser should hold, not only from what React can render, and enforces entitlement at the API.

desiredOutcomes.description: Enumerate what virtualization breaks and implement the mitigations.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Restores row position, keyboard navigation, in-app search, export, and focus behaviour.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Virtualization is a drop-in fix; install the library and the table is fast.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It is fast, and it also removes the dataset from the DOM. So the DOM stops telling the truth about the data: screen readers report the wrong position, keyboard navigation stops at the rendered window, find-in-page and printing see only visible rows, and a focused row that unmounts sends focus to the top of the page mid-task.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner virtualize a table and then complete a real task using only a keyboard and a screen reader. The list of what broke writes itself, and the experience of losing focus mid-task is more persuasive than the rule.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Sorting and filtering on the client is a performance choice that makes the table feel responsive.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It requires the entire dataset in the browser, where it is readable in developer tools, held in memory, and included in anything that exfiltrates browser data. If the rows contain personal data, a responsiveness decision has silently become a data-exposure decision that nobody reviewed as one, and a row-level filter in the table is presentation rather than authorization.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner open developer tools on their own client-sorted table and read a record they are not entitled to see. Then move sorting to the API and confirm the response contains only permitted rows.

competencies.title: Measured performance work
competencies.description: Reproduce at production scale under throttling, classify the dominant cost as volume, computation, or blast radius, fix one thing, and measure again.

desiredOutcomes.description: Run the measurement procedure and classify the dominant cost correctly.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reproduces at production volume with throttling, distinguishes many-small from one-large-self-time from unnecessary renders, and records one change per measurement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When something is slow, wrap components in memo and callbacks in useCallback.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Memoization addresses unnecessary re-renders. It does nothing for volume, where thousands of components each render once legitimately, and nothing for an expensive computation running during render. Applied speculatively it adds comparison cost and becomes permanent, because nobody can later prove it is safe to remove.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner apply blanket memoization to a slow table first and measure no improvement, then classify the cost and apply the matching fix. Then ask them to remove the memoization they added and justify the removal — the difficulty of that justification is the hidden cost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It runs smoothly when I test it, so performance is acceptable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Development fixtures are small and developer hardware is fast. The failure mode exists only at production data volume on the devices users actually have, which is why these defects reach production despite testing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require every performance claim to be accompanied by a number measured at production row counts with CPU and network throttling applied. An unthrottled measurement is treated as no measurement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Ship the features first; performance can be optimised afterwards.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: State placement, list strategy, and route splitting set the performance ceiling, and all three are structural. Changing them later means rewriting components rather than tuning them, which is why post-launch optimisation sprints achieve so little.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner estimate the cost of switching a finished, focus-managed table from client to server pagination, then compare with the cost of that decision at design time.

competencies.title: Accessible interfaces
competencies.description: Use native semantics first, treat focus management as a designed state machine, announce asynchronous outcomes to users whose focus is elsewhere, and verify with a keyboard and a screen reader.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement dialog focus management including restoration in the effect cleanup.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Moves focus in, traps, closes on Escape, restores on close, and explains why restoration belongs in the cleanup rather than in an onClose handler.

desiredOutcomes.description: Announce an asynchronous outcome with a live region that actually fires.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Mounts the region before the message, announces an outcome rather than an activity, debounces, and uses polite politeness.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding ARIA attributes makes a component accessible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: ARIA describes; it does not implement. A `div` with `role="button"` gains the role and none of the behaviour, so teams implement Enter and forget Space. Worse, assistive technology trusts ARIA, so an attribute that is wrong or never updates actively misinforms — which is worse than plain markup that makes no claim.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner replace a `div role="button"` with a real `<button>` and list what they no longer have to implement. Then have them find one ARIA attribute in their codebase that never updates, and hear what a screen reader announces for it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accessibility is a checklist you run before release.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Automated tools find roughly a third of issues, mostly labels, contrast, and invalid ARIA. Focus models in grids, dialogs, and multi-step flows are state machines that must be designed with the component; retrofitting one into a finished virtualized table means rewriting the table.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run an automated checker, fix everything it reports, and then complete a real task using only a keyboard. The defects found in the second pass, and their cost to fix at that stage, are the argument.

competencies.title: Tests that survive refactoring
competencies.description: Write tests coupled to observable behaviour, mock at the network boundary, test each layer where it belongs, and make coverage traceable to requirements.

desiredOutcomes.description: Rewrite an implementation-coupled test to assert on behaviour, and state what it now also verifies.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses role and label queries, survives a class rename, and identifies the accessibility assertion gained.

desiredOutcomes.description: Replace a module mock with network-boundary interception and demonstrate what it catches.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Configures failure on unhandled requests, resets handlers between tests, and shows a field-name mismatch failing under the new approach and passing under the old.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A thorough test checks the component's internal state and structure.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A test should fail when behaviour changes and pass when only implementation changes. Assertions on class names and internal state invert that, producing false failures on harmless edits — and the team's rational response is to stop refactoring, so a suite bought to enable change ends up preventing it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner rename a CSS class and run both versions of a test. Then have them use `getByRole` on an element that lacks an accessible name, so they discover the accessibility defect the query surfaces for free.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Mocking my API module is equivalent to mocking the network.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A module mock replaces your own code with your own assumption, so the fetch layer, cache keys, serialisation, error mapping, and retry logic are all excluded from the test. If the real endpoint returns a differently named field, the test passes and production fails.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner rename a field in the mock so it no longer matches the real API, and run both test styles. Only the network-boundary version fails, which is the demonstration.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: High line coverage means the feature is well tested.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Coverage counts executed lines, not verified behaviours. A configuration-driven renderer can show 96% coverage while nine of eleven configurations are never exercised, and assertions can be coupled to implementation while still executing every line.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list the behaviour paths of a configuration-driven component and compare that count with its line coverage. Then add a contract test that fails when a configuration references an unimplemented field type.

competencies.title: Client-side security boundaries
competencies.description: Treat the browser as untrusted, enforce authorization on the server, sanitize at save time, choose token storage by which risk you can mitigate, and recognise the quiet exposure paths.

desiredOutcomes.description: Demonstrate that a client-side permission check enforces nothing and implement the server-side equivalent.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Documents a successful unauthorised request before the fix, adds the server check, and handles 403 as a normal outcome.

desiredOutcomes.description: Audit an application for the quiet exposure paths.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Covers bundle-exposed variables, sensitive values in URLs, over-fetching, telemetry payloads, public source maps, and CSV formula injection.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Hiding the button for users without permission prevents them from performing the action.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Everything the browser holds, the user holds. The endpoint is visible in network traffic and can be called directly, so conditional rendering only prevents a predictable failure. The permission is a server concern, and 403 must be handled as a normal outcome because permissions change while tabs stay open.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call the endpoint with `curl` as an unauthorised user and paste the successful response into the ticket before writing any fix. Then add the server check and explicit 403 handling, and test the latter with a mocked forbidden response.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Our CORS configuration stops unauthorised callers from using the API.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: CORS is a browser policy governing which origins may read a response. It says nothing about who is asking, it is enforced by the browser rather than the server, and non-browser clients ignore it entirely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call their own API from a terminal, bypassing the browser, and observe the response arriving despite the CORS policy. Then separate the three concepts explicitly: authentication, authorization, and origin policy.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A CSV export is a formatting feature, so it does not need a security review.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A cell beginning with an equals sign or similar character is executed as a formula by spreadsheet applications. User-supplied fields are attacker-controlled input that will predictably be exported and opened by another team, so the injection is stored in one system and executed in another, against someone who was not the original target.
