commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner put a formula in a name field, export, and open the file in a spreadsheet application. Then add escaping plus a regression test asserting that a leading equals sign is neutralised.

competencies.title: Build discipline and delivery gates
competencies.description: Enforce quality mechanically with blocking checks and bundle budgets set from the target device, and promote a single artifact rather than rebuilding per environment.

desiredOutcomes.description: Configure blocking gates including a bundle budget that fails the build.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Sets budgets from a target device rather than current size, demonstrates a failing build, and treats raising a budget as a reviewed commit.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Reporting bundle size and lint results in the build log is enough; the team will act on them.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: An unenforced standard degrades quietly under delivery pressure, because reviewers are inconsistent and outnumbered by pull requests. Size regressions in particular are invisible in a diff, which is how an entry bundle grows from 210 kB to 1.4 MB without a single decision to allow it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner add a blocking budget, import a large library, and confirm a red build. Then have them raise the budget deliberately in a reviewed commit, so the difference between a decision and a drift is experienced directly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Building separately for staging and production is fine, since it is the same source code.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Different builds are different artifacts, so the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped. Configuration differences, dependency resolution, and build-time environment variables can all diverge. Loading configuration at runtime lets one verified artifact be promoted.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner compare build hashes across environments, then convert one build-time variable to a runtime one and promote a single artifact through both stages.

competencies.title: Server rendering orientation
competencies.description: Choose a rendering strategy per route, avoid hydration mismatches, place the client boundary correctly, and recognise which client-side habits become defects or security issues on a server.

desiredOutcomes.description: Assign rendering strategies across a set of routes with justification.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Chooses per route on change frequency, personalisation, and discoverability, rather than applying one strategy globally.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose and fix hydration mismatches using the preferred order of remedies.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Prefers determinism, then after-mount rendering, and reserves suppression for a single expected node.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Server rendering is strictly better, so every React app should use it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It adds infrastructure to run and monitor, a second runtime to debug, and a framework commitment that is expensive to reverse. An internal tool behind a login, whose first screen is authenticated and whose users are on managed devices, gains none of the benefits and pays all of the costs.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list the concrete benefits for a specific application — discoverability, social previews, first paint on cellular — and mark which apply. When none do, the exercise answers itself.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Our app is server-rendered, so crawlers can see our content.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Effects run only after mount in the browser, so a component that fetches in `useEffect` contributes an empty shell to the server-rendered HTML. The framework is doing server rendering; the component is opting out of it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner view the page source, rather than the inspected DOM, and compare against a version that fetches during server render. The difference between view-source and the element inspector is the whole lesson.

competencies.title: Architectural decisions and their record
competencies.description: Layer an application with an enforced dependency direction, evaluate dependencies on maintenance, size, exit cost, and overlap, and record structural decisions so they survive their authors.

desiredOutcomes.description: Organise a feature by domain rather than file type and enforce the dependency direction mechanically.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Produces a feature folder, adds a lint rule restricting cross-feature imports, and explains why a lint rule beats a team agreement.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a decision record for a structural choice made in this course.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Covers context, options considered, decision, and consequences including what becomes harder.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The reasoning behind our architecture is obvious from the code, so writing it down is bureaucracy.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Six months later nobody remembers why server state lives in the query cache while wizard state lives in a scoped store, or why tokens are in cookies. Without the record a new contributor reads the pattern as inconsistency and normalises it, reintroducing the exact problem the decision solved.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner examine a deliberate inconsistency in an unfamiliar codebase and try to reconstruct its reason from the code alone. Then read the corresponding decision record and compare. Then write one for a decision they made in this course.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding a library is a small decision that can be reversed later if it does not work out.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Exit cost varies enormously. A date formatter is replaceable in a day, but a state library or a form library embeds itself into every component and its replacement is a rewrite. Treating both as equally reversible means applying the same shallow diligence to both.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For each candidate dependency, have the learner estimate the work to remove it in twelve months, and set the depth of evaluation from that number. Then have them check for overlap with what is already installed.

options: A, B, C, D, E, F
A, D, F, C, E, B
A, D, F, B, C, E
A, C, D, E, F, B

optionFeedback.feedback: This is source order, which would only hold if nothing were asynchronous. The timer callback in particular cannot run before the synchronous code finishes.
Correct. A, D, and F are synchronous — note that the async body runs immediately to its first `await`. Then microtasks drain: C, then E. The timer, a macrotask, runs last.
This places the timer before the promise callbacks. Microtasks drain completely before the next macrotask, so C and E both precede B.
This assumes the promise callback runs before the remaining synchronous code. Nothing asynchronous runs until the call stack is empty, so F comes before C.

successCriteria: Correct order selected
Reasoning references the two queues rather than a memorised sequence
questions.reviewPromptOverride: State the two rules that determine output ordering between synchronous code, promise continuations, and timers.

questions.prompt: A dashboard loads 12 independent widget datasets with `for (const w of widgets) { data.push(await fetchWidget(w)); }`. Each call takes about 250 ms and the screen takes three seconds to appear. Rewrite the load, state the expected timing, and name one situation in which the original sequential form would have been the correct choice.
successCriteria: Starts all requests before awaiting, typically with Promise.all or Promise.allSettled
States the expected duration as roughly the slowest single request rather than the sum
Explains that the difference is when work starts, not how it is awaited
Names a legitimate sequential case: a dependent request, deliberate rate limiting, or ordered writes
Addresses what happens to error handling when one of the twelve fails

rubric.excellent: Rewrites correctly, states roughly 250 ms, explains the mechanism as start time rather than await syntax, names a legitimate sequential case with reasoning, and notes that Promise.all rejects on the first failure while allSettled reports all outcomes — choosing between them deliberately.
rubric.adequate: Rewrites correctly with Promise.all and states the timing improvement, but treats the mechanism loosely or names a sequential case without reasoning. Error behaviour not addressed.
rubric.weak: Suggests the rewrite as a memorised pattern without explaining why it is faster, or claims that sequential execution is never appropriate, or leaves the awaits inside the loop while adding Promise.all around it.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does moving from sequential awaits to Promise.all change the total time, and when is sequential still correct?

errorPatterns.description: Independent asynchronous work is awaited inside a loop, so requests execute one after another and total latency is the sum rather than the maximum.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log a timestamp at the start of each request in both forms. In the sequential version the start times are 250 ms apart; in the concurrent version they are milliseconds apart. Then require them to state one case where sequential is correct, so the rule learned is 'not by accident' rather than 'always parallelise'.

questions.prompt: A component holds `const [rows, setRows] = useState(initialRows)`. A handler runs `rows[2].status = 'done'; setRows(rows);` and nothing on screen changes. Why?
options: React batches the update and it will appear on the next render
The array reference did not change, so React's comparison reports no change and skips the re-render
Nested objects require a deep clone before any update will register
`setRows` must be called with a function rather than a value

optionFeedback.feedback: Batching groups updates within the same event; it does not delay them indefinitely. Here no update is registered at all.

Correct. React compares with `Object.is`. The mutation changed the contents but not the identity, so the comparison sees the same array. Produce a new array containing a new object for the changed row.
A deep clone would work but is unnecessary and wasteful. Structural sharing means you copy only the path to the change and reuse every unchanged branch.
The functional form solves stale-closure problems, not identity problems. Passing `prev => prev` with a mutation would fail in exactly the same way.

successCriteria: Identifies reference comparison as the mechanism

errorPatterns.description: State is modified in place and the same reference is passed to the setter, so change detection reports no change and the UI does not update.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log `Object.is(prev, next)` around both the mutating and the copying update. Then require an update to a value two levels deep, which forces copying the path rather than the leaf and makes structural sharing concrete.

questions.prompt: A module contains `export const requestCache = new Map()`. Which statement is accurate?
options: Each component that imports it receives its own Map
One Map exists per JavaScript context: per tab in a browser, per process on a server
A new Map is created each time the module is imported
The Map is created lazily on first access and garbage collected when unused

optionFeedback.feedback: Importers receive the same instance. A module is evaluated once and its exports are shared bindings.
Correct, and the consequence is the point: what is a harmless per-user cache in a tab becomes a structure shared between concurrent users on a server.
Module evaluation happens once, on first import. Later imports resolve to the already-evaluated module.
The Map is created when the module is evaluated, and it is reachable from the module binding, so it is not collected while the context lives.

successCriteria: Identifies per-context evaluation and the environment-dependent consequence

questions.prompt: A team is adding server rendering to an application whose store is created at module level. Explain what will go wrong, why it may not appear in staging, and what the fix is. Then describe how you would demonstrate the problem to a colleague who does not believe it.
successCriteria: Identifies that the store instance is shared across concurrent requests in a server process
Names the consequence as one user's data appearing in another user's response, in security terms
Explains that the defect is load-dependent and concurrency-dependent, so low-traffic staging may never exhibit it
States the fix as creating the store per request
Proposes a concrete demonstration with two concurrent requests carrying different user identities

rubric.excellent: Correctly identifies cross-request sharing, frames it as a data leak rather than a rendering bug, explains why staging traffic patterns hide it, prescribes per-request creation, and designs a reproducible two-request demonstration. May note that the same reasoning applies to any module-level mutable value, not only stores.
rubric.adequate: Identifies sharing and per-request creation, but treats the consequence as a correctness problem rather than a security one, or does not explain why testing missed it.
rubric.weak: Suggests clearing the store between requests, or adding a user ID key to the module-level store, which leaves the shared instance in place and merely narrows the window.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is a store created at module level safe in a browser and a security defect on a server?

errorPatterns.description: A mutable store or cache is created at module scope and therefore shared across all requests handled by a server process, allowing one user's state to reach another user's response.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run two concurrent simulated requests with different user identities against a module-level store and observe the leak, then repeat with per-request creation. Follow by auditing the codebase for every other mutable value at module scope, since stores are rarely the only one.

options: `showError` runs, because the 500 status rejects the fetch promise
`render` runs with the error body treated as an order, because fetch does not reject on error statuses
`res.json()` throws, so `showError` runs
Nothing happens; the promise stays pending

optionFeedback.feedback: `fetch` rejects only when the network request itself fails. A 500 is a completed HTTP exchange, so the promise resolves normally.
Correct, and this is why the defect is dangerous: the catch block exists, looks correct in review, and never runs. Check `res.ok` and throw a typed error.
The body is valid JSON, so parsing succeeds. It simply is not an order.
The promise settles normally. A pending promise would indicate a network stall, which is a different failure.

successCriteria: Identifies that fetch resolves on error statuses

errorPatterns.description: A fetch result is consumed without checking `response.ok`, so error responses are parsed and rendered as if they were valid data.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner call an endpoint returning 500 with a JSON error body and watch the success path execute. Then require a shared fetch wrapper that checks `ok` and throws a typed error carrying the status, and have them confirm the catch block now runs.

questions.prompt: A component wrapped in an error boundary throws from three places: during render, inside an `onClick` handler, and inside a `setTimeout` callback. Which does the boundary catch?
options: All three, since they all originate in the component
Only the render error; handlers and timers run outside React's render call stack
Render and the click handler, but not the timer
Only the timer, because it is asynchronous

optionFeedback.feedback: Boundaries catch errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. The other two escape to the global handler.
Correct. Handle the click error with `try`/`catch` in the handler, and the timer error inside the callback, backed by a global `unhandledrejection` listener so missed rejections become visible.
Event handlers are outside the boundary's reach too. React does not wrap handler invocation in the boundary's error path.
This inverts the rule. The timer is the one furthest from the boundary's scope.

successCriteria: Names render, lifecycle, and constructors as the boundary's scope

errorPatterns.description: An error boundary is relied on for failures in event handlers, timers, or async code, so those failures reach the user as a silent no-op or an unhandled rejection.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner throw from render, a click handler, and a timeout inside one boundary-wrapped component and observe which is caught. Then require correct handling for the two that escape, plus a global unhandledrejection listener wired to the error reporter.

successCriteria: Identifies the missing await, so a rejection escapes the try block entirely
Identifies the empty catch block as converting a failure into a wrong answer
Notes that `setStatus('saved')` runs regardless of whether the save succeeded
Rewrite awaits the call, handles the error visibly, and only reports success on success
States what the user sees in each case, including the current behaviour where a failed save displays as saved

rubric.excellent: Finds all three defects — missing await, empty catch, unconditional success message — and explains that the current code reports success for a failed save, which is worse than an error because the user has no reason to retry. Rewrite is correct and the user-facing outcome is described per case.
rubric.adequate: Finds the missing await and the empty catch and rewrites correctly, but does not articulate that the failure mode is a false success rather than a missing error message.
rubric.weak: Adds an await or an error log without addressing the unconditional status update, so the code still tells the user that a failed save succeeded.

questions.prompt: An API adds a required field and renames another. The client uses `as ApiOrder` on the response. Where does the failure appear?
options: At the fetch call, where the cast fails to apply
At compile time, because the declared type no longer matches the API
At an arbitrary point downstream, typically as a property access on undefined, far from the cause
Nowhere; TypeScript's structural typing tolerates extra and missing fields

optionFeedback.feedback: A cast performs no runtime work, so there is nothing at the fetch call to fail.
The compiler cannot know what the API returns. It knows only what you asserted, which is why the assertion is the problem.
Correct, and the distance between cause and symptom is the real cost. Validating at the boundary moves the failure to the fetch, with a message naming the offending field.
Structural typing governs compile-time assignability. At runtime the field is simply absent, and whatever reads it fails.

successCriteria: Identifies the delayed, displaced failure as the consequence

errorPatterns.description: External data is asserted into a type rather than validated, so shape mismatches propagate silently and fail at an unrelated location.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner change a field name on a mock server and trace how far the wrong data travels before anything fails. Then replace the cast with a schema parse and observe the failure relocate to the boundary with a field-level message.

questions.prompt: A shipment is `awaiting-pickup`, `in-transit`, `delivered`, or `lost`. Only `in-transit` has a current location, only `delivered` has a signature and delivery time, and only `lost` has a claim reference. Model this so that reading a signature on a lost shipment cannot compile. Then explain what happens to your code when the backend adds a fifth state, `returned-to-sender`, and why that is preferable to discovering it at runtime.
successCriteria: Produces a discriminated union in which each variant carries only its own fields
Includes an exhaustiveness check using a `never` assignment in the default branch
States that a new variant produces compile errors at every site that must handle it
Explains the preference in terms of when and to whom the problem appears
Notes that the type is derived from a validator, or that the same union is enforced at the parse boundary

rubric.excellent: Union is correct with no field appearing on a variant that should not have it, exhaustiveness check is present and explained, and the argument distinguishes a compile-time list of sites needing attention from a runtime failure that occurs for one user, in production, only when that state arises. Connects the model to boundary validation.
rubric.adequate: Union is correct and the exhaustiveness check is present, but the explanation is stated as a general benefit of type safety rather than as a specific contrast in when and how the problem surfaces.
rubric.weak: Uses a status enum with all other fields optional, or omits the exhaustiveness check so a new variant silently falls through the default branch.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: How does a discriminated union plus a never assignment convert a backend change into a compile-time task?

errorPatterns.description: State is modelled with optional fields, so combinations that cannot occur in the domain are representable and every consumer must defend against them.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner enumerate the combinations their optional-field interface permits and compare with the number of real states. The difference is the defect surface. Then rewrite as a union and repeat the count.

questions.prompt: A function parameter is typed `any` to unblock a merge. Six months later, what is the most likely consequence?
options: None; the annotation is local and only affects that parameter
The value has propagated through call chains, disabling checking at sites nobody associates with the original annotation
The compiler reports a warning wherever the value is used
The build fails once `strict` is enabled, making it easy to locate

optionFeedback.feedback: `any` is contagious. Every expression derived from it is also `any`, and it crosses function boundaries with return values.
Correct. The damage is non-local and invisible, which is why `unknown` is the better escape hatch: it defers the decision without disabling checks downstream.
There is no warning by default. `noImplicitAny` catches inferred `any`, not an explicit annotation.
`strict` does not flag explicit `any`. That is precisely why it survives.

successCriteria: Identifies propagation as the mechanism

errorPatterns.description: An explicit `any` spreads through derived expressions and return values, silently disabling type checking at sites remote from the annotation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner change one `any` to `unknown` and count the sites the compiler now flags. Establish that those sites were already unsafe and the annotation was concealing them, then narrow each one with a check or a parse.

questions.prompt: Support reports that in a task list, marking a task complete occasionally moves another task's unsaved comment onto the wrong task. It only happens when a task is removed from the middle of the list. What is the cause?
options: The comment state should be lifted to the parent
Rows are keyed by array index, so after a removal React reuses component instances against different data
The list is not memoized, so rows re-render and lose synchronisation
The comment field is uncontrolled and should be controlled

optionFeedback.feedback: Lifting would work around it by removing per-row state, but the identity claim is still wrong, and the same fault will reappear anywhere else the list is rendered.
Correct. The mid-list-only reproduction is the signature: a removal shifts indices, so the key no longer identifies the same task and the instance keeps its state against new data.
Re-rendering does not discard or move state. Here state is being preserved when it should be discarded.
Controlling the input changes where the value lives but not which component instance is matched to which task.

successCriteria: Identifies index keys from the reproduction pattern

errorPatterns.description: List items are keyed by index, so insertion, deletion, or filtering causes React to match component instances to the wrong data and preserve state against it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner reproduce the corruption with a mid-list deletion while a row holds unsaved input, then switch to stable keys. Then have them add exactly one reordering interaction to the existing test suite, so they learn which test would have caught it.

questions.prompt: For each case, decide whether an effect is the right tool: (a) computing a filtered list from props and state; (b) sending an analytics event when a user clicks Publish; (c) subscribing to a websocket for the currently selected room; (d) clearing form fields when the selected record changes. Justify each, and for any case where an effect is wrong, give the correct approach.
successCriteria: (a) rejected: compute during render, since an effect causes a second render and a moment of wrong output
(b) rejected: belongs in the click handler, since it responds to an event rather than synchronising with state
(c) accepted: a synchronization with an external system, with a cleanup unsubscribing on change or unmount
(d) rejected: use a key change to reset the subtree rather than an effect that clears fields
Applies the cleanup test explicitly as the discriminator

rubric.excellent: All four classified correctly with the cleanup test applied as the reasoning, not merely the outcomes recalled. Notes that (c) must re-subscribe when the room changes and that its cleanup must unsubscribe from the previous room. Recognises (d) as the clearest illustration of key-as-reset.
rubric.adequate: Three of four correct, with at least (c) justified by its cleanup. Reasoning is sound but partly stated as rules rather than derived from the synchronization definition.
rubric.weak: Accepts (a) or (b) as effects, or accepts (d) without recognising the key alternative, or classifies correctly while giving 'runs after render' as the reason.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: State the synchronization definition of useEffect and name two cases where an effect is the wrong tool.

errorPatterns.description: An effect sets state from props or other state, producing an extra render and a transient frame in which the displayed value is wrong.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log renders and displayed values through one prop change to make the intermediate wrong frame visible, then move the computation into render and confirm it disappears.

errorPatterns.description: An effect subscribes, listens, or opens a resource without a cleanup, so instances accumulate as dependencies change and stale handlers keep firing.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner change the effect's dependency several times while counting live subscriptions, then add the cleanup and re-count. Then run under Strict Mode, which surfaces the same class of defect automatically.

questions.prompt: A component re-renders 40 times per second but produces identical output each time. What is the DOM cost?
options: 40 DOM updates per second, which will cause visible stuttering
Effectively none, because reconciliation finds no differences and the commit does nothing
One update per second, since React throttles identical renders
It depends on whether the component is wrapped in memo

optionFeedback.feedback: Rendering produces a description; only differences reach the DOM. There is real JavaScript cost here, but not DOM cost.
Correct. The render work is real and worth measuring, but conflating render with commit leads to memoization applied where volume or computation is the actual problem.
React does not deduplicate identical renders. Each one runs your component function.
`memo` can skip the render entirely, but the question asks about DOM cost when the render does occur — which is the distinction being tested.

successCriteria: Separates render cost from commit cost

errorPatterns.description: All re-renders are treated as DOM cost, so memoization is applied speculatively instead of classifying the dominant cost.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner read render duration and commit duration separately in the profiler for a component that re-renders with identical output, then connect the reading to the classification step used in performance work.

questions.prompt: A `StatusChip` takes `colour`, `icon`, `bold`, `small`, `uppercase`, and `borderStyle`. It is used in 40 places. The design team changes which colour means 'blocked'. What happens, and what design would have prevented it?
options: One change in the theme file, because colour is centralised
Forty call sites must be reviewed, because each caller decided the colour; a `status` prop would have kept the mapping in one place
Nothing changes, since colour is a visual concern independent of meaning
The component must be duplicated for the new design

optionFeedback.feedback: The theme centralises colour values, not the decision about which value means which state. That decision currently lives at every call site.
Correct. Props expressing appearance push domain decisions to callers. A `status` prop lets the component own the mapping, so the design change is one edit.
The colour is carrying meaning here — it is how users identify a blocked item — so it is not independent of it.
Duplication multiplies the problem. The component is not wrong; its API is asking callers the wrong question.

successCriteria: Identifies the distributed decision as the cost

errorPatterns.description: A component accumulates appearance and toggle props, so callers must know presentation rules and the supported combinations exceed what is tested.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner count the combinations the prop set permits and identify how many are used and tested. Then convert to a composed API with children and recount, and replace appearance props with one domain-meaningful prop.

questions.prompt: A card component takes `variant: 'grid' | 'list' | 'compact'`, chosen by each parent from a viewport hook. Four separate bug reports describe it rendering incorrectly in a sidebar, in a modal, in a split pane, and in a print layout. Explain why these are one defect, propose a design that eliminates the prop, and say what evidence would confirm your diagnosis.
successCriteria: Identifies that the media query measures the viewport while the constraint is the container's width
Explains that every context where container width diverges from viewport width produces its own report
Proposes a container query that moves the decision inside the component and removes the prop
States that the confirming evidence is all four reports closing with a single change
Connects the removal of the prop to the principle that props should express meaning rather than presentation

rubric.excellent: Diagnoses the shared cause precisely, notes that simultaneous closure of unrelated-seeming tickets is the diagnostic signature of an architectural fault rather than four bugs, proposes the container query, and connects it to component API design as a single argument.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the viewport-versus-container mismatch and proposes container queries, but treats the four reports as coincidence rather than as evidence, or does not connect the fix to the API principle.
rubric.weak: Proposes adjusting breakpoint values, adding a fourth variant, or passing width down as a prop — all of which preserve the measurement error.

errorPatterns.description: A layout decision is exposed as a component prop and derived from viewport width, so the component renders incorrectly wherever container width and viewport width diverge.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner place the variant-driven component in a narrow sidebar on a wide viewport to reproduce the failure, then replace the prop with a container query and verify the same component in a grid, a sidebar, and a modal without any caller change.

questions.prompt: A utility class `.mt-0` fails to override a component rule, so a developer writes `.mt-0 { margin-top: 0 !important; }`. What is the durable fix?
options: Increase the utility's specificity by chaining selectors
Declare a cascade layer order placing utilities after components, so layer order decides precedence regardless of specificity
Move the utility later in the stylesheet
Use inline styles for utilities

optionFeedback.feedback: That wins this conflict and raises the ceiling for the next one. Specificity contests have no stable end state.
Correct. Layer order beats specificity, so a single-class utility reliably overrides a deeply nested component rule and no `!important` is needed anywhere.
Source order only breaks ties at equal specificity. The component rule is more specific, so it still wins.
Inline styles win by force and are unoverridable, which recreates the `!important` problem at the highest level.

successCriteria: Identifies layer order as beating specificity

errorPatterns.description: Style conflicts are resolved by increasing specificity or using `!important`, permanently raising the override threshold for all later work.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner remove one existing `!important` by declaring a layer order, then ask what the next override would cost under each approach. Establish the layer list as a project-wide decision recorded once.

questions.prompt: Your product has no plans to support right-to-left languages. Argue for or against adopting logical properties today, and quantify the decision as precisely as you can.
successCriteria: States that logical properties behave identically to physical ones in left-to-right languages, so adoption costs nothing now
Explains that retrofitting requires judging each directional declaration individually, since some must not mirror
Notes that the failures are visual rather than compile-time, so verification is manual across every screen
Reaches a defensible conclusion rather than restating both sides
Optionally identifies which categories must not mirror, such as numbers, phone numbers, logos, and media time controls

rubric.excellent: Argues for adoption with a clear asymmetry: zero cost now against a manual, screen-by-screen migration later that no automated transform can perform safely, because the decision to mirror is per-declaration. Names non-mirroring categories and may note that the RTL migration is usually the visible budget line while the silent formatting defects are the expensive ones.
rubric.adequate: Argues for adoption on the grounds that it is free now and expensive later, but does not explain why the migration cannot be automated.
rubric.weak: Argues against adoption on the grounds that RTL is not planned, treating a zero-cost present decision as if it had a cost.

errorPatterns.description: Physical CSS directions are used throughout, creating a manual per-declaration migration whenever mirroring is required.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner set `dir="rtl"` on a component built with physical properties, count the defects, convert to logical properties, and record what proportion that single change fixed. Then add a lint rule discouraging physical directions in new code.

questions.prompt: A reveal-on-hover implemented with `useState` and `onMouseEnter` passes an automated accessibility scan. What defect does the scan miss?
options: The revealed content lacks an accessible name
The content is unreachable for keyboard users, because `onMouseEnter` never fires without a pointer
The content has insufficient contrast in its revealed state
There is no defect; the scan is correct

optionFeedback.feedback: A missing name is exactly the kind of defect automated tools do find. The gap here is behavioural.
Correct, and it is invisible to scanners because the markup is valid — the content simply never becomes visible without a mouse. `:hover, :focus-within` covers both input modes.
Contrast is checkable automatically, and is not what the pointer-only implementation causes.
Passing a scan means no detectable violations, not that the interface is operable. Roughly a third of issues are machine-detectable.

successCriteria: Identifies the keyboard gap and the limits of automated scanning

errorPatterns.description: Interaction styling is implemented with React state and pointer events, costing a render per pointer movement and excluding keyboard users entirely.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner build both versions, profile a pointer traverse under CPU throttling, then unplug the mouse and tab through each. Require them to record both the timing difference and the content that was unreachable in the JavaScript version.

questions.prompt: For each requirement, decide CSS or JavaScript and justify it in one sentence: (a) a row highlights when the pointer is over it; (b) a progress bar's width reflects a percentage from the server; (c) a header sticks to the top while scrolling; (d) a tooltip flips above the trigger when it would overflow the viewport; (e) a panel fades out before being removed from the DOM.
successCriteria: (a) CSS, using :hover and :focus-within to cover keyboard users
(b) JavaScript supplies the value, ideally through a custom property so styling stays in the stylesheet
(c) CSS position: sticky, which runs off the main thread rather than in a scroll handler
(d) JavaScript, because it requires measurement the browser does not expose declaratively
(e) JavaScript involvement is required because React removes the node, but the animation itself can remain CSS
Applies the test of what information the browser does not already have

rubric.excellent: All five correct with the decision rule applied consistently rather than five separate judgements. Recognises (b) as a hybrid where JavaScript supplies one number, and (e) as a capability gap in React's unmounting rather than a general argument for animation libraries.
rubric.adequate: Four of five correct with sound reasoning, though (b) or (e) may be treated as wholly JavaScript concerns without noting the hybrid nature.
rubric.weak: Assigns interaction styling or sticky positioning to JavaScript, or reaches for an animation library for (a) or (c).

questions.reviewPromptOverride: State the test that decides whether a behaviour belongs in CSS or JavaScript.

errorPatterns.description: A component's layout responds to viewport width rather than to the width of its container, so it renders incorrectly in sidebars, modals, and split panes.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner reproduce the sidebar failure, replace the media query with a container query, and verify the component in three contexts. Then check whether other open layout tickets close at the same time.

questions.prompt: A drawer animates open by transitioning `width` from 0 to 320px. It stutters on mid-range devices. What is happening and what is the fix?
options: The duration is too long; shorten it
`width` forces layout recalculation every frame on the main thread; animate `transform: translateX` instead
The drawer needs `will-change: width`
The device is too slow; accept the degradation

optionFeedback.feedback: Duration affects how long the stuttering lasts, not whether it occurs.
Correct. `transform` and `opacity` can be handled by the compositor without recalculating layout, so they hold frame rate even while the main thread is busy.
`will-change` promotes the element to its own layer but cannot make a layout-triggering property cheap. It adds memory cost for no benefit here.
The animation is doing avoidable work. Mid-range devices are what most users have.

successCriteria: Identifies layout-triggering properties and the compositor alternative

errorPatterns.description: `will-change` is applied broadly as a general performance measure, costing memory and sometimes reducing performance without addressing the actual cause.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner measure memory and frame rate with `will-change` on every card, then removed. Then demonstrate the narrow legitimate use: applied immediately before a known-expensive animation and removed afterwards.

questions.prompt: A user reports that your product makes her nauseous. The interface has parallax hero images, a 700 ms slide between sections, and a looping pulse on the notification badge. There is no reduced-motion handling anywhere. Describe your immediate response and your considered response, and explain why the immediate one is insufficient on its own.
successCriteria: Immediate response ships a blunt global reduced-motion rule within a day, prioritising stopping the harm
Explains that the blunt version removes necessary feedback and leaves the interface confusing
Considered response addresses each animation individually: parallax removed, slide replaced with a short cross-fade, looping stopped, durations shortened
States that the state-change signal is retained in every case
Documents per animation what was removed and what was kept, with reasons

rubric.excellent: Gives a genuinely staged response, justifying the sequence: harm first, communication second. Recognises that removing all motion trades one accessibility problem for another, and produces a per-animation record. May note that the fix belongs in the design system so new animations inherit it.
rubric.adequate: Proposes the global reset and a later per-component pass, but does not clearly articulate why the reset alone is inadequate.
rubric.weak: Proposes only the global reset and treats the issue as closed, or proposes only the considered pass and leaves the user affected while it is designed.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What is the correct response to prefers-reduced-motion, and why is turning all animation off the wrong answer?

errorPatterns.description: Reduced-motion support is implemented as a binary switch, so users who need it lose the feedback that indicates what changed.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner navigate their own interface with all animation disabled and note where they cannot tell what happened. Then rebuild each animation as a reduced variant that keeps the state change and removes the travel.

errorPatterns.description: Animation is added for visual appeal without communicating a change, delaying interaction and increasing motion exposure for no informational benefit.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require a one-sentence statement of what each animation tells the user. Remove any animation without an answer, which converts a subjective discussion into a content question with a decidable outcome.

questions.prompt: A defect is reported that you have not seen. What must happen before you open any file?
options: Read the component you suspect, to build context
Reproduce the defect reliably, because without a reproduction you cannot distinguish a fix from a coincidence
Add logging throughout the suspected area
Check whether anyone else has changed that code recently

optionFeedback.feedback: Suspicion before reproduction is a guess, and reading code to confirm a guess tends to produce confirmation rather than diagnosis.
Correct. Reproduction also converts 'sometimes' into a specific condition, which usually narrows the search dramatically before any code is read.
Logging before you can trigger the defect produces output you cannot interpret, because you do not know which run was the failing one.
Recent-change history is genuinely useful, and it comes after reproduction rather than instead of it.

successCriteria: Identifies reproduction as the gate on everything else

errorPatterns.description: Several speculative changes are made without a reproduction or a stated hypothesis, so no change is attributable and failed attempts accumulate in the file.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require a written hypothesis before any file is opened, and require reverting a failed attempt before the next is tried. Then show a file containing three overlapping previous fixes and ask which can safely be removed.

questions.prompt: A dashboard's summary count stops updating after the first change, while the underlying list updates correctly. Two previous developers have already 'fixed' this: one added a forced refresh interval, another added a key to the summary component. Both are still in the code. Describe your diagnosis, your fix, and what you do about the two previous fixes.
successCriteria: Reproduces first and states a hypothesis before reading code
Identifies a stale closure as the likely mechanism, given that the value is one update behind rather than wrong
Locates the callback capturing an earlier render's bindings, typically an effect with an empty dependency array
Fixes with a functional update or a corrected dependency, rather than with a refresh
Removes the two previous fixes and explains why leaving them is a cost, having verified the real cause

rubric.excellent: Diagnoses from the symptom's shape — stale rather than wrong indicates a captured value — verifies with the profiler or a breakpoint, fixes the mechanism, and removes both earlier workarounds after confirming the real cause. Notes that each previous fix probably introduced its own artefact and that leaving them makes the next defect harder to diagnose.
rubric.adequate: Diagnoses the stale closure and fixes it correctly, but leaves the previous fixes in place or removes them without explaining why that is part of the work.
rubric.weak: Adjusts the refresh interval, adds another key, or adds a further effect to force an update, treating the symptom rather than the mechanism.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A displayed value is consistently one update behind. What mechanism does that shape of symptom indicate, and how do you confirm it?

errorPatterns.description: A workaround suppresses the visible symptom while the causal mechanism remains, so the defect recurs elsewhere and the workarounds accumulate.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require a one-sentence mechanism explanation before any ticket is closed, and treat inability to write one as the work being unfinished. Then have the learner search the codebase for other instances of the same mechanism.

assessments.title: Finding your way in unfamiliar code

questions.prompt: You have twenty minutes in a repository you have never seen, and a ticket about one incorrect value on one screen. What is the most productive use of that time?
options: Read the entry file and follow the imports to build a mental model
Trace that one value backwards: the text on screen, its props, its owner, its data source, then the real network response
Read the README and the folder structure documentation
Run the test suite and read the failing tests

optionFeedback.feedback: This has no natural end point and produces recall rather than orientation. It also rarely reaches the specific code the ticket concerns.
Correct. One backwards trace terminates, answers the ticket, and incidentally teaches the routing convention, the data layer, the state library, and the folder rule.
Worth ten minutes if it exists and is current, but documentation describes intentions and the trace shows what is actually there.
Useful when tests are failing. Here nothing is failing in CI; the defect is in behaviour the tests do not cover.

successCriteria: Chooses tracing over reading and can say why it terminates

errorPatterns.description: A learner attempts to understand a codebase by reading it in structural order, producing broad shallow recall and no path to the code relevant to the task.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner one value to trace end to end in twenty minutes, then ask them to describe the architecture from memory. Compare with an equal period spent reading files, and make the trace the standard onboarding step.

questions.prompt: A production error reads `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total')` with a stack trace whose first eight frames are inside `react-dom.production.min.js` and whose ninth is `a.chunk.js:1:48221`. Describe how you would work with this, and what you would change so the next such error is easier to diagnose.
successCriteria: Skips framework frames and looks for the first frame in first-party code
Recognises that the minified frame is unreadable without source maps
Prescribes uploading source maps to the error reporter rather than serving them publicly
Reads the message literally: something expected to be an object was undefined, and identifies the likely boundary where it originated
Connects the fix to validating data where it enters the application so the failure occurs at the boundary

rubric.excellent: Works the trace correctly, prescribes source map upload with the security qualification, reads the message literally to narrow the candidate values, and connects the recurrence to missing boundary validation rather than treating it as a one-off null check.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the need for source maps and the first-party frame, but treats the fix as adding optional chaining at the crash site.
rubric.weak: Proposes defensive optional chaining or a default value at the point of failure, which produces wrong output instead of a crash and removes the only signal that something is wrong.

questions.prompt: You fix a one-line defect and also rename six variables and extract a helper in the same file. Why should these be separate commits?
options: Commit hygiene is a team convention with no functional consequence
The reviewer cannot see which line is the fix, and a regression in the refactor cannot be reverted without also losing the fix
Large commits slow down the build
Separate commits make the history easier to search

optionFeedback.feedback: There are two concrete consequences: the fix is effectively unreviewed, and revert becomes a choice between two defects.
Correct. The revert argument is the sharper one — it is what you need at the worst moment, when a regression is live.
Build time is unaffected by commit granularity.
True and useful, but a secondary benefit compared with reviewability and revertability.

successCriteria: Names both the review and the revert consequence

errorPatterns.description: A defect fix and an unrelated refactor share a commit, so the corrective change is unreviewable and cannot be preserved through a revert.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner produce both a mixed commit and a split pair for the same work and review each as a reviewer would, then ask which they could revert safely during an incident.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing a 900-line pull request that adds a new feature. You have thirty minutes. Describe what you check, in what order, and what you do about the size.
successCriteria: Checks scope against the ticket first: does it do what was asked, and only that
Checks where new state lives against the codebase's existing placement rule
Checks keys, dependency arrays, and cleanups as the concentration points for React defects
Checks the error and empty paths, not only the successful path
Checks keyboard operability and whether tests assert behaviour rather than implementation
Addresses the size explicitly, requesting a split rather than approving what cannot be reviewed

rubric.excellent: Orders the checks by defect yield, addresses all six areas, and treats the size as a first-class problem — stating that approving an unreviewable diff creates a false record of scrutiny, which is worse than declining to review. Proposes a concrete split.
rubric.adequate: Covers most of the checks in a reasonable order and notes the size, but approves with comments rather than requesting a split.
rubric.weak: Reviews for style and naming, or approves on the grounds that the tests pass, without examining state placement, failure paths, or keyboard operability.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What do you check when reviewing a React change, in order of defect yield?

errorPatterns.description: A pull request is large enough that review degrades into approval, so it consumes review time while providing no defect-finding value and creating a false record of scrutiny.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner review a very large diff under a time limit and list what they actually verified, then repeat with a small one. Use the difference to set a team size guideline and a splitting practice.

questions.prompt: A team finds that unrelated screens re-render when one feature updates, the global store contains entries nobody can explain, and features must remember to clear their own state on unmount. What do these symptoms indicate?
options: State is placed too low and should be lifted
State is placed too high; entries belong in feature-scoped or local tiers
The store needs better memoized selectors
The application needs a second store for feature state

optionFeedback.feedback: Too-low placement shows as repeated lifting, prop drilling, and diverging sibling copies. These symptoms are the opposite set.
Correct. All three are classic too-high symptoms: wide blast radius, accumulation nobody dares delete, and manual lifecycle management the tier does not provide.
Selectors would reduce the re-renders while leaving the accumulation and the manual clearing untouched. That treats one symptom of three.
A second store may eventually be justified, but adding one before correcting placement moves the misplaced state rather than removing it.

successCriteria: Distinguishes too-high from too-low symptoms

errorPatterns.description: State is placed in the global store without a stated reason, widening the blast radius and accumulating entries whose readership is unknown.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner audit the store and annotate each entry with the number of distinct screens that read it. Single-reader entries are the evidence. Move one down a tier and record the diff size and what improved.

questions.prompt: A veterinary appointment system holds: the signed-in vet, today's appointments from the server, which appointment row is expanded, a consultation note in progress that must survive an accidental navigation, the practice colour theme, and a filter by species. Assign each a tier, justify using the five questions, and identify the one item where two tiers are defensible — then argue for one.
successCriteria: Signed-in vet to global client state, justified by application-wide audience and session lifetime
Appointments to the server cache, justified by server ownership, and explicitly not copied into a client store
Expanded row to local state, justified by single-component audience and short lifetime
Species filter to the URL, justified by shareability
Theme to global client state or a root custom property, with the render cost noted
Identifies the consultation note as the genuinely contested item and argues a position

rubric.excellent: All six assigned with the five questions applied explicitly rather than by resemblance to earlier examples. Identifies the consultation note as contested — local state is simplest but does not survive navigation, so a scoped store or a draft persisted through the server cache is arguable — and commits to a position with reasoning about data loss versus complexity.
rubric.adequate: Five of six assigned correctly with reasonable justification, and a contested item identified, though the argument for one side is thin.
rubric.weak: Assigns most items to the global store for convenience, or copies the appointment list into a client store, or treats the filter as local because only one screen uses it.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Give the five questions that decide which tier a piece of state belongs in.

errorPatterns.description: Shareable view state is held in both the URL and a store, so the two disagree after a back navigation that changes the URL without notifying the store.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner build the mirrored version, press the back button, and observe the disagreement. Then rebuild with the URL as the single source and the store deriving from it, or with the store removed entirely.

questions.prompt: A memoized selector is used by two components with different filter arguments. Profiling shows it recomputing on every render of either component. Why?
options: The store is being replaced rather than updated
The default memoization holds one result, so alternating arguments miss the cache every time and return new references
The selector's input selectors are not themselves memoized
Memoized selectors do not work with React's concurrent rendering

optionFeedback.feedback: That would invalidate everything, but the described pattern — alternating between two callers — points specifically at the cache size.
Correct, and the second-order damage matters: the new reference returned each time defeats memoization downstream as well. Use a per-instance selector factory or configure the cache.
Unmemoized inputs can cause recomputation, but here the inputs are stable and the arguments differ, which is the single-result cache.
Memoized selectors work under concurrent rendering. This is a cache-size property, not a scheduling interaction.

successCriteria: Identifies the single-result cache and the downstream reference consequence

errorPatterns.description: One memoized selector instance is shared by components passing different arguments, so every call misses the single-result cache and returns a fresh reference.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log recomputations from two components with differing arguments, then apply a per-instance factory and log again. Establish the count difference as the acceptance criterion for the fix.

questions.prompt: Compare `setPickedQuantity({ sku, qty })` with `itemScanned({ sku, qty })` as action designs. Explain what the second communicates that the first does not, and what happens to each when a second slice must also respond to the same user activity.
successCriteria: Identifies that the setter records a decision already made at the call site, so the reasoning lives in the component
Identifies that the event names what happened, leaving each slice to decide how to respond
States that adding a second responding slice requires a component change under the setter design and none under the event design
Notes that an event-shaped action log reads as a record of user activity rather than a list of assignments
Confirms that reducers remain pure under both designs

rubric.excellent: Draws the distinction as ownership of the decision rather than as naming style, and demonstrates the second-slice consequence concretely. May note that event actions make time-travel debugging genuinely informative, because the log describes what the user did.
rubric.adequate: Explains the naming distinction and the multi-slice benefit, but treats it as a convention rather than as a question of where reasoning lives.
rubric.weak: Treats the two as equivalent with different names, or argues for setters on grounds of explicitness without addressing the multi-slice case.

errorPatterns.description: Actions are named after the state they assign, so the reasoning stays in the component and additional responders require component changes.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner write both forms, then introduce a second slice that must react to the same activity. The setter version requires a second dispatch from the component; the event version requires no component change at all.

questions.prompt: A reducer stores `state.currentLine` into a module-level variable so a later selector can reuse it. The application crashes with an error about a revoked proxy. What happened?
options: The store was recreated, invalidating the reference
The saved reference is an Immer draft, which is revoked once the reducer returns; only the produced state may be held
Selectors cannot access state outside the store
The reducer mutated state, which is not permitted

optionFeedback.feedback: Store recreation would produce a different failure. The revoked-proxy message names the mechanism specifically.
Correct. Drafts exist only for the duration of the reducer. Immer produces the new immutable state on return and disables the proxy, so any escaped reference is unusable.
Selectors read state routinely. The problem is which object was retained, not where it was read.
Mutating the draft is exactly what Immer permits. Retaining it beyond the reducer is what is not permitted.

successCriteria: Identifies draft lifetime as the mechanism

errorPatterns.description: A reference to an Immer draft is retained beyond the reducer, producing a revoked-proxy crash when it is later read.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner reproduce the crash deliberately, then explain what Immer produced at the moment the reducer returned. Establish the rule that only the produced state, never the draft, may leave the reducer.

questions.prompt: A component uses `const { total, currency } = useCartStore(s => ({ total: s.total, currency: s.currency }))` and re-renders whenever anything in the store changes. Why?
options: The store notifies all subscribers on every change regardless of selectors
The selector returns a new object each call, and the default comparison is by reference, so the result always appears changed
Destructuring in the selector is unsupported
The component is missing `React.memo`

optionFeedback.feedback: Selector subscriptions are precisely how the store avoids that. The subscription is working; the comparison is being defeated.
Correct. Use a shallow comparison for multi-value selections, or select each value with its own subscription.
Destructuring the result is fine. The object literal inside the selector is the problem.
`memo` compares props from a parent. It cannot help when the hook itself reports a change on every store update.

successCriteria: Identifies reference comparison of a fresh object literal

errorPatterns.description: A store selector returns a newly created object, so reference comparison reports a change on every store update and the component re-renders for unrelated changes.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner count renders while mutating an unrelated part of the store, then apply shallow comparison and count again. Establish shallow comparison as the default for any selector returning more than one value.

questions.prompt: Two picking sessions must run side by side with completely independent state. Describe how you would create and distribute the store, and explain why using context here does not reintroduce the re-render problem that context is usually criticised for.
successCriteria: Creates the store once per instance, using lazy initialisation so it is not recreated on re-render
Passes the store handle through a context provider scoped to each instance
Explains that the context value is a stable handle rather than changing data
States that consumers subscribe through selectors, so updates bypass context propagation entirely
Notes that a single module-level store would make the two sessions share state

rubric.excellent: Correct construction with lazy initialisation, and a precise account of why context is appropriate: it carries an unchanging reference, so it never re-renders consumers, while the actual updates flow through selector subscriptions. Connects back to context being dependency injection rather than storage.
rubric.adequate: Correct construction and distribution, with the stability of the context value noted but not clearly connected to why the usual criticism does not apply.
rubric.weak: Creates the store at module level and attempts to namespace it by session ID, which leaves both sessions sharing one instance, or recreates the store on every render.

assessments.title: Caching data you do not own

questions.prompt: After a successful mutation, a list does not refresh. Which sequence of checks finds the cause fastest?
options: Clear the whole cache, then reintroduce granular invalidation later
Check that the query provides the tag, that the mutation invalidates that tag, that the tag IDs match, and that the component is subscribed
Add a refetch interval to the query
Check whether the mutation returned an error

optionFeedback.feedback: Clearing everything hides the fault and refetches data that was fine, and the granular version rarely returns.
Correct. Nearly always one of these four, and nearly always the third — a tag with an ID on one side and without it on the other.
An interval masks the defect with a delay, and the data is still stale between ticks.
Worth thirty seconds, and the premise states the mutation succeeded, so it is not where the sequence should start.

successCriteria: Reproduces the four ordered checks

errorPatterns.description: Server responses are copied into a client store, creating a second source of truth with no invalidation story that drifts from the cache.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner trace one field held in both places and find the code responsible for keeping them equal. Usually none exists. Then delete the copy and read from the cache, confirming the affected screens still work.

questions.prompt: A list shows a full-page skeleton every thirty seconds when its background refresh runs, losing the user's scroll position. What is wrong?
options: The refresh interval is too aggressive
The skeleton is rendered on `isFetching` rather than `isLoading`, so a refresh over existing data replaces the content
The query key is unstable, causing a full cache miss
The list should be virtualized

optionFeedback.feedback: A longer interval reduces how often the problem occurs without changing the behaviour when it does.
Correct. `isLoading` means there is nothing to show yet; `isFetching` includes refreshes over existing data. Keep the rows visible and show a subtle indicator instead.
An unstable key would cause endless refetching rather than a periodic one, and it is a plausible neighbouring defect worth ruling out.
Virtualization addresses row volume, which is unrelated to which flag drives the skeleton.

successCriteria: Distinguishes the two flags and their correct UI treatment

errorPatterns.description: A loading skeleton is shown during background refreshes, replacing visible content and destroying scroll position and focus.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log both flags through a background refetch, then implement the skeleton-versus-indicator split and verify that scroll position and focus survive a refresh.

questions.prompt: For each action, choose optimistic or pessimistic and justify from the consequence of being wrong: (a) marking a message as read; (b) opening a remote irrigation valve; (c) adding an item to a shopping basket; (d) issuing a customer refund. Then describe what a correct rollback looks like for whichever of these you made optimistic.
successCriteria: (a) optimistic: a wrong display is trivially recoverable
(b) pessimistic: showing 'open' for a failed command means a field is not watered
(c) optimistic, though noting stock or pricing failures may require a visible correction
(d) pessimistic: a financial action whose false confirmation causes downstream work and loss of trust
Rollback is described as visible to the user rather than silent
Reasoning is consistently based on consequence rather than on perceived speed

rubric.excellent: All four justified from consequence, with the rollback design specifying what the user sees and what they can do next. Recognises that a silent rollback is worse than a slow confirmation, because it removes the user's opportunity to notice and retry.
rubric.adequate: Classifies correctly with consequence-based reasoning, but describes the rollback only as reverting state without addressing user notification.
rubric.weak: Chooses optimistic throughout on responsiveness grounds, or pessimistic throughout to be safe, without weighing consequence per action.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What determines whether an update should be optimistic or pessimistic?

errorPatterns.description: An optimistic update is applied to an action with real-world consequences, and the rollback is silent, so the user believes a failed action succeeded.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner classify five actions by the cost of a false success, then implement one optimistic and one pessimistic case, ensuring the optimistic rollback produces a visible message with a retry path.

questions.prompt: Which async state is most often omitted, and why is its absence particularly difficult to detect?
options: Loading, because developers test with fast local data
Partial, because the page renders normally while one value is silently wrong or missing
Error, because errors are rare in development
Empty, because test fixtures always contain data

optionFeedback.feedback: Loading is the state most reliably implemented, because it is the first thing anyone sees while building.
Correct. A complete failure is reported immediately; a dashboard where one of six panels quietly failed looks correct, so it is neither noticed nor reported.
Error states are frequently under-designed, but their absence is visible when they occur. Partial failure is not.
Empty states are often missing and are worth designing, but they are visibly missing when reached.

successCriteria: Identifies partial and explains its detection difficulty

errorPatterns.description: Only the successful path is designed, so empty, error, and partial states appear as blank regions, generic messages, or silently missing values.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner force all four states deliberately, including failing one of two parallel requests, and write the user-facing copy for each. Requiring copy exposes empty states that offer no next action and error states that offer no retry.

questions.prompt: Design the four async states for an emergency room triage board that several clinicians view at once. Specify what each state shows, what the user can do in it, and how a screen reader user whose focus is in the filter field learns that anything happened.
successCriteria: Loading uses a skeleton matching the final layout dimensions to avoid shifting content
Empty distinguishes 'no patients' from 'no patients matching this filter' and offers a way to clear the filter
Error states what failed, whether it is retryable, and provides a retry control
Partial indicates which portion of the data is stale or missing rather than rendering as if complete
A polite live region announces the outcome, mounted before the message and debounced
Recognises that stale data on a triage board is a clinical risk, so staleness must be visible

rubric.excellent: All four states specified with a user action in each, dimension-matched skeletons, and an announcement strategy that distinguishes outcomes from activity. Treats visible staleness as a safety requirement in this domain and may address concurrent editing by other clinicians.
rubric.adequate: Four states specified with reasonable copy and a live region present, but the partial state is thin or the announcement describes activity rather than outcome.
rubric.weak: Specifies loading and error only, or provides a generic failure message with no retry, or omits the screen reader case entirely.

questions.prompt: Which item does NOT belong in the URL?
options: The selected tab on a detail page
A password reset token used to authenticate the reset request
The current sort column and direction
The page number in a paginated list

optionFeedback.feedback: A tab determines what the user is looking at, so it should be shareable and survive a refresh.
Correct. URLs are recorded in browser history, server logs, referrer headers, and analytics, so a credential in a query string is exposed in several systems at once.
Sort state is view state a user would reasonably share, so the URL is the right tier.
Page number is a clear case: shareable, bookmarkable, and expected to survive navigation.

successCriteria: Applies both the shareability rule and the sensitivity exception

errorPatterns.description: Filters, sorting, and tab selection are held in memory, so views cannot be shared, do not survive a refresh, and do not respond to browser navigation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner list the complaints a memory-held filter produces and confirm that moving it to the URL resolves all of them at once. Then have them handle a hand-edited invalid value so the route degrades rather than crashing.

questions.prompt: Your router blocks `/admin` for users without the admin role. A colleague argues that the admin endpoints therefore do not need their own permission checks, since the UI is the only client. Respond.
successCriteria: States that the guard is client code and the endpoints remain callable directly
Notes that 'the UI is the only client' is an assumption the server cannot verify
Prescribes independent authorization on every endpoint
Notes that the client should still handle 403 as a normal outcome, because permissions change during long sessions
Optionally proposes demonstrating the bypass rather than arguing about it

rubric.excellent: Rebuts clearly, distinguishes the guard's user-experience purpose from enforcement, prescribes server-side checks plus explicit 403 handling, and proposes demonstrating the bypass with a direct request — because a documented successful unauthorised call ends the discussion faster than the argument does.
rubric.adequate: Correctly identifies that the server must check, but does not address 403 handling or the long-lived-session case.
rubric.weak: Suggests obscuring the endpoint, moving the check earlier in the router, or adding a client-side token check as sufficient.

errorPatterns.description: Route guards are relied on as an access control, leaving the underlying endpoints unprotected against direct requests.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner call a guarded route's endpoint directly while signed in as an unauthorised user and record the successful response in the ticket, then implement the server-side check and explicit 403 handling in the UI.

questions.prompt: A cross-field rule requires the incident date to be no later than today. It is written as a refinement without a `path`. Users report that the submit button 'does nothing'. What is happening?
options: The rule never runs, because refinements require a path to execute
The rule runs and fails, but the error attaches to the form root, so no field shows a message and submission is blocked silently
The date field is not registered with the form
The resolver is not configured

optionFeedback.feedback: The rule runs regardless. `path` controls where the resulting error is attached, not whether the check happens.
Correct, and the user's description is precise: from their side the button genuinely does nothing, because there is no message anywhere to explain the refusal.
An unregistered field would produce a missing value rather than a blocked submit with no message.
Without a resolver no validation would run at all and the form would submit, which is the opposite symptom.

successCriteria: Identifies root attachment as the cause of the silent block

errorPatterns.description: A cross-field validation error attaches to the form root rather than to a field, so submission is blocked with no visible message.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner build the rule without `path`, attempt submission, and experience the dead button. Then add `path` and confirm the message appears. Add a test asserting the message is rendered next to the named field.

questions.prompt: Users of a long claims form report three problems: typing is sluggish; after saving, the form still warns about unsaved changes on every navigation; and when the server rejects a policy number, the message appears only in a banner at the top of a form that requires scrolling. Diagnose all three and describe the fixes, including what a screen reader user should experience for the third.
successCriteria: Sluggishness attributed to controlled inputs re-rendering the whole form per keystroke, fixed with uncontrolled inputs and per-field subscriptions
Persistent dirty warning attributed to not resetting with the saved values after a successful save
Notes that recreating the defaults object each render also produces a permanently dirty form
Server error mapped onto the named field using the form library's error API
Focus moved to the first invalid field, with the message linked by aria-describedby and the field marked aria-invalid
Notes that a warning users always see is a warning they learn to dismiss

rubric.excellent: All three diagnosed with the correct mechanism, and the third answered for both sighted and screen reader users. Observes that the persistent dirty warning trains users to dismiss it, so the defect degrades a safety feature rather than merely annoying people.
rubric.adequate: All three diagnosed and fixed correctly, but the accessibility requirements for the third are partial — for example focus is moved but the message is not programmatically associated.
rubric.weak: Attributes sluggishness to needing memoization, or resolves the dirty warning by removing the unsaved-changes prompt, or leaves the server error in the banner.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Name two common causes of a form that reports unsaved changes permanently, and state where a server field error should appear.

errorPatterns.description: A large form uses controlled inputs, re-rendering every field on each keystroke and producing visible input lag.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner profile keystroke renders on an eight-field form in both implementations and extrapolate to the real field count, then convert the largest form in the codebase and measure again.

questions.prompt: A German user enters `1.234,56` into an amount field parsed with `parseFloat`. What is stored, and why did this survive review?
options: `1234.56`, because JavaScript normalises separators
`1.234`, because parsing stops at the comma — and the result looks like a plausible amount, so nothing appears wrong
`NaN`, which would have been caught immediately
`123456`, because separators are ignored

optionFeedback.feedback: `parseFloat` applies English conventions only. It has no knowledge of the user's locale.
Correct, and the plausibility is the danger: an error by a factor of one thousand that produces a well-formed number can persist for months without being reported.
`NaN` would be an easier defect, because it fails loudly. This one succeeds quietly with the wrong value.
Separators are not ignored; parsing halts at the first character it cannot interpret.

successCriteria: Identifies the value and the reason it goes unnoticed

errorPatterns.description: Locale-formatted numeric input is parsed with English separator conventions, producing a plausible but wrong value that passes review.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner enter a German-formatted amount into their own form and inspect the stored value. Then implement locale-aware parsing and add a test using a locale whose separators differ from English.
