questions.prompt: A confirmation message uses `${nights} ${nights === 1 ? 'night' : 'nights'}`. A translator reports it cannot be translated correctly into Arabic. Explain why this is not a translation problem, and describe the fix.
successCriteria: States that Arabic has six plural categories and the code provides only two branches
Explains that the translator cannot supply categories that do not exist in the code
Prescribes ICU MessageFormat so the translator supplies their language's categories
Notes that the code passes only the count, leaving grammar to the message
Optionally connects this to fragment concatenation, which fails for the same structural reason

rubric.excellent: Identifies the structural nature of the fault precisely, explains why such tickets cycle between market teams and vendors without resolution, prescribes ICU, and generalises to concatenated fragments and any other place where code makes grammatical decisions.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the category mismatch and prescribes ICU, but does not explain why the translator is unable to fix it.
rubric.weak: Suggests adding more branches for the languages in scope, or asking translators for a workaround phrasing, both of which preserve the structure.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why can a count-based ternary for plurals not be fixed by translators?

errorPatterns.description: Pluralization is expressed as a two-branch condition in code, which cannot represent the plural categories of most languages.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Show the learner the CLDR plural rules for Arabic and Polish, then have them convert one ternary to an ICU message and verify that the categories resolve. Add a lint rule flagging count-based ternaries around user-facing text.

questions.prompt: A team estimates adding a new language at two weeks: 'extract the strings and send them to a vendor.' Name four categories of work this estimate omits, and identify which single practice would have found the most defects before any translator was paid.
successCriteria: Names layout expansion, since translated text runs 20–35% longer into several languages
Names formatting and parsing of numbers, dates, and currency
Names collation, since code-point sorting mis-orders accented names
Names mirroring for right-to-left languages, and the cost of physical CSS directions
Identifies a pseudo-locale pass as the highest-yield pre-translation practice, finding truncation and unextracted strings together

rubric.excellent: Names four or more omitted categories, distinguishes the visible costs from the silent ones such as parsing and collation, and identifies the pseudo-locale pass with a clear explanation of the two defect classes it surfaces in a single run for roughly half a day of effort.
rubric.adequate: Names three or four categories and identifies the pseudo-locale, but treats all categories as equally visible.
rubric.weak: Names only text length and right-to-left support, or proposes machine translation as the pre-check, which produces an impression rather than a finding.

errorPatterns.description: Internationalization is scoped as string extraction, leaving formatting, parsing, collation, layout expansion, and mirroring undiscovered until after translation is commissioned.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Run a pseudo-locale pass before commissioning translation, and audit one numeric input and one sorted list, which is where the silent value-level defects concentrate. Add the pseudo-locale check as a blocking CI step.

questions.prompt: A support tool sorts 340,000 meter records on the client 'for responsiveness'. Each record includes a customer address. Contractors are scoped to a single substation. What is the most serious problem?
options: The initial download is large and slow on poor connections
Every contractor's browser now holds all 340,000 customer addresses, because the scope filter is applied in the table rather than by the API
Sorting 340,000 rows will block the main thread
Memory usage may cause the tab to crash on low-end devices

optionFeedback.feedback: Real, and the least serious of the four. Bandwidth is recoverable; disclosed personal data is not.

Correct. A filter in the table is presentation, not authorization. The data is readable in developer tools and in anything that exfiltrates browser storage, so a performance decision has silently become a disclosure.
A genuine performance concern, and still secondary to shipping records the user is not entitled to see.
Possible, and a crash is a far better outcome than a quiet disclosure.

successCriteria: Ranks disclosure above performance and identifies where entitlement must be enforced

errorPatterns.description: Sorting or filtering on the client requires the full dataset in the browser, disclosing records the user is not entitled to see while entitlement is enforced only in the table.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner open developer tools on their own client-sorted table and read a record outside their entitlement. Then move sorting and filtering to the API and confirm the response contains only permitted rows.

questions.prompt: You virtualize a 200,000-row grid. List everything you must now design that you did not need before, and for each, state the specific mitigation. Then explain why doing this after the grid is built costs far more than doing it during.
successCriteria: Screen reader row position, mitigated with aria-rowcount on the grid and aria-rowindex per row
Keyboard navigation beyond the rendered window, mitigated by holding the focused cell in state, scrolling to index, and restoring focus after mount
Find-in-page, mitigated by in-app search across the full dataset with the limitation communicated
Printing and export, mitigated by a server-side export path
Focus loss when a focused row unmounts, mitigated by keeping it rendered or restoring focus explicitly
Explains that the focus model is a state machine the virtualizer must cooperate with, so retrofitting means rewriting row rendering

rubric.excellent: All five with correct mitigations, plus a clear account of why retrofit is expensive: the focus model must be designed jointly with the virtualizer, so adding it later means rewriting row rendering rather than adding attributes. May quantify with the two-days-versus-six-weeks contrast.
rubric.adequate: Four of five with correct mitigations, and a general statement that retrofitting is costly without explaining the structural reason.
rubric.weak: Lists accessibility attributes only, or treats the whole set as something a library handles automatically.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Name five things virtualization breaks and the mitigation for each.

errorPatterns.description: Virtualization is added without restoring row position, keyboard navigation, in-page search, export, or focus behaviour, making the grid unusable without a mouse.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner complete a real task in their virtualized grid using only a keyboard and a screen reader, recording every point of failure. Then implement the mitigations and repeat the same task as the acceptance test.

questions.prompt: A profile shows one commit of 3,800 ms in which a row component rendered 12,400 times at about 0.3 ms each. What is the correct fix?
options: Wrap the row in `memo` and its callbacks in `useCallback`
Reduce the number of rendered rows through virtualization or pagination, since this is a volume problem
Move the row data into a memoized selector
Split the route so the table loads later

optionFeedback.feedback: Memoization prevents unnecessary re-renders. Here 12,400 components each rendered once, legitimately, so there is nothing for it to skip.
Correct. Many components with small individual self time is the signature of volume, and the fix is to render fewer of them.
That addresses one component with large self time, which is the different classification. The per-row cost here is already small.
Route splitting defers the cost rather than removing it. The table will still take 3,800 ms when it loads.

successCriteria: Classifies as volume from the many-small signature

errorPatterns.description: Memoization is applied speculatively without classifying the dominant cost, adding comparison overhead and becoming permanent because its removal cannot later be justified.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner apply blanket memoization first and measure no improvement, then classify and apply the matching fix. Then require them to remove the memoization and justify the removal, which demonstrates the hidden long-term cost.

questions.prompt: A screen is reported as slow. Describe your measurement procedure from first report to closing the ticket, including what you record. Then explain why fixing two problems between measurements is a mistake, using the example of a second bottleneck hidden inside a larger one.
successCriteria: Reproduces at production data volume rather than with development fixtures
Applies CPU and network throttling representative of the target device
Records with the profiler and classifies the dominant cost before changing anything
Makes one change, measures again, and records the number each time
Explains that a second bottleneck is often invisible until the first is removed, so batched fixes cannot be attributed
Notes that unattributable memoization becomes permanent because nobody can prove it is safe to remove

rubric.excellent: Full procedure with recorded numbers at each step, and a precise account of the hidden-bottleneck effect: a 210 ms computation inside a 3,800 ms commit is undetectable until the commit shrinks. Connects this to why the measurement log itself is the deliverable.
rubric.adequate: Correct procedure with throttling and one change per measurement, but the hidden-bottleneck argument is stated as a general principle rather than shown.
rubric.weak: Describes profiling without production-scale data or throttling, or proposes a list of optimisations applied together and measured once at the end.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Give the performance measurement procedure in order, and say why only one change is made between measurements.

errorPatterns.description: Performance is assessed with development-sized fixtures on developer hardware, so the failure mode that exists only at production volume is never observed.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require every performance claim to carry a number measured at production row counts with CPU and network throttling. Treat an unthrottled measurement as no measurement, and keep a production-scale fixture in the repository.

errorPatterns.description: Performance is deferred to a later phase, after state placement, list strategy, and route boundaries have already fixed the ceiling.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner estimate the cost of converting a finished, focus-managed table from client to server pagination, then compare with making that decision at design time. Add list strategy and state placement to the design review checklist.

questions.prompt: A team replaces `<div role="button" tabIndex={0} onClick={…}>` with `<button onClick={…}>`. What do they no longer have to implement?
options: Only the role attribute
Focusability, activation by both Enter and Space, disabled semantics, and form participation
Nothing; the two are equivalent once tabIndex is present
Only keyboard activation, which they had already implemented

optionFeedback.feedback: The role is the smallest part. The behaviours are what teams reimplement incompletely.
Correct, and Space is the reliable omission: teams implement Enter, test with Enter, and ship a control that native semantics would have handled for free.
`tabIndex` provides focusability only. Activation, disabled state, and form participation all remain unimplemented.
Even that is usually partial, and disabled semantics and form participation are also gained.

successCriteria: Enumerates the behaviours native semantics provide

errorPatterns.description: A generic element is given an ARIA role instead of using the native element, so the role is announced while the associated behaviours are missing or partial.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner list every behaviour they must implement for the div version and test each with a keyboard, then substitute the native element and delete the code that becomes unnecessary.

errorPatterns.description: A state-carrying ARIA attribute such as aria-expanded is set once and never updated, so assistive technology reports a state that contradicts the interface.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner find one state-carrying ARIA attribute in the codebase, toggle the component with a screen reader running, and hear the announcement. Establish that any ARIA state must be driven by the same value that drives the visual state.

questions.prompt: A filter above a data grid updates results asynchronously. A keyboard and screen reader user applies a filter with focus still in the filter input. Describe what they currently perceive, what they should perceive, and how you implement it. Then explain why dialog focus restoration belongs in an effect cleanup rather than in an onClose handler.
successCriteria: Currently they perceive nothing, since focus does not move and no announcement occurs
A polite live region announces the outcome, such as the number of matching records
The region is mounted before the message appears, or it is frequently not announced
The announcement is debounced so rapid typing does not produce continuous speech
Focus restoration belongs in the cleanup because an effect is a synchronization with an explicit undo
Notes that an onClose handler misses unmounts caused by navigation or a parent removing the dialog

rubric.excellent: Describes the current silence accurately, specifies a correct live region including mount order and debouncing, distinguishes outcome announcements from activity announcements, and explains focus restoration through the effect's synchronize-and-undo definition, naming navigation-driven unmount as the case an onClose handler misses.
rubric.adequate: Specifies the live region correctly and states that restoration belongs in the cleanup, but justifies it by convention rather than by the effect definition.
rubric.weak: Proposes moving focus to the results after filtering, which removes the user from the filter input mid-task, or uses an assertive region for routine updates.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: How does a screen reader user learn that an asynchronous filter has completed, and where does dialog focus restoration belong?

errorPatterns.description: Focus models and announcements are deferred to a pre-release accessibility pass, after components whose structure must support them are complete.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner add focus management to a finished virtualized grid and record the effort, then design it into a new component from the start and compare. Add keyboard operability and announcement design to the component definition of done.

questions.prompt: Replacing `container.querySelector('.submit-btn')` with `screen.getByRole('button', { name: /submit claim/i })` gives you two benefits. What are they?
options: It runs faster and produces clearer failure messages
It survives markup and styling changes, and it fails when the control lacks an accessible name — which is also an accessibility defect
It works in more test runners and supports async queries
It avoids querying the DOM directly, which is discouraged

optionFeedback.feedback: Failure messages are better, but that is a side benefit rather than a reason to prefer the query.
Correct. The second benefit is the one usually overlooked: the query cannot find what a screen reader could not find, so the test doubles as an accessibility assertion.
Runner support is unrelated, and both forms can be awaited.
Both query the DOM. What differs is whether the query describes something a user perceives.

successCriteria: Names both refactor resilience and the accessibility assertion

errorPatterns.description: Tests assert on class names, test IDs, or internal state, so harmless implementation changes produce false failures and the team stops refactoring.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner rename a CSS class and run both versions of a test. Then have them apply a role query to an element with no accessible name, so they discover the accessibility defect the query surfaces without extra work.

questions.prompt: A test passes in CI while the feature fails in production, because the API returns `balancePence` and the test's mock returns `balance`. Explain how the mocking approach allowed this, what you would change, and what two configuration settings prevent the neighbouring failure modes.
successCriteria: Identifies that mocking the application's own API module replaces real code with an assumption written by the same author
States that the fetch layer, cache keys, serialisation, error mapping, and retry logic were excluded from the test
Prescribes intercepting at the HTTP boundary so the real data layer runs
Names failing on unhandled requests, so unmocked calls are loud rather than silent
Names resetting handlers between tests, so per-test overrides do not leak and cause order-dependent failures

rubric.excellent: Explains the circularity of module mocking precisely — the test verifies the component against the author's belief about the API — lists what network-boundary interception restores to the test, and names both settings with the specific failure each prevents. May add a contract or end-to-end check against the real API shape.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the module-mock problem and prescribes boundary interception, and names one of the two settings.
rubric.weak: Proposes adding more assertions, raising coverage, or adding a snapshot, none of which detect a wrong assumption about the API shape.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What does network-boundary mocking put under test that a module mock does not?

errorPatterns.description: The application's own API module is mocked, so tests verify the component against an assumed response shape that can diverge from the real API without any test failing.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner rename a field in the mock so it no longer matches the real API and run both test styles; only the boundary version fails. Then enable failure on unhandled requests and handler resetting, and observe what each surfaces.

errorPatterns.description: Line coverage is treated as evidence of testing, so configuration-driven behaviour paths go unexercised despite high reported coverage.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner enumerate the behaviour paths of a configuration-driven component and compare that count with its line coverage, then add a parameterised test across all configurations and a contract test that fails on an unimplemented field type.

questions.prompt: You add server-side authorization to an endpoint that was previously protected only by a hidden button. What must the client also do?
options: Nothing further; the server check is sufficient
Handle 403 as a normal outcome, because permissions can be revoked while a long-lived tab is open
Retry the request with elevated credentials
Remove the client-side permission check, which is now redundant

optionFeedback.feedback: The server is now correct, but a UI that treats 403 as impossible will show an unhandled error to a user whose permissions changed mid-session.
Correct. A tab open for six hours can outlive a role change, so 403 is an expected outcome deserving a clear message rather than a crash.
Retrying an authorization failure with the same identity cannot succeed, and requesting elevation automatically would be a defect of its own.
The client check should stay, so users are not offered actions that will fail. It is user experience, and it always was.

successCriteria: Identifies 403 handling and retains the client check as user experience

errorPatterns.description: Authorization is enforced only by conditional rendering or a route guard, leaving the endpoint callable by anyone who can reach it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner call the endpoint directly as an unauthorised user and paste the successful response into the ticket before writing any fix, then add the server-side check and a test that asserts the forbidden response.

errorPatterns.description: A forbidden response is treated as an impossible state, so a permission change during a session produces an unhandled error rather than a clear message.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner simulate a forbidden response with a mocked handler and implement an explicit message with a next action, then add it to the standard set of states every mutation must handle.

questions.prompt: A finance analyst opens a monthly export and the spreadsheet prompts about an external data connection. A customer's display name, entered through a self-service portal, began with an equals sign. Explain the vulnerability, the fix, and why this surface is routinely missed in review.
successCriteria: Explains that spreadsheet applications execute cells beginning with certain characters as formulas
Notes that the name field is attacker-controlled input that will predictably be exported
Prescribes escaping risky leading characters, plus correct quoting of delimiters
Prefers server-side generation with access logging where practical
Explains that it is missed because the injection is stored in one system and executed in another, against a third party
Adds a regression test asserting the escaping

rubric.excellent: Explains the mechanism and the cross-system nature of the attack, prescribes escaping with correct quoting and server-side generation, adds a regression test, and articulates why exports are reviewed as formatting features rather than as security surfaces — the reviewer, the storer, and the victim are three different people.
rubric.adequate: Explains the mechanism and prescribes escaping, but does not articulate why the surface is systematically overlooked.
rubric.weak: Proposes validating names to reject unusual characters, which breaks legitimate names, or treats it as a spreadsheet configuration problem for the finance team.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What must a CSV export escape, and why is this surface routinely missed?

errorPatterns.description: Exported cells beginning with formula-triggering characters are written unescaped, so user-supplied content executes when the file is opened in a spreadsheet application.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner place a formula in a name field, export, and open the file in a spreadsheet application. Then implement escaping plus correct quoting, add a regression test, and add exports to the security review checklist.

questions.prompt: A team restricts their API's allowed origins to their own domain and concludes the API is protected against unauthorised use. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: The origin list is too permissive and should include only the exact subdomain
CORS governs which origins a browser permits to read a response; it does not identify the caller, and non-browser clients ignore it entirely
CORS requires credentials mode to be effective
Nothing is wrong, provided preflight requests are configured correctly

optionFeedback.feedback: Tightening the list is reasonable housekeeping and does not address the category error.
Correct. It is enforced by the browser, not the server, so a request from a terminal or a script is unaffected. Authentication and authorization are separate server-side concerns.
Credentials mode changes cookie handling on cross-origin requests. It does not turn an origin policy into authorization.
Preflight configuration affects which cross-origin requests browsers permit, which is still not who is asking.

successCriteria: Separates origin policy from authentication and authorization

errorPatterns.description: A CORS configuration is treated as access control, leaving endpoints unauthenticated and unauthorized for any client that is not a browser.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner call their own API from a terminal and observe the response arriving despite the origin policy. Then separate the three concepts explicitly in a short written note and check each endpoint for an independent authorization step.

questions.prompt: An entry bundle grew from 210 kB to 1.4 MB over two years without anyone noticing. Which response addresses both the symptom and the cause?
options: Print the bundle size in the build log for reviewers to monitor
Add blocking budgets set from the target device, analyse the bundle, lazy-load heavy routes, and consolidate overlapping dependencies
Ask reviewers to watch for large imports during code review
Analyse and lazy-load now, and create a ticket for budgets

optionFeedback.feedback: Information nobody is obliged to act on is exactly the condition under which the bundle grew unnoticed.
Correct. It fixes the current state and installs the mechanism preventing recurrence, with the budget derived from what users' devices can load rather than from what the bundle currently weighs.
This relies on the human vigilance that has already failed across two years of pull requests.
Better than nothing, but the deferred ticket competes with feature work and the drift resumes immediately.

successCriteria: Addresses both the current state and the preventive mechanism

errorPatterns.description: Quality checks report rather than block, so standards degrade under delivery pressure and regressions accumulate invisibly.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner add a blocking budget, import a large library, and confirm a red build. Then have them raise the budget deliberately in a reviewed commit, so the difference between a decision and a drift is experienced directly.

questions.prompt: Your pipeline builds separately for staging and production from the same commit. Explain the risk, and describe what changes if configuration is loaded at runtime instead.
successCriteria: States that two builds are two artifacts, so the tested artifact is not the shipped one
Names concrete divergence sources: build-time environment variables, dependency resolution, and build tooling differences
Explains that runtime configuration allows one verified artifact to be promoted through environments
Notes that the promoted artifact can be identified by hash, making the deployed version traceable
Optionally notes that secrets must still not be embedded in the client bundle regardless of when configuration loads

rubric.excellent: States the risk precisely, names several divergence sources, explains artifact promotion and hash-based traceability, and adds that runtime configuration does not license placing secrets in client-readable configuration.
rubric.adequate: Identifies that the tested artifact differs from the shipped one and prescribes runtime configuration, without detailing the divergence sources.
rubric.weak: Treats the difference as theoretical, or proposes comparing build outputs manually rather than eliminating the second build.

errorPatterns.description: Each environment receives its own build, so the artifact verified in staging is not the artifact deployed to production.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner compare build hashes across environments, convert one build-time variable to runtime configuration, and promote a single artifact through both stages, verifying the hash is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A site uses a server-rendering framework, yet search engines index an empty shell and social previews show no headline. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server is too slow and crawlers time out
Content is fetched in `useEffect`, which does not run on the server, so the initial HTML contains only a shell
The sitemap is missing or incorrect
The framework is configured for static generation instead of server rendering

optionFeedback.feedback: A slow server produces a slow page, not an empty one. The distinction is visible in the response body.

Correct. The framework is server-rendering the component, and the component is opting out by deferring its data to an effect. Check view-source rather than the element inspector, which shows the post-hydration DOM.
A sitemap affects discovery, not what is found on the page once crawled.
Static generation also produces HTML at build time, so content fetched during generation would still be present.

successCriteria: Identifies effects not running server-side and names view-source as the check

errorPatterns.description: Data is fetched in an effect within a server-rendered route, so the server emits markup without content and the benefit of server rendering is lost.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner compare view-source with the element inspector for the same page, then move the fetch into the server component and confirm the headline appears in the response body.

questions.prompt: A publisher has four routes: an article that changes rarely and receives most search traffic; a section front updated every few minutes; a live blog updated constantly; and a subscriber account area that is personalised and behind authentication. Assign a rendering strategy to each with justification. Then identify which client-side habits in an existing codebase would become defects on the server.
successCriteria: Article: static generation with on-demand revalidation, justified by low change frequency and high search value
Section front: incremental revalidation on a short interval
Live blog: server rendering, ideally streamed, justified by constant change
Account area: client rendering, justified by personalisation and no search value
Identifies module-level store creation as a cross-user leak
Identifies non-deterministic first renders such as clocks, randomness, and browser-only globals as hydration mismatches

rubric.excellent: Assigns all four with reasoning from change frequency, personalisation, and discoverability, and identifies both the module-level store leak and hydration mismatch sources. May add that passing whole server-side objects as props to client components serialises them into the page, and that server actions are public endpoints requiring their own authorization.
rubric.adequate: Assigns all four sensibly and names at least one habit that becomes a defect, though the account area may be over-engineered with server rendering it does not need.
rubric.weak: Applies one strategy to all four routes, or recommends server rendering everywhere on the grounds that it is faster.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: How do you choose a rendering strategy per route, and which client-side habits become defects on a server?

errorPatterns.description: Server rendering is adopted uniformly, adding infrastructure, a second runtime, and framework commitment to routes that gain nothing from it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner list the concrete benefits — discoverability, social previews, first paint on cellular — and mark which apply per route. Where none apply, keep client rendering and record the decision.

questions.prompt: Your team agrees that features must not import each other's internal files. Six months later it happens in four places. What went wrong, and what would have prevented it?
options: The agreement was not documented clearly enough
An agreement depends on every reviewer noticing every time; a lint rule enforces the boundary mechanically and fails the build
The folder structure needs reorganising
The team needs more experienced reviewers

optionFeedback.feedback: Documentation helps people who read it at the right moment. It does not catch the import written under deadline pressure at 6pm.
Correct. Structural rules that are not enforced mechanically degrade, because reviewers are inconsistent and outnumbered. This is the same argument as blocking CI gates, applied to architecture.
The structure may be fine. What is missing is enforcement of the rule about crossing it.
Experienced reviewers still miss imports in large diffs, and this places the burden on people rather than on a tool.

successCriteria: Identifies mechanical enforcement as the fix

questions.prompt: Write a decision record for the state placement rule your team will follow. Cover context, options considered, decision, and consequences. Then explain what specifically goes wrong six months later if this record does not exist.
successCriteria: Context describes the problem that forced a decision, not merely the topic
At least two genuine options are considered, with the trade-off between them stated
The decision is specific enough to settle a code review disagreement
Consequences include what becomes harder, not only what improves
Explains that without the record a newcomer reads deliberate variation as inconsistency and normalises it
Notes that the record is stored alongside the code so it is found when the question arises

rubric.excellent: A record that would actually settle a disagreement, with honest consequences including the costs accepted. The explanation identifies the specific failure: an unexplained pattern is indistinguishable from an accident, so a well-intentioned newcomer removes the variation and reintroduces the original problem. May note that this is how architectures decay without anyone deciding to change them.
rubric.adequate: All four sections present with a specific decision, but consequences list only benefits, or the six-month explanation is generic.
rubric.weak: Records the decision without alternatives or consequences, or writes it so generally that it cannot resolve a concrete disagreement.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What are the four parts of a decision record, and what goes wrong when a structural decision is not recorded?

errorPatterns.description: A structural decision is made without a written record, so its reasoning is unavailable when the pattern is questioned and the variation is later removed as inconsistency.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner examine a deliberate inconsistency in an unfamiliar codebase and attempt to reconstruct its reason from the code alone, then read the corresponding record. Require a record for every decision made during this course.

errorPatterns.description: A dependency is added without assessing maintenance, size, exit cost, or overlap, so deeply embedded libraries receive the same shallow evaluation as trivially replaceable ones.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: For each candidate, have the learner estimate the work required to remove it in twelve months and scale the evaluation depth to that number. Then audit the existing dependency list for overlap, which commonly reveals duplicate date or utility libraries.

retrievalSystem.algorithm: Expanding-interval scheduling driven by each item's own schedule block. An item's first review falls at initialReviewDays after its originating experience is completed; successful recalls advance through subsequentReviewDays, and the interval is multiplied by decayParameters.strengthMultiplier at each success, bounded by minimumIntervalDays and maximumIntervalDays. A failed recall resets the item to initialReviewDays. When confidenceSchedulingEnabled is true, a correct recall given at low confidence is scheduled at initialReviewDays rather than advancing, and an incorrect recall given at high confidence is flagged miscalibrated so the review surfaces the calibration gap alongside the content. Items entering the queue through reviewOnMiss follow missedItemSchedule and are keyed by their originating questionId or interactionId.
retrievalModes: free-recall — an unaided prompt with no cues, used for principles the learner must be able to state unprompted, such as the state placement questions or the CSS decision rule
cued-recall — a partial cue supplying the situation and asking for the mechanism, used where the concept is only useful when triggered by a symptom
application — a small novel case requiring the principle to be applied rather than restated
scenario-analysis — a multi-factor situation with competing considerations, used for judgement competencies such as tier selection and optimistic-versus-pessimistic updates

contrast — two superficially similar cases whose correct treatments differ, used to prevent overgeneralisation, for example isLoading against isFetching, or a legitimate sequential await against an accidental one
error-explanation — the learner is shown a defective snippet and must name the mechanism, which is the retrieval mode closest to the actual work of the debugging section

track: experience-completion — which experiences were opened, completed, or abandoned, with time on each
interaction-responses — every answer with its timestamp, including free-text responses for later review
confidence-ratings — the rating attached to each answer, retained as a pair with the eventual score
calibration-gap — the signed difference between confidence and correctness, aggregated per competency and per section
retrieval-success-rate — recall accuracy per item and per competency, over time
review-adherence — scheduled reviews completed against reviews due, which predicts decay before it appears in scores
mastery-trajectory — evidence-weighted competency estimates across sessions, with decay applied
misconception-frequency — how often each misconceptionId is selected, and whether selection persists after remediation
error-pattern-recurrence — repeated instances of the same errorPatternId across different assessments, which distinguishes a slip from a stable wrong model
assessment-attempt-history — attempts, scores, and difficulty served per question under adaptive rules
adaptive-path — the difficulty sequence each learner was served, used to check that adaptive serving is not stalling at a level
transfer-performance — scores on transfer exercises separated from scores on in-context assessments, since the gap between them is the measure of genuine transfer
written-response-self-rating — learner self-assessment on rubric-scored items, compared against later auto-scored performance on the same competency
time-to-first-response — response latency per item, which distinguishes fluent retrieval from effortful reconstruction
hint-usage — how often progressive hints were requested before answering
prior-knowledge-routing — which probe outcomes triggered which routing actions, and whether learners routed past material later underperformed on it

glossary.definition: The runtime mechanism that empties the microtask queue completely, runs one macrotask, and repeats. It explains why promise callbacks always run before timers.
A promise reaction or `queueMicrotask` callback. Microtasks are drained exhaustively before the next macrotask, so a self-scheduling chain can delay timers indefinitely.
A timer, input-output callback, or DOM event. Exactly one runs between microtask drains.
A function together with the scope in which it was created. It captures the binding, meaning the storage location, rather than the value at the moment of creation.
The storage location for a variable. `let` and `const` create a fresh binding for each loop iteration; `var` creates one shared by all iterations.
A callback reading values captured from an earlier render, producing a value that is consistently one update behind. The usual fix is a functional update or a corrected dependency.
The span in which a `let` or `const` binding exists but cannot be read, turning ordering mistakes into a clear ReferenceError rather than a silent undefined.
An ES module is evaluated once per JavaScript context, so module scope is a singleton for that context's lifetime. Safe per-user in a browser tab; shared across users in a server process.
A rejected promise that was never awaited or caught. A global listener makes these visible rather than silent.
The check `fetch` requires, because it rejects only on network failure. A 404 or 500 resolves normally and will otherwise be parsed as data.
A React component that catches errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. It does not catch errors in event handlers, timers, or async code.
Comparison by identity using `Object.is`, which is how React, Redux, and memoization decide whether something changed. Mutating an object changes its contents but not its identity.
Producing a new value by copying only the path that changed and reusing every unchanged branch, which makes immutable updates inexpensive.
A set of variants separated by one shared field with a literal value, so that narrowing on the tag gives exactly the fields that state has.
Assigning a narrowed value to `never` in a default branch, so adding a variant produces a compile error at every site that must handle it.
Validating external data once, where it enters the application, so failures occur at the edge with a message naming the offending field.
A primitive marked with a phantom tag so that two identifiers sharing the same underlying type become distinct at compile time, at no runtime cost.
A TypeScript operator that checks a value against a type without widening the inferred type, unlike an annotation, and without suppressing checks, unlike a cast.
The three separate phases: producing a description of the UI, comparing it with the previous one, and applying the differences to the DOM. A re-render is not a DOM update.
One of four causes: the component's own state changed, its context value changed, its parent re-rendered, or a hook it uses signalled a change.
A claim that an element is the same conceptual item as before. An incorrect key causes React to reuse a component instance against different data and preserve its state.
Deliberately changing a component's key to discard its subtree state, which is cleaner than an effect that clears fields when a prop changes.
An effect that keeps an external system in sync with React state and whose cleanup reverses exactly what it did. If a cleanup cannot be written, the work usually belongs in render or a handler.
Passing a function to a state setter so it receives the current value, which prevents stale-closure defects when the next state depends on the previous one.
A component providing behaviour and state while rendering no markup, leaving presentation to the caller. This is why such libraries survive redesigns.
Accepting children rather than accumulating boolean props, so variation lives at the call site instead of expanding the component's API surface.
React's dependency injection mechanism. Every consumer re-renders when the provided value's identity changes, so contexts should be split by change frequency and their values memoized.
A CSS query responding to an ancestor container's size rather than the viewport, which lets a component adapt to the space it was given without a prop.
An explicit precedence order declared with `@layer`. Layer order beats specificity, so a utility can override a component rule without `!important`.
A runtime, inheritable CSS variable. Changing one re-themes the application without a single React render.
A flow-relative CSS direction such as `margin-inline-start`, identical to its physical equivalent in left-to-right languages and mirroring automatically in right-to-left ones.
`transform` and `opacity`, which can be animated without recalculating layout and often off the main thread.

First, Last, Invert, Play: measuring an element's start and end positions, applying a transform that returns it visually to the start, then animating that transform to zero, giving layout-accurate motion using only transforms.
A user preference for reduced movement. The correct response removes travel such as parallax and large translations while keeping the signal that something changed.
An attribute removing an element and its subtree from focus order and the accessibility tree, needed when a mounted element is hidden only visually.
Diagnosing by working from the rendered value to its props, then its owner, then its data source, then the actual network response — rather than reading a codebase in structural order.
The first stack-trace frame in your own code, which is where diagnosis normally begins. Production traces require uploaded source maps to be readable.
A breakpoint that pauses only when an expression is true, which makes a defect occurring on one record in a thousand practical to inspect.
How much of the application re-renders when one piece of state changes. It is one of the five questions deciding where state belongs.
One of six homes for state: server cache, URL, global client, scoped store, injected context, or local. Each piece of state belongs to exactly one.
A function producing the same output for the same state and action, with no side effects and no mutation of the original, which is what makes it trivially testable.
A Proxy permitting mutating syntax inside a reducer while producing immutable state on return. The draft is revoked once the reducer returns and must not be retained.
An action naming what happened rather than what to assign, so multiple slices can respond independently and the action log reads as a record of user activity.
A derived-state function that recomputes only when its inputs change. The default cache holds one result, so sharing one instance across differing arguments defeats it.
Storing records keyed by ID alongside an ordered list of IDs, so updating one record does not touch the others and lookups do not scan an array.
Comparing an object's own enumerable values rather than its identity, required when a store selector returns a newly constructed object.
A cached copy of data the client does not own. It can be stale, can fail, can arrive out of order, and can be changed by someone else while it is on screen.
The endpoint plus arguments identifying a cache entry. Unstable argument objects create a new key on every render, causing endless refetching.
`isLoading` is true only when no cached data exists yet; `isFetching` is true for any request in flight, including a background refresh over visible data.
Marking cached entries stale after a mutation. When data fails to refresh, check that the query provides the tag, the mutation invalidates it, the IDs match, and the component is subscribed.
Applying a change before the server confirms it, requiring a rollback path that is visible to the user. Chosen by the consequence of being wrong, not by perceived speed.
Loading, empty, error, and partial. Partial — some data present, some failed — is the state most often omitted and the hardest for users to notice.
A client-side check preventing navigation to a screen. It improves the experience and enforces nothing, so every guarded route needs server-side authorization.
A form's current values differing from its defaults. It breaks when the form is not reset with saved values after a successful save, or when the defaults object is recreated each render.
The adapter connecting a validation schema to a form library, so one schema serves as both the runtime validator and the source of the TypeScript type.
A language plus a region, governing date order, separators, currency position, first day of week, sort order, and text direction. It is independent of currency.
The platform's built-in formatting, pluralization, and collation APIs. Formatters should be constructed once and always given an explicit locale.
A message syntax expressing plurals and placeholders so translators supply their own language's categories, which a two-branch condition in code cannot do.
A generated locale that lengthens and decorates every string, revealing both truncated layouts and strings that were never extracted, in a single pass.
Locale-correct string ordering. Sorting by code point places accented names at the end of a list and mis-orders non-Latin scripts.
Rendering only the rows near the viewport with a spacer preserving scroll height. It also removes the dataset from the DOM, which breaks row position, keyboard navigation, find-in-page, and printing.
Attributes supplying the true dataset size and a row's true position, needed because virtualization makes the DOM unrepresentative of the data.
A pattern giving exactly one cell `tabIndex={0}` so Tab enters and leaves a grid in one step while arrow keys move within it.
A component's own render duration excluding its children. Many components with small self time indicates volume; one component with large self time indicates computation during render.
The DOM mutation, layout, style recalculation, and paint that follow reconciliation. When React time is small but frames are long, the cost is here.
Largest Contentful Paint for perceived load, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift for visual stability.
The wait a user feels, which skeletons, retained content during refetch, and prefetching reduce without changing any measured work.
An element whose content changes are announced by assistive technology. It must be mounted before the message appears, should announce outcomes rather than activity, and should be debounced.
Confining Tab within an open dialog, and returning focus to the element that opened it on close. Restoration belongs in the effect cleanup so it survives unmounts caused by navigation.
Observable behaviour versus how code is currently built. A test should fail when the first changes and pass when only the second does.
The Testing Library ranking from `getByRole` through `getByLabelText` and `getByText` to `getByTestId`, ordered by resemblance to how a real user finds an element.
Intercepting HTTP so the application's real fetch layer, cache keys, serialisation, and error mapping remain under test, unlike a module mock.
Per-test request overrides persisting into later tests, producing failures that depend on execution order.
A requirement identifier embedded in a test name, making coverage of a requirement answerable mechanically rather than by reading the suite.
A response header restricting where scripts may come from, which converts a successful injection into a blocked one when configured without unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval.
Cookie attributes making a token unreadable to scripts and limiting cross-site sending. The token storage decision is about which risk you can mitigate, not which is riskless.
A browser policy governing which origins may read a response. It does not identify the caller and is ignored entirely by clients that are not browsers.
A cell beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` being executed as a formula by spreadsheet applications, which makes exports a security surface rather than a formatting feature.
An enforced size ceiling that fails the build when exceeded, set from the target device rather than from the bundle's current size.
A CI check that prevents merging rather than reporting. A standard that is not enforced mechanically degrades under delivery pressure.
Loading environment values at run time so one verified artifact is promoted between environments, rather than rebuilding and shipping something that was never tested.
A one-page record of context, options considered, decision, and consequences, stored beside the code. It is how a design survives the departure of the people who made it.
Attaching React's handlers and state to server-rendered HTML rather than recreating the DOM. It asserts that the client's first render reproduces the server's output exactly.
A difference between the client's first render and the server's HTML, caused by anything the server could not know: clocks, randomness, browser globals, or stored preferences.
A component running only on the server, shipping no JavaScript, unable to use state or effects, and able to await data directly.
The directive marking where code begins shipping to the browser. Everything imported below it is included, so the boundary should be pushed down to interactive leaves.
A server function invocable from the client. It is a public HTTP endpoint and requires its own authorization regardless of which interface calls it.
Sending HTML progressively as segments resolve, so primary content renders while slower regions arrive later behind Suspense boundaries.

sections.title: JavaScript Foundations: The Runtime Beneath React
sections.description: Most defects that look like React defects are not. A dropdown shows last week's value, a spinner never stops, a save writes the wrong record, a change never appears on screen. Trace each far enough and you reach the JavaScript runtime: a variable captured at the wrong moment, a promise that finished in an unexpected order, an object changed in place, a module evaluated once when you expected it once per user. This section builds that foundation, then closes with the shape an application takes and the rule that keeps it that shape. All examples come from a parcel depot dispatch console.

learningObjectives.description: Predict the execution order of synchronous code, promise continuations, and timers, and justify the order by naming the queue each item enters.
Distinguish sequential from concurrent asynchronous work, restructure accidentally sequential code, and name a case where sequential execution is correct.
Explain that a closure captures a binding rather than a value, and predict the behaviour of deferred callbacks created in a loop.
Predict whether a value declared at module level is shared, and by whom, in a browser tab and in a server process, and state the consequence in security terms.
Choose the correct error-handling mechanism for synchronous, promise-based, event-handler, and render-time failures, and recognise the patterns that produce silent wrong answers.
Explain why a mutated object does not trigger a re-render, and apply structural sharing to update nested state.
Organise an application into layers with a single dependency direction, and enforce that direction mechanically rather than by agreement.

motivationHooks.prompt: A depot dispatch console took six seconds to show a bay manifest. No server was slow, no query was missing an index, and no profiler flagged a component. The cause was a `for` loop with an `await` inside it: thirty rows, each waiting 200 ms for the previous one to finish. The fix was four characters of structure and no new code. Defects of this shape are common, cheap to fix, and almost impossible to find if you do not know the mechanism.

Before you read anything else, write down your answer to this. A file contains one line: `export const cache = new Map()`. Two other files import it. **How many Maps exist?** Then write down whether your answer changes if this code runs on a server that handles requests from many users at once. Keep both answers. You will check them at the end of the section.

Every later section in this course depends on this one. Stale values in React are closures. Selector memoisation and re-render decisions are reference equality. Per-request store creation under server rendering is module evaluation. Failed invalidation that looks like a caching bug is often an unchecked response status. You are not learning background theory here; you are learning the mechanisms the rest of the course names by shorthand.

Return to your two written answers. **One Map exists**, not two: a module is evaluated once and every importer receives the same instance. And yes, the second answer must change. In a browser each user has their own tab and therefore their own context, so one shared Map is one Map per user. On a server the process handles many users' requests in the same context, so that one Map is shared between all of them — and a cache holding one user's data can be read into another user's response. The code did not change. Only the environment did. That is the whole lesson, and it is why Section 6 insists that stores are created per request and Section 11 treats this as a security finding rather than a rendering bug.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about the ground your React code stands on.

**One thread, two queues.** Microtasks drain completely before the next macrotask, and an async function body runs immediately up to its first `await`. Ordering is predictable, not mysterious.

**`await` yields; it does not parallelise.** The difference between three seconds and 250 milliseconds is when the work starts, not how you wait for it. Sequential is correct sometimes — just never by accident.

**Closures capture bindings, not values.** This single fact explains stale-value defects in React, in intervals, in subscriptions, and in event handlers registered once.

**Modules are evaluated once per context.** That is per-user in a browser and shared across users on a server, which turns a harmless pattern into a data leak when the environment changes.

**Errors go where the call stack goes, and async has no call stack.** `try`/`catch` needs an `await`, `fetch` needs an `ok` check, and error boundaries cover render but not events, timers, or async work.

**Change is detected by reference.** Mutation is invisible to React, Redux, and every memoisation you will meet later. Structural sharing makes copying cheap.

**Structure is a rule, and rules decay unless a machine enforces them.** Layer the application, point every dependency downward, and let lint hold the line.
keyTakeaways: Promise callbacks always run before timers, and an async body runs synchronously to its first await.
Start independent work together, then await the aggregate. Serial by accident is the defect.
A closure reads the storage location, so it sees later writes; `let` gives a fresh binding per loop iteration and `var` does not.
Module scope is a singleton for its JavaScript context — safe in a tab, dangerous in a server process.
try/catch needs await; fetch needs an ok check; error boundaries do not catch handlers, timers, or async code.
An empty catch block converts a loud failure into a silent wrong answer.
React compares references, so copy the changed path rather than mutating in place.
Enforce dependency direction with a lint rule, not with a team agreement.
