learningExperiences.title: One thread, two queues

contentBlocks.content:
## One thread

JavaScript in the browser runs your code on a **single thread**. There is one call stack. While your code is running, nothing else runs: no click handler, no network callback, no painting.

So how does anything asynchronous happen? The runtime keeps queues of work to do **after** the stack becomes empty.

## Two queues

The event loop works like this. When the call stack is empty, the runtime empties the **microtask** queue completely. Then it takes **one** item from the **macrotask** queue and runs it. Then it empties the microtask queue again. Then it repeats.

- **Macrotasks** include `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, input and output callbacks, and most DOM events.
- **Microtasks** include promise reactions (`.then`, `.catch`, `.finally`), the code after an `await`, and `queueMicrotask`.

The difference matters. Microtasks are emptied **completely** before the next macrotask runs. So a promise chain that keeps creating new promises can block a `setTimeout(…, 0)` for a long time.

The output is: `1`, `4`, `6`, `3`, `5`, `2`.

Work through why, line by line.

1. `1` prints. Synchronous.
2. The timer is registered. Its callback goes to the macrotask queue. Nothing prints.
3. The promise is already resolved, so its callback goes to the microtask queue. Nothing prints.
4. The async function is **called**, so its body starts running immediately. `4` prints. Then `await null` suspends the function and schedules the rest as a microtask.
5. `6` prints. The call stack is now empty.
6. Microtasks drain: `3`, then `5`.
7. One macrotask runs: `2`.

Two rules to remember. First, **the body of an async function runs immediately until it reaches the first `await`**. Second, **promise callbacks always run before timers**.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the answer: in the depot scanning snippet above, which number prints **third**?
options: `3 microtask`, because promise callbacks are prioritised
`6 scan-end`, because all synchronous code runs before anything queued
`2 timeout`, because it was scheduled with a delay of zero
`5 after-await`, because the async function was already running

optionFeedback.feedback: Promise callbacks are prioritised over timers, but not over synchronous code. Nothing queued runs until the call stack is empty, and `console.log('6 scan-end')` is still on the stack.
Correct. The order so far is `1`, then `4` (the async body runs immediately up to its `await`), then `6`. Only after that does the runtime look at any queue.

A delay of zero means 'as soon as possible', not 'immediately'. The callback still waits for the stack to empty and for the entire microtask queue to drain first, which is why it prints last of all six.
The async function did start running immediately, and that is why `4` prints second. But `await null` suspends it, and the resumption is a microtask, so `5` waits behind the synchronous code.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The rule that decides this question is the one people most often skip: **nothing in either queue runs while synchronous code is still executing**. The queues are drained when the call stack empties, not opportunistically. Once you hold that, the rest follows mechanically — first all synchronous statements in source order, then every microtask, then one macrotask.
hints: Ask first: has the call stack emptied yet at this point in the file?
The async function body is synchronous up to its first `await`. Where does that put `4`?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt: A function schedules itself with `Promise.resolve().then(loop)` on every call, and a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is also pending. What happens to the timer?
options: It runs after the current microtask, since the runtime alternates between the queues
It may never run, because the microtask queue is drained exhaustively and keeps refilling itself
It runs immediately, because timers have higher priority than promises
It runs once the promise chain reaches a fixed depth limit

optionFeedback.feedback: The runtime does not alternate. It empties the microtask queue **completely**, and a self-scheduling chain refills it faster than it empties, so the loop never reaches the macrotask stage.

Correct, and this is a real way to freeze an interface. Recursive promise scheduling starves timers, rendering, and input handling. If you need to yield to the browser between iterations, schedule with a macrotask such as `setTimeout` or `scheduler.postTask`.
Priority runs the other way. Promise callbacks are microtasks and always run before the next timer.
There is no depth limit on microtask scheduling. Recursion depth on the call stack is limited, but each `.then` starts a fresh stack, so the chain can continue indefinitely.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the practical consequence of 'drains exhaustively'. It is also worth carrying into Section 9: when a screen is unresponsive but the profiler shows little React work, a starving main thread is one of the candidates. The fix is to yield deliberately with a macrotask rather than assuming the runtime will interleave for you.
hints: What exactly does 'the microtask queue is emptied completely' mean if the queue refills while it is being emptied?

steps: Identify what is synchronous. `console.log('A start')` and `console.log('E end')` run on the call stack, so `A` prints first and `E` prints second.

Identify what is scheduled and where. The `setTimeout` callback enters the **macrotask** queue. The `queueMicrotask` callback enters the **microtask** queue. The `.then` callback also enters the **microtask** queue, because the promise is already resolved.
Determine the order within the microtask queue. Microtasks run in the order they were queued, so `C` was queued before `D` and therefore runs first.
Apply the event loop. The call stack empties after `E`. The runtime then drains the microtask queue completely: `C`, then `D`.
Run one macrotask. With the microtask queue empty, the timer callback finally runs: `B`.
Assemble the result: `A start`, `E end`, `C microtask`, `D promise`, `B timeout`.
workedExamples.conclusion: The output is `A`, `E`, `C`, `D`, `B`. Notice what determined it: not the order the callbacks were written, and not the delay value on the timer, but **which queue each callback entered**. `queueMicrotask` and `.then` are interchangeable for ordering purposes because they use the same queue; `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is in a different category entirely and always loses to both. When you are reasoning about ordering in real code, classify each callback by its queue first and the answer usually falls out without further thought.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Without looking: state the two rules that determine ordering between synchronous code, promise continuations, and timers.
A callback is scheduled with `queueMicrotask(fn)` and another with `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, in that order. Which runs first, and would swapping the two lines change the answer? Explain why.

learningExperiences.title: `await` does not create parallelism

contentBlocks.content:
## Sequential by accident

```js
const a = await fetchManifest('bay-1');   // 400ms
const b = await fetchManifest('bay-2');   // 400ms — this call does not start until a finishes
const c = await fetchManifest('bay-3');   // 400ms → about 1200ms in total
```

```js
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([     // all three requests start immediately
  fetchManifest('bay-1'), fetchManifest('bay-2'), fetchManifest('bay-3'),
]);                                       // about 400ms
```

The difference is **when the work starts**, not how you wait for it. A `for` loop containing an `await` is fully sequential. Thirty rows, each waiting 200 ms, produces a screen that takes six seconds to load.

`await` gives control back to the event loop. It does not make things run at the same time.

## When sequential is correct

Sequential code is right when request two needs the result of request one, or when you are limiting the request rate on purpose, or when writes must be ordered. The mistake is being sequential **by accident**.

## One caution about error behaviour

`Promise.all` rejects as soon as any single promise rejects, and you lose the results of the ones that succeeded. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them and reports each outcome separately. Choose deliberately: `all` when a partial result is useless, `allSettled` when you want to show what did load. That choice reappears in Section 7 as the partial async state.

interactionSequence.prompt: A loader runs `for (const id of bayIds) { manifests.push(await fetchManifest(id)); }` over 20 bays, each request taking about 200 ms. Roughly how long does the loop take, and why?
options: About 200 ms, because `await` lets the requests overlap
About 4 seconds, because each request is not created until the previous one settles
About 200 ms, because the browser batches requests to the same host automatically
Unknowable from the client code, since it depends entirely on the server

optionFeedback.feedback: This is the most common misreading of `await`. It suspends the function and returns control to the event loop, but the next `fetchManifest` call is a later statement that has not been evaluated yet, so no second request exists to overlap with.
Correct. Twenty requests at roughly 200 ms each, one after another. Start them all first, then await the aggregate, and the total drops to roughly the slowest single request.
Browsers do limit and multiplex connections per host, but that affects requests already in flight. Here only one request exists at any moment, so there is nothing to batch.
Server latency is a variable, but the structure of the client code decides whether that latency is paid once or twenty times. That much is knowable from the code alone.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The diagnostic habit worth forming: when you see `await` inside a loop, ask whether iteration N+1 needs anything from iteration N. If it does not, the loop is sequential by accident. The measurement that proves it takes seconds — log a timestamp at the start of each request. In the sequential version the start times are 200 ms apart; in the concurrent version they are milliseconds apart.
hints: When is the second `fetchManifest(...)` call actually evaluated?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: describe one place in a project you have worked on where requests were probably sequential without needing to be. What was the user-visible effect, and what would you have measured to confirm it?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer names a concrete screen, describes the effect in the terms a user would use ('the page sat blank', 'the list filled in one row at a time'), and proposes a specific measurement — request start timestamps, or the waterfall shape in the Network tab, where sequential requests form a staircase and concurrent ones form a block. Note that the waterfall alone identifies this defect in about ten seconds once you know what the staircase means, which is why it is worth recognising visually as well as conceptually.

steps: Map the real dependencies. `getRoute` must come first, because `route.bays` and `route.vehicleId` do not exist until it resolves. Nothing else depends on anything else.
Classify each remaining call. The six manifest requests are independent of each other. The inspection request depends only on `route`, not on any manifest.
Total the current cost: 300 + (6 × 250) + 300 = 2100 ms. Three separate sequential stages, two of which did not need to be sequential.
Start the six manifest requests together with `Promise.all`, mapping over the bays rather than looping with an `await` inside.
Notice that the inspection request can start at the same time as the manifests, since it only needs `route`. Group both into one `Promise.all`.
Total the new cost: 300 ms for the route, then roughly 300 ms for the slowest item in the concurrent group, giving about 600 ms.

Decide the error behaviour deliberately. With `Promise.all`, one failed manifest discards the other five and the inspection. If the screen can usefully show five of six bays, use `Promise.allSettled` for the manifest group and render the failed one as a partial state.
workedExamples.conclusion: 2100 ms becomes about 600 ms, and no new code was written — only the structure changed. Two lessons generalise beyond this example. First, **the dependency graph, not the source order, tells you what must be sequential**: `getInspection` was written last but only ever needed `route`, so it belonged in the concurrent group. Second, **restructuring for concurrency forces an error-handling decision you were previously making by default**, because sequential code fails at the first problem while concurrent code must decide whether a partial result is worth showing. Make that decision explicitly rather than inheriting whichever behaviour `Promise.all` happens to give you.

retrievalPractice.prompt: You see `await` inside a `for` loop during a code review. What single question tells you whether this is a defect?
Give one situation where sequential `await` calls are correct, and one where they are a defect. What distinguishes them?
Six independent requests must all succeed for the screen to be meaningful, and a seventh is optional extra detail. Which combination of `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled` would you use, and why?

learningExperiences.title: Closures capture bindings, not values

contentBlocks.content:
## What a closure captures

A **closure** is a function together with the scope where it was created. When the function runs later, it reads the variables from that scope.

The important detail: a closure captures the **binding**, which means the storage location. It does not capture the value at the moment of creation.

```js
let scanned = 0;
setInterval(() => console.log(scanned), 1000);   // this sees every later change
scanned = 12;                                     // the closure reads this new value
```

If closures captured values, that interval would print `0` forever. It prints `12`, because it reads the same storage location that the assignment wrote to.

## Bindings per iteration

`let` and `const` create a new binding for each loop iteration. `var` creates one binding that all iterations share.

```js
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));   // prints 3, 3, 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));   // prints 0, 1, 2
```

With `var`, all three callbacks close over the same `i`. By the time any of them runs, the loop has finished and `i` is `3`.

## Why this matters for React

This is the mechanism behind stale-value defects in React. A callback created inside a render captures the variables **from that render**. A render's `const` bindings never change, so the callback keeps reading the value from the render that created it — however long it lives.

Section 3 returns to this as the stale closure, and Section 5 lists it first among the five symptoms you will meet in real codebases. When a displayed value is consistently one update behind rather than simply wrong, this is almost always the mechanism.

## Two related points

`let` and `const` are hoisted, but you cannot read them before their declaration line. That period is called the **temporal dead zone**, and it turns a class of ordering mistakes into a clear `ReferenceError` instead of a silent `undefined`.

Also note that `function` declarations are fully hoisted, but `const fn = () => …` is not.

options: `bay A`, `bay B`, `bay C`
`bay undefined` three times, because all three callbacks read `i` after the loop has set it to 3
`bay C` three times, because the last value assigned wins
Nothing, because the timers are cleared when the loop ends

optionFeedback.feedback: This is what `let` would produce, because `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration. With `var` there is one shared binding, and all three callbacks read it after the loop finishes.

Correct, and the `undefined` is the useful detail. The shared `i` is `3` when the callbacks run, and `bays[3]` does not exist. This is the same mechanism as the classic `3, 3, 3` example, made slightly nastier because the symptom is a missing value rather than a wrong number.
Close in spirit, but check the arithmetic. The loop exits when `i` reaches `3`, not `2`, so the callbacks read `bays[3]`, which is `undefined`.
Timers are not cleared when a loop ends. They persist until they fire or until `clearTimeout` is called explicitly.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Note how the symptom presents: not an error, not a crash, just `undefined` where data should be. That is characteristic of binding defects and is why they are hard to spot in review. Changing `var` to `let` fixes it entirely, because `let` gives each iteration its own binding for the callback to close over.
hints: What is the value of `i` at the moment the first timer callback actually runs?
How many separate `i` bindings does a `var` loop create?

interactionSequence.prompt: A depot dashboard registers a subscription once when it loads, and its callback logs a `total` variable declared alongside it. The total updates correctly everywhere else on screen, but the subscription always logs the original value. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The subscription is firing before the total is updated
The callback closed over a binding created in an earlier scope that is never reassigned, so it reads that scope's value permanently
The subscription needs to be re-registered on every change
The total is being mutated in place rather than reassigned

optionFeedback.feedback: Timing would produce an occasional stale reading, not a permanently frozen one. 'Always the original value' points at capture rather than at ordering.

Correct. The callback reads the binding from the scope in which it was created. If that scope is recreated on each update — as a React render is — and the callback is not, the callback keeps reading the original scope's binding forever.

Re-registering would work by creating a new closure each time, but it treats the symptom expensively. The better fixes are to read the current value through a function or a ref rather than through a captured binding.

Mutation in place is a real and separate defect, covered later in this section, but it causes a value to change without anything noticing. Here the opposite is happening: everything else notices and only this callback does not.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The shape of the symptom is the diagnostic. **Consistently stale** means a captured binding. **Occasionally stale** means ordering or a race. **Wrong rather than late** means the data itself, so check the network response. Learning to separate those three saves hours, and Section 5 builds the full symptom-to-cause table on top of this distinction.
hints: Was the callback created once, while the variable it reads is recreated many times?

steps: Read what the interval callback closes over. It closes over `scannedCount`, which is a `let` binding in the enclosing function scope.
Check whether that binding is ever reassigned. `recordScan` assigns to the same binding, so the interval should see the new value. This code, as written, actually works.

So the reproduction does not yet match the bug. Look for what differs in the real component: the real screen recreates its scope on every update, because a React render creates fresh bindings each time.

Now the defect reproduces. `count` is a fresh binding on every call to `renderStatus`, but the interval was created during the first call and closed over that first binding. Later calls create new bindings the interval never sees.
Choose a fix. Option one: read through a function rather than a value, so the closure captures the reader instead of the reading — `setInterval(() => console.log(getCount()), 1000)`.

Option two: hold the value in a single mutable container that outlives the scope, and have each update write to it — a ref, in React terms. The closure then captures the container, and the container's contents are current.

Option three, where applicable: recreate the interval when the value it depends on changes, clearing the previous one. This is exactly what a React effect with a dependency and a cleanup does, and Section 3 formalises it.
workedExamples.conclusion: The defect was never in the interval and never in the variable. It was in the **mismatch of lifetimes**: a callback that lives once, reading a binding that is recreated many times. Whenever you find a value that is permanently stale, look for that mismatch rather than for a bug in the update logic, which is usually working perfectly. All three fixes work by removing the mismatch — either the closure stops capturing the short-lived binding, or the callback is recreated as often as the binding is.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What exactly does a closure capture? State it in one sentence, then give the practical consequence for a `for` loop using `var`.

A value displayed on screen is consistently one update behind, while everything else is current. Name the likely mechanism, and name one alternative mechanism you would rule out first if the value were only *occasionally* stale.

learningExperiences.title: Modules are evaluated once per context

contentBlocks.content:
## Evaluated once

An ES module is evaluated **once**, the first time something imports it. Every later import receives the same instance.

This means that code at the top level of a module is a **singleton** for the lifetime of that JavaScript context.

```js
// telemetry.js
export const cache = new Map();          // ONE map, shared by every file that imports it
console.log('evaluated');                // prints exactly once
```

In a browser this is usually what you want, and it is safe. Each user has their own tab, so each user has their own context.

## On a server this is not safe

A store or cache at module level is shared across **every request that the server process handles**. One user's data can appear in another user's response.

This is not a rendering bug. It is a data leak, and it has three properties that make it dangerous:

- It depends on concurrency, so it appears under load and not in quiet testing.
- It is intermittent, so it is easy to dismiss as a one-off.
- The code that causes it has usually worked correctly for years in the browser.

This is the cause of the leak described in Section 11, and the reason for the rule in Section 6 that stores are created **per request** when you use server rendering.

## Two more consequences

Import order does not control evaluation order in the way people expect, because a module's dependencies are evaluated before the module itself.

And side effects at module level run when the file is imported. A `fetch` call, a subscription, or a timer at the top level of a module fires whether or not anyone uses the export.

interactionSequence.prompt: A module contains `export const requestCache = new Map()`. Four different files import it. How many Maps exist, and does the answer depend on the environment?
options: Four — each importing file receives its own copy
One per JavaScript context: one per tab in a browser, one per process on a server
One per import statement evaluated, so the count depends on bundling
One, created lazily on first access and discarded when no file is using it

optionFeedback.feedback: Importers receive the same instance. A module is evaluated once and its exports are shared bindings, not copies.
Correct, and the environment clause is the part that matters. The same code is a per-user cache in a tab and a structure shared between concurrent users in a server process.

Bundling can duplicate a module if it is resolved through two different paths, which is a real and separate problem worth knowing about. But the language rule is one evaluation per module per context, regardless of how many import statements reference it.
The Map is created when the module is evaluated, and it stays reachable from the module binding for as long as the context lives, so it is never discarded.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The habit to build: whenever you see mutable state at the top level of a module, ask **'who shares this?'** In the browser the answer is 'this user'. On a server the answer is 'everyone this process serves'. Nothing in the code distinguishes the two, which is why the defect survives code review — the reviewer is mentally running it in a browser.
hints: How many times is the module body executed, and what decides that number?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your team is adding server rendering to the depot console. A colleague says the module-level store has worked without incident for two years, so it can stay. Write the argument you would make, including how you would demonstrate the problem rather than debate it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer makes three moves. First, it explains that two years of correct behaviour is evidence about the *browser*, not about the server, because the sharing scope changes with the environment while the code does not. Second, it names the consequence in security terms — one dispatcher's draft manifest appearing in another dispatcher's page — rather than as a correctness annoyance, because that framing changes how the ticket is prioritised. Third, and most usefully, it proposes a demonstration instead of an argument: fire two concurrent requests with different user identities against the module-level store and show the crossover, then repeat with per-request creation. The demonstration matters more than the explanation here, because the defect is load-dependent and therefore easy to disbelieve. A very good answer adds that quiet staging traffic may never reproduce it, so 'we tested and it was fine' is not evidence either.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this argument?

workedExamples.problem:
**Case study — the depot console that leaked between dispatchers.**

A parcel depot ran a dispatch console used by 40 dispatchers across three sites. The console was client-rendered for two years without incident. The team added server rendering to improve first paint on the warehouse tablets. Within a week, a dispatcher at the Leeds site reported seeing a half-completed manifest belonging to a dispatcher in Bristol. It happened perhaps once a day, could not be reproduced on demand, and had not appeared at all during two weeks of staging. Work out what happened.
steps: Establish what changed. The application code did not change; only the execution environment did. That immediately makes environment-dependent behaviour the leading hypothesis, and it rules out the recent feature work everyone was suspicious of.
Look for state whose sharing scope depends on the environment. The team found `export const draftStore = createDraftStore()` at the top of a module — created once when the module is first imported.

Apply the rule. In a browser, that module is evaluated once per tab, so each dispatcher had their own `draftStore`. On the server, it is evaluated once per Node process, and one process serves many requests. Every dispatcher rendered by that process shared one store.

Explain the intermittency. A leak only becomes visible when two dispatchers are served by the same process closely enough in time that one's draft is still in the store when the other's page renders. That requires concurrency, which is why it appeared roughly once a day in production and never in staging.

Explain why testing missed it. Staging received a handful of requests per hour from one or two testers, usually sequentially. The condition for the defect — concurrent requests from different users in one process — essentially never occurred.

Confirm the diagnosis by reproducing it deliberately. The team wrote a script issuing two simultaneous render requests with different user identities and asserted that neither response contained the other's data. It failed immediately, which converted an intermittent field report into a deterministic test.
Fix it by creating the store per request and passing it down through the request context, so no two requests can reach the same instance.

Audit for the same pattern elsewhere. The team searched for mutable values at module scope and found three more: a memoised permissions lookup, a request cache, and a module-level `let currentUser` used by a logging helper. All three were leaks of the same kind, and none had caused a visible report yet.
workedExamples.conclusion: The defect was invisible for two years because the environment guaranteed isolation for free, and it appeared the moment that guarantee was withdrawn. Three transferable lessons. **First, 'it has always worked' is evidence about one environment only** — when the environment changes, every assumption the environment was silently enforcing must be re-checked. **Second, the reproduction is the deliverable.** An intermittent field report is nearly impossible to act on; a failing two-request script is a ticket anyone can pick up and verify. **Third, one instance of this pattern predicts others.** The audit found three more leaks with no reports attached, which is the normal ratio: reported defects of this class are a small sample of the ones present, because most of them leak data nobody happens to recognise.

retrievalPractice.prompt: How many times is a module's top-level code evaluated, and what determines the scope of sharing?
Why is a `Map` created at module level a safe per-user cache in a browser and a cross-user data leak on a server? Name the single fact that differs.
You are reviewing a pull request that adds `export const featureFlagCache = new Map()` to a module in a server-rendered application. What do you ask, and what would you accept as a fix?

transferExercises.context: Hospital medication administration — a different domain from the depot examples used in this section.
transferExercises.scenario: A ward medication app lets nurses scan a patient wristband and then scan a drug barcode. The two scans call different services. The app has run on ward tablets for three years. The hospital is now adding a server-rendered summary view so that the first screen appears instantly on slow ward Wi-Fi. Within days, a nurse reports seeing the previous patient's allergy list on the summary screen. It happens rarely, and the ward's test environment has never reproduced it.
transferExercises.task: Write a diagnosis and a plan. Name at least two distinct mechanisms from this section that could produce this symptom, and say what evidence would distinguish them. Then, for whichever mechanism you consider most likely given that the symptom appeared only after server rendering was introduced, describe the demonstration you would build to make it reproducible, and the fix. Finally, state what else you would audit once the first instance is confirmed, and why the audit is likely to find more.
successCriteria: Names module-level state shared across requests as a candidate mechanism, and explains why the timing of the report points at it

Names at least one alternative mechanism — a stale closure capturing an earlier patient, or an unchecked response status returning stale or error data — and states what evidence would separate it from the first
Explains why the defect is intermittent by referring to concurrency, and why a low-traffic test environment does not reproduce it
Describes a concrete reproduction using two simultaneous requests with different patient identities, with an assertion that neither response contains the other's data
Prescribes per-request creation of the shared state rather than clearing it between requests or keying it by patient ID
States that the codebase should be audited for other mutable values at module scope, and explains that reported instances of this class are a small sample of those present
Frames the consequence in patient-safety and data-protection terms rather than as a rendering inconsistency

learningExperiences.title: Where errors go, and where they do not

options: `showError` runs, because the 500 status causes the fetch promise to reject
`renderManifest` runs with the error body treated as a manifest, because fetch resolves on error statuses
`res.json()` throws, so `showError` runs
The promise never settles and the screen stays on its loading state

optionFeedback.feedback: `fetch` rejects only when the network request itself fails — no connection, DNS failure, CORS block. A 500 is a completed HTTP exchange from the browser's point of view, so the promise resolves normally.

Correct, and this is why the defect is so durable: the `catch` block exists, looks correct in review, and simply never runs. `renderManifest` receives `{ error: 'database unavailable' }` and renders whatever that produces — usually blanks or `undefined`.

The body is valid JSON, so parsing succeeds without complaint. It is just not a manifest. `res.json()` would only throw if the body were not parseable, which is a different failure worth handling separately.
The promise settles normally with a response object. A permanently pending promise would indicate a network stall, which produces a different symptom.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two things make this worth memorising. First, the symptom is not an error message but **wrong content**, which means it is reported as a rendering bug rather than as a failed request. Second, the fix belongs in one shared place: a fetch wrapper that checks `res.ok` and throws a typed error carrying the status. Adding the check at each call site guarantees that someone will forget it.
hints: What does `fetch` consider a failure? Is a completed request with a 500 response a failure by that definition?

interactionSequence.prompt: A component is wrapped in an error boundary. It throws from three places: during render, inside an `onClick` handler, and inside a `setTimeout` callback. Which does the boundary catch?
options: All three, because all three originate inside the component
Only the render error; handlers and timers run outside React's render call stack
The render error and the click handler, but not the timer
Only the timer, because asynchronous errors are what boundaries are designed for

optionFeedback.feedback: Boundaries catch errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. The other two escape to the global handler, where nothing is listening unless you added a listener.

Correct. Handle the click error with `try`/`catch` inside the handler, and the timer error inside its callback, backed by a global `unhandledrejection` listener so missed rejections become visible rather than silent.
Event handlers are outside the boundary's reach as well. React does not invoke handlers inside the boundary's error path, which surprises most people the first time.
This inverts the rule exactly. The timer callback is the furthest of the three from anything the boundary can see.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The reliable way to remember this: a boundary catches what React itself called. React calls your render function, so it can wrap that call. React does not call your `setTimeout` callback — the runtime does — and it does not wrap handler invocation in the boundary's error path either. Anything React did not call is your responsibility to catch.
hints: Which of the three does React itself invoke?

steps: Check whether the promise is awaited. `submitDispatch(draft)` returns a promise that is never awaited, so any rejection escapes the `try` block entirely and becomes an unhandled rejection. The `catch` is unreachable for the failure it was written for.

Check what the `catch` does if it ever runs. It is empty. An empty catch converts a loud failure into a silent one, which is strictly worse than no `try` at all, because at least an uncaught error appears in the console and in error reporting.
Check the ordering of the success message. `setStatus('dispatched')` runs immediately after the call is made, not after it succeeds. So the status is set even when the dispatch fails.

Name the user-visible consequence of the current code: **a failed dispatch displays as dispatched**. The parcel is not on a van, and nobody has any reason to look again. This is the most serious defect of the three, and it is caused by the combination rather than by any single line.

State what the user now sees in each case. On success: 'dispatching', then 'dispatched'. On a rejected promise: 'dispatching', then 'failed' with an explicit statement that the parcel was not assigned and a retry path. On an unexpected throw: the same failure path, and the error reaches the reporting service.

Note the remaining gap. If `submitDispatch` uses `fetch` internally without checking `res.ok`, a 500 response resolves successfully and this handler will still report success. The fix must reach into the fetch layer, not only the handler.
workedExamples.conclusion: Three defects, one mechanism: **each one converts a failure into a false success**. The missing `await` means the failure is never seen, the empty `catch` means it is never reported, and the unconditional status update means it is actively contradicted. Note the order of severity — the most damaging is not the missing error message but the wrong success message, because an error prompts a retry while a false success does not. And note the final step: fixing a handler is not enough if the layer beneath it is swallowing status codes, which is why the `ok` check belongs in one shared wrapper.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the four rules of error propagation from this section: what `try`/`catch` requires, what `fetch` does on a 500, what an error boundary does not catch, and what an empty catch block costs you.
Name three kinds of error a React error boundary will not catch, and say what handles each one instead.
A team reports that their error handling 'does not work' — the catch blocks never run even though the API is clearly failing. Give the two most likely causes and the check that distinguishes them.

learningExperiences.title: Reference equality and structural sharing

contentBlocks.content:
## Change is detected by reference

React, Redux, and memoisation all answer the question 'did this change?' by comparing **references** with `Object.is`. They do not compare contents.

If you change an object in place, its contents change but its identity does not. The comparison reports no change, and the render is skipped.

```js
parcels.push(newParcel);               // the same array reference — React sees no change
setParcels([...parcels, newParcel]);   // a new reference — React re-renders
```

## Structural sharing makes this cheap

The objection people raise is cost: surely copying is wasteful? It is not, because the new array reuses every element that did not change. You copy one level, not the whole data tree.

Updating one field of one parcel in a list of 5,000 creates one new array, one new parcel object, and reuses 4,999 existing objects untouched. That is **structural sharing**.

## Two operators worth knowing

Optional chaining (`?.`) returns `undefined` instead of throwing when part of a path is missing. Nullish coalescing (`??`) uses the fallback value only for `null` and `undefined` — unlike `||`, which also replaces `0` and `''`.

```js
const count = data?.summary?.scanned ?? 0;   // a real 0 stays 0
const label = bay.nickname || 'Unnamed';     // an empty string becomes 'Unnamed' — often a bug
```

This matters more than it looks in a depot context, where `0` parcels scanned and `0` failed scans are both meaningful values that `||` would quietly replace.

options: React batches the update, so it will appear on the next render
The array reference did not change, so React's comparison reports no change and skips the re-render
Nested objects need a deep clone before any update will register
`setRows` must be called with a function rather than a value

optionFeedback.feedback: Batching groups updates that occur within the same event; it does not defer them indefinitely. Here no update is registered at all, because React concluded nothing changed.

Correct. React compares with `Object.is`. The mutation changed the array's contents but not its identity, so the comparison sees the same array. Produce a new array containing a new object for the changed row.
A deep clone would work, and it is wasteful and unnecessary. Structural sharing means copying only the path to the change — the array and the one row object — and reusing everything else.
The functional form solves stale-closure problems, not identity problems. Passing `prev => { prev[2].status = 'loaded'; return prev; }` would fail in exactly the same way.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is one idea you will meet in five costumes across this course. It is the re-render decision here and in Section 3. It is selector memoisation in Section 6 and the `useShallow` rule for lightweight stores. It is the blast-radius diagnosis in Section 9. Each time, the underlying question is the same: **did the reference change?** Learning it once as a mechanism, rather than five times as five library rules, is the point of grouping them.
hints: What does `Object.is(oldArray, newArray)` return here?
Did the array's identity change, or only its contents?

interactionSequence.prompt: A depot summary shows `bay.scannedCount || '—'`. Bay 4 has genuinely scanned zero parcels and displays `—`. What is the correct fix, and what does the current code communicate?
options: Use `bay.scannedCount ?? '—'`, since `??` falls back only on `null` and `undefined`, so a real zero displays as zero
Use `bay.scannedCount != null ? bay.scannedCount : '—'`, since `??` is unsupported in production browsers
Leave it; displaying `—` for zero is a reasonable design choice
Use `String(bay.scannedCount) || '—'`, which converts the zero to a truthy string first

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. `||` replaces every falsy value, including `0` and `''`. Here that means a bay with zero scans is indistinguishable from a bay with no data at all — two states with very different operational meanings.
The logic is correct and equivalent, but the premise is not: `??` is supported across all current browsers. Prefer the shorter form; the explicit null check is only needed for older build targets.

It conflates 'zero parcels scanned' with 'no information available'. In a depot those mean different things — one is a bay running behind, the other is a scanner that is offline — and the display cannot distinguish them.
This works by accident, because `'0'` is a truthy string. It is fragile, obscures the intent, and breaks the moment someone removes the conversion during a refactor.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The rule worth carrying: use `||` for fallbacks where every falsy value should be replaced, and `??` wherever `0`, `''`, or `false` are legitimate values. In domains that count things — parcels, doses, transactions, errors — zero is nearly always legitimate, so `??` is the safer default and `||` is the one that needs justifying.
hints: Which values does `||` treat as absent, and is zero one of them?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words, explain to a colleague why copying an array to update one item is not as expensive as it sounds. Use a concrete number, and say what is actually reused.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong explanation names structural sharing and quantifies it: updating one parcel in a list of 5,000 creates one new array and one new parcel object, and the other 4,999 objects are the same objects, referenced from the new array. Nothing is deep-copied. The cost is proportional to the depth of the path you changed, not to the size of the data. A very good answer adds the reason this design is worth its cost: because unchanged branches keep their identity, any consumer comparing references can skip work for every part of the tree that did not change — which is the same property memoised selectors and `React.memo` rely on later in the course.

steps: Identify the path from the root to the value being changed: `state` → `state.bays` → the bay with id `B-02` → that bay's `parcels` array → the parcel with id `P-4417` → its `status` field. Five levels.
Apply the rule: **every object on that path gets a new identity, and nothing else does.** That is five new objects in total, regardless of how much data hangs off the tree.

Write the update from the inside out. The new parcel object:

```js
const newParcel = { ...oldParcel, status: 'loaded' };
```

The new parcels array for that bay, replacing only the matching element and reusing the other 199 objects by reference:

```js
const newParcels = bay.parcels.map(p => p.id === 'P-4417' ? newParcel : p);
```

The new bay object, reusing everything except the parcels array:

```js
const newBay = { ...bay, parcels: newParcels };
```

The new bays array, replacing only `B-02` and reusing `B-01` and `B-03` by reference:

```js
const newBays = state.bays.map(b => b.id === 'B-02' ? newBay : b);
```

The new root:

```js
const newState = { ...state, bays: newBays };
```

Count what changed. New objects: `newState`, `newBays`, `newBay`, `newParcels`, `newParcel` — five. Reused by reference: 599 parcel objects, two bay objects, two parcel arrays, and the `depotId` string. Nothing was deep-copied.

Verify the consequences. `Object.is(state, newState)` is `false`, so React re-renders. `Object.is(state.bays[0], newState.bays[0])` is `true`, so anything comparing bay `B-01` by reference can skip its work entirely.
workedExamples.conclusion: Five new objects updated a tree containing more than six hundred. That ratio is the whole argument for structural sharing: **the cost of an immutable update is proportional to the depth of the change, not to the size of the data.** And the second half of the conclusion is the more useful one — because unchanged branches keep their identity, every consumer that compares by reference gets to skip work for the parts that did not change. Mutation would have been marginally cheaper to write and would have destroyed that property for the entire tree, which is exactly the trade this design refuses to make.

retrievalPractice.prompt: You changed a value in state and nothing re-rendered. What is the first thing to check, and what function does React use to make that decision?
Updating one field of one item in a list of 5,000 — how many new objects are created, and what is reused? Explain what property that reuse preserves for consumers downstream.
When would `||` be the right operator for a fallback, and when would `??`? Give one value that behaves differently under the two, and a domain where that difference is dangerous.

learningExperiences.title: The shape of the application, and holding that shape

contentBlocks.content:
## Five layers, one direction

Use five layers. Each layer may depend only on the layers below it.

**Routes and pages → features → shared components → domain logic → infrastructure (API, storage).**

Organise folders by **feature**, not by file type. A folder such as `features/manifests/` should contain that feature's components, hooks, store slice, and types. This is better than separate `components/`, `hooks/`, and `store/` folders, which spread every feature across four places.

## The one rule that keeps it working

**A feature may import from `shared/`, but never from another feature's internal files.**

If two features need the same thing, either export it explicitly through the feature's public entry point, or move it down into `shared/`.

## Enforce it with a machine

Use a lint rule such as `import/no-restricted-paths`. Do not rely on a team agreement.

Agreements depend on every reviewer noticing every time, in every diff, under deadline pressure. They weaken with team turnover and with the size of the pull request. Lint rules do not weaken. This is the same argument that Section 10 makes about blocking CI gates, applied to architecture rather than to quality checks.

## Key terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Event loop** | Empties all microtasks, runs one macrotask, then repeats. |
| **Microtask / macrotask** | Promise callbacks / timers, input-output, and DOM events. |
| **Closure** | A function plus the scope where it was created. It captures bindings, not values. |
| **Binding** | The storage location for a variable. |
| **Temporal dead zone** | The period where a `let` or `const` variable exists but cannot be read yet. |
| **Module evaluation** | Happens once per context. Module scope is a singleton for that context. |
| **Singleton** | One shared instance for the whole context. |
| **Unhandled rejection** | A rejected promise that nobody awaited or caught. |
| **`response.ok`** | The check that `fetch` requires, because it does not reject on 4xx or 5xx. |
| **Error boundary** | Catches errors in render and lifecycle. Not events, timers, or async code. |
| **Reference equality (`Object.is`)** | How React decides that something changed. |
| **Structural sharing** | Copying only the part that changed and reusing everything else. |
| **`?.` / `??`** | Stop safely on a missing value / use a fallback only for `null` and `undefined`. |
| **Dependency direction** | Features import downward, never sideways. |

## ⚠️ Common errors

1. **Using `await` sequentially in a loop** for work that could run at the same time.
2. **Believing that `await` makes code parallel.**
3. **Reading an old value from a closure** and blaming React for it.
4. **Mutable state at module level.** Safe in a browser, a cross-user leak on a server.
5. **Side effects at module level** that run as soon as the file is imported.
6. **Using `try`/`catch` around a promise you did not await.**
7. **Not checking `response.ok`.**
8. **Expecting an error boundary to catch an event handler error or an async error.**
9. **Empty `catch` blocks** that turn failures into wrong answers.
10. **Changing state in place** and then wondering why nothing re-rendered.
11. **Using `||` where `??` is correct**, which replaces valid `0` and `''` values.
12. **Organising folders by file type**, so one small change touches eleven files.
13. **Relying on a team agreement** to hold a structural rule that a lint rule could enforce.

## Summary

- One thread, two queues. Microtasks are emptied fully before the next macrotask. An async function body runs immediately until the first `await`.
- `await` gives back control. It does not create parallelism. Start independent work together, then wait for all of it.
- Closures capture **bindings**. `let` creates a new binding per loop iteration. `var` does not.
- **Modules are evaluated once per context.** This is safe in a browser tab and dangerous on a server.
- `try`/`catch` needs `await`. `fetch` needs an `ok` check. Error boundaries do not catch events or async errors.
- React detects change by **reference**, so copy instead of mutating. Structural sharing keeps copying cheap.
- Layer the application and **enforce dependency direction with a lint rule**, not with an agreement.

interactionSequence.prompt: A depot console is organised by file type. Adding one column to the manifest table requires editing eleven files across four folders. A colleague proposes reorganising by feature. What is the strongest argument, and what must accompany the change?
options: Feature folders are the current convention, and consistency with the wider ecosystem has value
A change to one feature should touch one folder; the reorganisation must be accompanied by a lint rule preventing features from importing each other's internals
Feature folders reduce the total number of files in the project
Feature folders improve build performance by grouping related modules

optionFeedback.feedback: Convention is a weak argument on its own, and it does not tell you what to do when the convention is ambiguous. Locality of change is the reason the convention exists.
Correct on both halves. The reorganisation delivers locality, and the lint rule is what stops the structure decaying into a folder layout with the same tangled dependencies it replaced.
The file count is roughly unchanged; the files are grouped differently. What changes is how many of them one task touches.
Build tooling resolves modules by graph, not by folder proximity, so grouping has little effect on build time.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The second half of the answer is the part teams skip, and skipping it is why 'we tried feature folders and it did not help' is a common report. Without an enforced dependency direction, features quietly import each other's internals within weeks, and you end up with the old coupling wearing a new folder structure. The rule is the change; the folders are just where it becomes visible.
hints: What prevents the new structure from decaying back into the old one within six months?

interactionSequence.prompt: Think about a codebase you work in now. Where does a typical small change land — one folder, or several? If several, name one rule that, if it had been enforced from the start, would have reduced that number.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The number of folders a small change touches is one of the cheapest available proxies for structural health, and you can measure it this week without changing anything. The most common answers are a dependency-direction rule, a rule about where shared code lives, or a rule that a feature exposes a single public entry point. Notice that all three are rules about **imports** rather than about folders — the folder layout follows from the rule, not the other way round, which is why reorganising folders without adding a rule tends not to hold.

workedExamples.problem: The depot console has `features/manifests/` and `features/routing/`. A developer needs the manifest formatting helper inside the routing feature, and writes `import { formatManifestLine } from '../../manifests/utils/format'`. The lint rule rejects it. Work out the correct resolution.
steps: Confirm the rule that was broken: a feature may not import another feature's **internal** files. The import reaches into `manifests/utils/`, which is internal by construction.

Ask the first question: is this helper genuinely part of the manifests feature, or is it general-purpose code that happens to live there? Read what it does. If it formats a manifest line using manifest-specific domain rules, it belongs to manifests. If it just pads and joins strings, it is generic and misfiled.

Take the generic case first. If the helper is not manifest-specific, move it down to `shared/formatting/`. Both features may then import it legally, and the dependency direction is preserved because both are importing downward.

Take the domain-specific case. If the helper really is manifest logic, decide whether routing should depend on manifests at all. Sometimes the answer is that it should, in which case manifests must export it deliberately through its public entry point — `features/manifests/index.ts` — and the lint configuration permits imports from that path only.

Consider the third possibility, which is often the correct one and is easy to miss: routing does not need manifest logic, and the requirement is a sign that a concept is missing. Perhaps both features need a shared notion of a 'consignment line' that belongs in domain logic, below both of them.

Whichever resolution applies, record it. A one-line comment in the feature's entry point, or an entry in a decision record, explains to the next person why this particular export is public while its neighbours are not.
workedExamples.conclusion: The lint rule did not merely block an import; it forced a design question that would otherwise have been answered by accident. Notice the three resolutions and what distinguishes them: **move it down** when the code is general, **export it deliberately** when the dependency is real and intended, and **introduce the missing concept** when the requirement reveals that two features are reaching for something neither of them owns. An unenforced agreement would have produced none of these conversations — the developer would have written the deep import, the reviewer would probably have approved it, and the coupling would have been discovered eighteen months later when someone tried to delete the manifests feature.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the five layers and the single rule about imports between features. Then say why the rule is enforced by lint rather than by agreement.
A feature needs a helper that lives inside another feature. Give the three possible resolutions and say what distinguishes them.

learningExperiences.title: Practical activity: prove each mechanism yourself

contentBlocks.content:
## Why do this rather than read it again

Every item below asks you to **predict first, then run, then explain any difference**. That order matters. A prediction you got wrong is worth more than three correct readings, because it tells you precisely where your model of the runtime diverges from the runtime's actual behaviour.

Work in a scratch project or a browser console. No framework is needed for most of it.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: You are building a small scratch harness that reproduces, in isolation, the five mechanisms responsible for most defects that get misfiled as React bugs. Everything here maps directly onto something you will meet in a real codebase within a month of joining one.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Demonstrate each mechanism from this section with your own running code, so that you can recognise the symptom in unfamiliar code rather than only recognise the explanation on a page.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A browser with developer tools, or Node 18 or later
A scratch folder — no framework or build tooling required for items 1 to 6
Optional for item 6: any small React setup, or read the described behaviour if you have none available
instructions: **1. Ordering.** Write down your predicted output of the six-line ordering example from the first experience before running it. Run it. If the actual output differs from your prediction, write one sentence naming the rule you had wrong. Do not skip the writing step.

**2. Concurrency.** Write a loader that fetches three endpoints sequentially with `await`, logging a timestamp immediately before each call. Note the gaps between the start times. Convert it to `Promise.all` and re-run. Record both total durations and both sets of start-time gaps. Then answer in one sentence: which number proves the mechanism, the total or the gaps?

**3. Concurrency, error behaviour.** Make one of the three endpoints fail. Observe what `Promise.all` returns. Switch to `Promise.allSettled` and observe the difference. Write one sentence on which you would choose for a screen that can usefully display two of three results.

**4. Closures.** Write a loop using `var` that schedules three timeouts logging the loop variable. Predict, then run. Change `var` to `let` and run again. Then write a version that prints the intended values while still using `var`, and explain in one sentence what your fix actually did.

**5. Modules.** Create a module exporting `new Map()` and a `console.log` at the top level. Import it from two separate files. Write to the Map from one file and read from the other. Record how many times the log line printed and what the second file read. Write one sentence explaining what would change if this ran in a server process handling two users at once.

**6. Error propagation.** Write a `fetch` wrapper and point it at an endpoint returning 500 with a JSON body. Show that your `catch` block does not run and that your success path receives the error body. Then add an `res.ok` check that throws, and confirm the `catch` now runs. If you have a React setup available, additionally throw from an `onClick` handler inside an error boundary and confirm the boundary does not catch it.

**7. Immutability.** Build a nested structure of at least three levels. Update one leaf value by mutation and log `Object.is(before, after)` on the root. Then update the same value immutably and log it again. Count how many objects you created in the second version, and how many you reused.

**8. Nullish handling.** Display a counted value that is legitimately zero using `||` and then using `??`. Record what each displays, and name one field in a system you have worked on where this distinction would have mattered.
reflectionPrompts: Which prediction were you most confident about and still got wrong? That gap is the most valuable single finding in this activity — what specifically was your model doing differently from the runtime?
Item 5 asked you to imagine a server context you probably did not run. How convinced are you by that reasoning without having seen it fail? If you are not fully convinced, what would convince you?
Of the mechanisms here, which do you think you are most likely to encounter first in real code, and what would the symptom look like from a user's point of view rather than from the code's?
Item 2 asked which number proves the mechanism. If a colleague showed you only a total duration improvement, what alternative explanations would still be open?

selfAssessmentCriteria: I wrote each prediction down before running the code, rather than after
For every prediction that was wrong, I wrote one sentence naming the rule I had misunderstood
Item 2 records both total durations and the start-time gaps, and I can say which of the two actually demonstrates the mechanism
Item 4 includes a working `var` version, and I can explain what my fix changed about the binding
Item 5 records the number of times the module-level log printed, and I can state the sharing scope in both environments
Item 6 demonstrates the silent success path before the `ok` check was added, not only the corrected version
Item 7 records a count of created and reused objects, not just working code

retrievalPractice.prompt: From memory, list the five mechanisms this section covered that commonly produce defects misfiled as React bugs.

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Check your understanding

Answer without scrolling back. Retrieval that feels effortful is the retrieval that lasts; looking up the answer first feels better and teaches less.

Three true/false questions, then three short-answer questions.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** `await` inside a `for` loop runs the requests at the same time.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Each `await` suspends the function until the previous request settles, so the next request is not even created yet. Start independent work together and await the aggregate with `Promise.all`.
Correct. The loop is strictly sequential. Concurrency comes from when the work starts, not from how you wait for it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The measurement that settles this in ten seconds: log a timestamp at the start of each request. Sequential requests start one latency apart and produce a staircase in the Network tab; concurrent ones start milliseconds apart and produce a block.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** `fetch` rejects its promise when the server returns 500.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. `fetch` rejects only when the network request itself fails. A 500 is a completed HTTP exchange, so the promise resolves and your success path runs with the error body.
Correct. You must check `response.ok` yourself, ideally in one shared wrapper that throws a typed error carrying the status.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Remember the shape of this defect: it presents as wrong content rather than as an error, so it gets reported as a rendering bug. That misdirection is why it survives so long in codebases.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** A `Map` created at module level is a per-user cache in a browser, and also on a server.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It is per-user in a browser because each user has their own tab and therefore their own context. On a server, one process serves many users' requests in one context, so the Map is shared between them — a cross-user data leak.
Correct. Module scope is per-context, and what a context contains depends entirely on the environment. Create per-request instances when server rendering.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the answer to the prediction you wrote at the start of the section. The code never changes; only the sharing scope does. That is why the defect passes review — the reviewer is mentally running it in a browser.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Explain what a closure captures. Then give the practical consequence for a `for` loop that uses `var` to schedule deferred callbacks.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** A closure captures the *binding* — the storage location — not the value at the moment of creation. So it reads whatever that location holds when the closure eventually runs, including changes made after the closure was created. With `var`, every iteration of the loop shares one binding, so all the deferred callbacks read the same location, and by the time any of them runs the loop has finished and left its final value there. With `let`, each iteration gets its own binding, so each callback reads its own iteration's value. **Accept** answers that use different wording for 'binding' — storage slot, variable reference, memory location — provided the distinction from 'value' is clear. **Reject** answers saying the closure 'copies' or 'remembers' the value, which is the model this question exists to correct.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Name three kinds of error a React error boundary will not catch, and say what handles each one instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** (1) Errors in **event handlers** — handle with `try`/`catch` inside the handler itself. (2) Errors in **timers and other scheduled callbacks**, such as `setTimeout` — handle inside the callback. (3) Errors in **async code**, including rejected promises — handle with `try`/`catch` around the `await`, backed by a global `unhandledrejection` listener so anything missed is reported rather than silent. Boundaries cover render, lifecycle methods, and constructors only. **Accept** 'errors thrown after the component has rendered' as a rough grouping if the three specific mechanisms and their handling are named. **Reject** answers that name only the categories without saying what handles each, since the practical value is in the second half.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A colleague updates one field of one item in a 5,000-item list by copying rather than mutating, and objects that this must be wasteful. Answer them. Include a count, and state what property the copying preserves that mutation would destroy.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** The update creates a new array and a new object for the changed item — two new objects in a flat list, or one per level of nesting on the path to the change. The other 4,999 items are not copied at all; they are the same objects, referenced from the new array. This is structural sharing, and it means the cost is proportional to the *depth* of the change rather than the *size* of the data. The property it preserves is identity for everything that did not change: because unchanged branches keep their references, any consumer comparing by reference — React's re-render decision, a memoised selector, a shallow-comparing store subscription — can skip work for those branches entirely. Mutation would be marginally cheaper to write and would destroy that property for the whole tree, because nothing downstream could tell what had changed. **Accept** any correct count with the reuse explained. **Reject** answers that only assert 'it is fast enough' without naming structural sharing or the identity property, since the second half is the actual argument.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

retrievalPractice.prompt: Recall the seven summary claims of this section without looking: the two queues, what `await` does, what closures capture, how often modules evaluate, the three error rules, how change is detected, and how structure is held.

transferExercises.context: Concert ticketing platform — a different domain from both the depot examples and the hospital transfer above.
transferExercises.scenario: A ticketing platform releases seats for a large venue at a fixed time. In the sixty seconds after release, three defects are reported. First, the seat map takes eleven seconds to appear for some users, though the API responds in under 300 ms per request and the map has 40 seating blocks. Second, the 'seats remaining' counter on the header freezes at whatever number it showed when the page loaded, while the seat map itself updates correctly. Third, several users complete a purchase and see a confirmation screen, but no ticket is issued and no error is recorded anywhere.
transferExercises.task: Diagnose all three defects using only the mechanisms from this section. For each one: name the mechanism, state the specific evidence you would gather to confirm it before changing any code, describe the fix, and explain how you would prevent the same class of defect from recurring across the codebase rather than only at this site. Then rank the three by severity and justify your ranking — noting that the ranking is not the same as ranking them by how loudly they were reported.
successCriteria: Identifies the eleven-second load as accidentally sequential requests across the 40 blocks, and proposes concurrent loading with an explicit decision between `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled`
Names the evidence for the first defect as request start timestamps or the staircase shape in the Network waterfall, rather than the total duration alone

Identifies the frozen counter as a stale closure — a callback created once reading a binding that is recreated on each update — and distinguishes 'consistently stale' from 'occasionally stale' as the diagnostic signature
Proposes a fix for the counter that removes the lifetime mismatch, such as reading through a function or a ref, or recreating the subscription when its dependency changes

Identifies the silent failed purchase as some combination of an unchecked `response.ok`, an un-awaited promise, and an unconditional success message, and explains that the success path ran with an error body or before any result existed
Names the fix for the third defect as a shared fetch wrapper that checks `ok` and throws a typed error, plus awaiting the call and setting the confirmation only on success
Proposes at least one systemic prevention: a shared fetch wrapper, a global `unhandledrejection` listener, or a lint rule against empty catch blocks and un-awaited promises

Ranks the silent failed purchase as most severe, with a justification based on a false success removing the user's reason to retry, and explicitly notes that it was the least loudly reported of the three

sections.title: TypeScript for React: Modelling Data So Wrong States Cannot Be Written
sections.description: The point of types here is not to satisfy a compiler. It is to make invalid states impossible to write, so that the reviewer, the editor, and the build all catch a class of defect before any test has to. Two techniques carry most of the value: discriminated unions, which remove impossible combinations from your domain model, and validating data where it enters the application, which moves failures from three components downstream back to the boundary that caused them. Branded types and `satisfies` close the remaining gaps. All examples come from a clinical pathology laboratory that tracks specimens.

learningObjectives.description: Convert a model built from optional fields into a discriminated union, and explain which impossible states the conversion removed.
Add an exhaustiveness check with a `never` assignment, and explain how it converts a backend change into a compile-time task list.
Validate external data at the boundary and derive the TypeScript type from the validator, so the two cannot drift apart.
Distinguish `unknown` from `any`, and predict how an explicit `any` propagates through a codebase over time.
Apply branded types to identifiers that share a primitive type, and mint branded values at the validation boundary rather than by scattered casts.
Choose correctly between a type annotation, an `as` cast, and `satisfies`, and predict what each does to the inferred type.
Configure `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and judge whether the resulting errors represent real latent defects.

motivationHooks.prompt: A pathology console modelled a specimen result with a `status` string and three optional fields, then called `value.toFixed(2)` whenever the status was not `'failed'`. The backend team added a fourth status, `cancelled`, which carries no value. The results grid crashed for every cancelled specimen, in production, for the users least able to work around it. The change that caused this was one word in a backend enum. With a discriminated union and an exhaustiveness check, that same change would have produced compile errors in eleven files before anyone ran the code.

Write this down before reading on. An interface has a `status: string` field plus three optional fields: `value`, `error`, and `isLoading`. **How many distinct combinations of those fields does that interface permit?** Now write down how many states your domain actually has. Keep both numbers. The gap between them is not a rounding error — it is the surface area every consumer of that type has to defend against, and you will calculate it exactly at the end of this section.

Here is a line that appears in almost every React codebase: `const user = await res.json() as User`. It compiles. It passes review. It has type annotations. And it provides **exactly zero** protection against the server returning something different. Why does a language built to catch type errors accept this one without complaint — and what should be written instead?

Return to your two numbers. With `status: string` there are infinitely many status values, but hold `status` aside and count only the three optional fields: each is present or absent, giving **2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations**, multiplied by every possible string. Your domain has **four** states. So the type permits at least eight shapes where four are meaningful, and it permits nonsense such as a result that is simultaneously loading, failed, and complete — or a `'complete'` result with no value at all, which is exactly the crash described in the opening. A discriminated union permits four shapes and no others. That is the whole argument, and everything else in this section is a refinement of it.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about typing a React application.

**Types are a modelling tool before they are a checking tool.** Their highest value is making invalid states unwritable, which removes defects rather than detecting them.

**Optional fields cannot express a state machine.** They say which fields may be absent individually, not which combinations are legal, so every consumer inherits the job of defending against nonsense.

**A discriminated union plus a `never` assignment converts a backend change into a task list.** When a new variant appears, the compiler names every site that must handle it, at build time, for the developer who caused it — rather than at runtime, in production, for one affected user.

**External data is `unknown` whatever the annotation says.** A cast is a claim the compiler agrees to stop checking; validation is a check that actually runs. Validate once at the boundary and derive the type from the validator.

**`any` is not local.** It propagates through derived expressions and return values, disabling checks at sites nobody connects to the original annotation. `unknown` gives the same freedom without the contagion.

**Brand identifiers that share a primitive type.** Two IDs both typed `string` will eventually be swapped, and the compiler cannot help unless you make them distinct.

**`satisfies` checks without widening; an annotation widens; `as` suppresses.** Knowing which you want is the difference between keeping your inference and losing it.
keyTakeaways: Model with discriminated unions so each variant carries only its own fields.
Add a `never` assignment in the default branch so new variants break the build everywhere they must be handled.
Validate external data at the boundary, and derive the type with `z.infer` rather than writing a parallel interface.
A cast asserts and checks nothing; validation checks and can fail loudly at the edge.
Prefer `unknown` to `any`, because `any` spreads silently through everything it touches.
Brand identifiers that share a primitive type, and mint branded values at the parse boundary.
`satisfies` constrains a value while preserving its narrow inferred type.
Turn on `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`; the second one finds real defects teams routinely skip.

furtherReading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing
furtherReading.author: TypeScript team
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Read the sections on discriminated unions and exhaustiveness checking. The `never` technique is presented here as a language feature rather than as a pattern, which is worth seeing — it explains why the compiler behaves the way it does rather than just that it does.

furtherReading.title: Zod: Basic usage and type inference
furtherReading.author: Colin McDonnell and contributors
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Focus on `infer`, `safeParse`, and `discriminatedUnion`. The boundary pattern in this section is three lines of Zod, and the documentation is short enough to read in one sitting rather than sampled through search results.

furtherReading.title: The satisfies operator
furtherReading.citation: Pocock, M. Clarifying the satisfies operator.
furtherReading.author: Matt Pocock
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Short, and it settles the annotation-versus-cast-versus-satisfies question with side-by-side examples. Read it if the distinction in this section felt like three similar things rather than three different ones.

furtherReading.title: Parse, don't validate
furtherReading.author: Alexis King
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Written for Haskell but the argument is language-independent and it is the clearest statement of why boundary validation is a design principle rather than a defensive habit. The core idea — that parsing returns a more precise type while validating returns only a yes or no — reframes the whole section.

furtherReading.author: TypeScript team
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The rationale here is more persuasive than the compiler-options reference. It explains why `array[i]` returning `T | undefined` is the honest type, which is the argument you will need when a colleague asks why the build suddenly has forty new errors.

furtherReading.author: Egghead
furtherReading.rationaleNote: A practical walkthrough of the brand pattern including where to mint branded values. Useful if you want to see the technique applied across a whole client rather than in the isolated examples used here.
