learningExperiences.title: Render, reconcile, commit — and what actually triggers a re-render

contentBlocks.content:
## Three separate things

React does three things, and people often treat them as one. That conflation causes most confusion about performance.

1. **Render** — React calls your component function to produce a description of the UI. This is pure. It touches no DOM.
2. **Reconcile** — React compares the new description with the previous one.
3. **Commit** — React applies the differences to the real DOM, then runs effects.

**A re-render is not a DOM update.** A component can re-render and produce exactly the same output, in which case the commit does nothing at all.

Rendering is comparatively cheap. Commits are expensive, because that is where layout, style recalculation, and paint happen. Section 9 depends on this distinction: when a screen is slow, the first question is which of the three phases is costing the time, and the answer decides which fix applies.

interactionSequence.prompt: A `SeatMap` parent re-renders because a toggle changed. It renders three children — `SeatGrid`, `Legend`, and `FareSummary` — and none of their props changed. What happens?
options: None of the three re-render, because React compares props and skips children whose props are unchanged
All three re-render, but reconciliation finds no differences, so the commit does nothing to the DOM
All three re-render and all three update the DOM, since a render always produces DOM work
Only children that consume context re-render; the others are skipped

optionFeedback.feedback: React does not compare props by default. Doing so would require a comparison for every child on every render, so React makes the opposite choice: re-render children and let reconciliation find that nothing changed. `memo` opts into the comparison where it is worth paying for.

Correct on both counts, and the two counts are separate. Three renders happened — real JavaScript ran — and zero DOM updates followed. Holding both facts at once is what stops you misdiagnosing performance later.
Rendering produces a description of the UI. Only differences between the new and old descriptions reach the DOM, and here there are none.
Context is one of the four triggers, but a parent re-rendering is another, and it applies to all children regardless of what they consume.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The practical consequence: seeing many components in the profiler does not by itself mean you have a problem, and seeing few does not mean you do not. What matters is the **self time** of those renders and whether a commit followed. Section 9 turns this into a formal classification, but the habit starts here — always ask whether the cost you are looking at is render cost or commit cost.
hints: Does React compare a child's props before calling it?
What does the commit phase do when the new output matches the old?

interactionSequence.prompt: A component re-renders forty times per second and produces identical output every time. Where is the cost?
options: In the DOM, which is being written to forty times per second
In the render phase — your component function runs forty times — while the DOM cost is effectively zero
There is no cost at all, since React deduplicates identical renders
Entirely in the commit phase, since that is where effects run

optionFeedback.feedback: Nothing reaches the DOM, because reconciliation finds no differences. There is real cost here, but it is not DOM cost.

Correct. Forty function calls per second, plus whatever those functions compute, is worth knowing about — but the fix is different from a commit-cost fix, which is exactly why the distinction matters.
React does not deduplicate. Each render calls your component function, runs any computation inside it, and produces a fresh description to compare.
Effects do run after commit, but with identical output there are no DOM mutations and dependency arrays will typically prevent effects re-running. The recurring cost here is the render itself.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This distinction determines which of three fixes is right, and applying the wrong one wastes weeks. **Render cost from too many components** means reduce the number rendered — pagination or virtualization. **Render cost from one expensive computation** means move it out of render into a memoized derivation. **Render cost from components that need not have rendered** means fix state placement or narrow the subscription. Memoization only helps the third, which is why applying it to the first two feels like it should work and does not.
hints: What runs on a render, and what runs on a commit?

steps: Identify which state changed. Typing updates `query`, which lives in `CheckInPage`.
Apply trigger 1: `CheckInPage` re-renders because its own state changed. That is correct and unavoidable — something must render the new query value.
Apply trigger 3 to the children. `SeatMap`, `PassengerList`, and `FareSummary` all re-render because their parent re-rendered, even though `flight` did not change and their props are identical.
Follow it down. `SeatMap` renders 300 seat components, each of which re-renders for the same reason. That accounts for the 340.

Separate render cost from commit cost. Each of those renders produces output identical to the previous one, so reconciliation finds no differences and the commit does essentially nothing. The DOM is not being thrashed; your JavaScript is.

Consider the memoization fix and reject it as the first move. Wrapping `SeatMap` in `memo` would work, but it adds a props comparison on every render, must be maintained as props change, and treats a symptom: the state is simply in the wrong place.
Re-measure. Typing now re-renders `SearchSection` and its children only. The 300 seat components are untouched, because nothing above them changed.

Note the case where the state genuinely must live high — say the search result filters the passenger list. Then the composition fix applies instead: pass the expensive subtree as `children` so it is created by the parent that does not re-render, rather than by the one that does.
workedExamples.conclusion: Three hundred and forty renders, zero DOM updates, and the correct fix involved no memoization at all. Two lessons generalise. **The blast radius of a state change is determined by where the state lives**, which is why Section 6 treats placement as an architectural decision rather than a convenience. And **the first response to too many renders should be to ask why they are happening**, not to prevent them: memoization stops the renders while leaving the structural cause in place, so the next piece of state added at the same level recreates the problem.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the three phases React goes through, and state which of them touches the DOM.
List the four things that trigger a re-render. Which one do people most often forget, and what does forgetting it cause them to misdiagnose?
A keystroke causes 340 components to render but produces no DOM changes. Give two fixes that are better first moves than memoization, and say when each applies.

learningExperiences.title: Keys are a claim about identity

contentBlocks.content:
## What a key means

A `key` tells React: **this is the same conceptual item as before.** It is not a way to silence a warning. It is a claim, and React acts on it.

If the claim is wrong, React reuses the wrong component instance. The instance keeps its state — but the state is now attached to different data.

```tsx
{passengers.map((p, i) => <SeatRow key={i} passenger={p} />)}      // ✗
{passengers.map((p)    => <SeatRow key={p.id} passenger={p} />)}   // ✓
```

## Why index keys corrupt state

Delete the second of five passengers. Every later passenger shifts up one index. React sees that "item 1 still exists" and keeps the component instance that was previously showing passenger 2, now feeding it passenger 3's data.

That instance still holds its own local state: a half-typed meal preference, an open dropdown, a checked special-assistance box. All of it now belongs to a different passenger.

This is the most common data-corruption defect in React, and it has a specific property that makes it durable: **it only appears when the list changes order.** A test suite built on a fixed fixture will never trigger it, which is why it survives QA cycles.

contentBlocks.title: The same rule, used deliberately
contentBlocks.content:
Because a changed key discards the instance and its state, **changing a key on purpose is how you reset a subtree.**

```tsx
<SeatMap key={flightId} flight={flight} />
```

Every time `flightId` changes, React unmounts the old `SeatMap` and mounts a fresh one with clean state. No effect, no clearing logic, no risk of forgetting a field.

Compare that with the alternative: an effect watching `flightId` that resets six pieces of state. The effect version has a second render with stale values, has to be updated whenever a seventh piece of state is added, and is exactly the kind of effect the next experience argues against.

interactionSequence.prompt: A seat-selection list is keyed by index. Each row has a local "meal preference" input. An agent is halfway through typing a meal note for passenger 4 when passenger 2 is removed from the list. Predict what the agent sees.
options: The correct passenger is removed and the half-typed note stays with passenger 4
The half-typed note can end up attached to a different passenger than the one it was typed for
React logs a key warning and the list refuses to update
All rows lose their local state, because the list re-rendered

optionFeedback.feedback: This is what index keys appear to do until a list reorders. Removing an item shifts every later index down by one, so React matches instances to data by position rather than by identity.

Correct — and note what makes this dangerous in an airline context: the corrupted state is a passenger requirement, and nothing on screen indicates that anything went wrong. The list looks entirely normal.
React warns only when keys are missing entirely. An index is a perfectly valid key, so there is no warning at all. The corruption is silent, which is why it survives for months.
A re-render does not discard state. State is discarded when a component unmounts or when its key changes. Here the opposite is happening: state is preserved when it should have been discarded.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The diagnostic signature to memorise: **the defect appears only on mid-list changes.** Deleting the last item is fine. Deleting the first or middle item shifts indices and corrupts. If a bug report says 'only sometimes' and you can find a reordering interaction in the flow, index keys should be your first hypothesis. Section 5 lists this second among the five symptoms for exactly that reason.
hints: After removing item 2, which item now occupies index 2?
Does React discard a component instance whose key it still recognises?

interactionSequence.prompt: A form must reset when the selected flight changes. Two implementations are proposed. **A:** `useEffect(() => { setSeat(null); setMeal(''); setBags(0); setNotes(''); }, [flightId])`. **B:** `<SeatForm key={flightId} />`. Which is better, and why?
options: A, because it is explicit about which fields are cleared
B, because it discards all state by construction — no field can be forgotten, and there is no intermediate render showing stale values
They are equivalent; the choice is stylistic
A, because remounting a component is expensive and should be avoided

optionFeedback.feedback: Explicitness is real, and it is also the liability: the list must be maintained by hand. Add a fifth field and forget to clear it, and one passenger's note leaks into the next flight — a defect nothing will flag.

Correct on both counts. The completeness argument is the obvious one; the timing argument is the one people miss. The effect runs *after* a render, so there is one frame in which the new flight is displayed alongside the previous flight's form values.
They differ in two observable ways: whether a forgotten field is possible, and whether a stale intermediate render occurs. Neither is stylistic.

Remounting is generally cheap for a form-sized subtree, and here it replaces four state updates plus an extra render. If the subtree were genuinely expensive that would be worth measuring — but it would be an argument for restructuring, not for the effect.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Notice that both arguments for B come from mechanisms in this section rather than from taste. The completeness argument comes from what a key change does — discard the instance entirely. The timing argument comes from when effects run — after the commit, which means the stale frame is visible. This is what it looks like to reason from the model rather than from a rule you memorised.
hints: What happens to state when a key changes?
When does an effect run relative to the render that scheduled it?

workedExamples.problem: **Case study — the wheelchair that moved.** A check-in console at a mid-sized carrier handled about 900 flights a day. Over eight months, agents filed eleven vague reports about special-assistance flags 'looking wrong'. Each was closed as unreproducible. Then a passenger who had not requested assistance was met at the gate with a wheelchair while a passenger who had requested one was not. Reconstruct the diagnosis.
steps: Collect what the reports had in common. All eleven involved the passenger list. None had reproduction steps. Several mentioned the agent had been 'in the middle of something' when it happened.

Attempt reproduction with the standard test flight. Load the list, set a flag, verify it. Correct every time. This is why the reports were closed — the test fixture was a fixed list of eight passengers that nobody ever removed anyone from.
Notice what the test never did. Real agents remove passengers constantly: no-shows, rebookings, upgrades. The fixture never exercised the one interaction that matters.

Reproduce with a mid-list removal. Open the list, tick the special-assistance box on passenger 5, remove passenger 2, and observe the tick now sitting on passenger 4 — because the passenger formerly at index 5 is now at index 4, and React kept the instance holding the checked state at index 5, which now displays a different person.

Read the render code and confirm the mechanism:

```tsx
{passengers.map((p, i) => <PassengerRow key={i} passenger={p} />)}
```

The special-assistance checkbox was local state inside `PassengerRow` rather than a field on the passenger record, so it lived in the instance rather than in the data.

Note the second contributing decision. Had the flag been stored on the passenger object and rendered from props, the wrong key would have produced a visual glitch that corrected on the next render, rather than persistent corrupted state. **Local state plus a wrong key is what makes this dangerous**; either alone is much less severe.

Fix the key:

```tsx
{passengers.map((p) => <PassengerRow key={p.passengerRef} passenger={p} />)}
```

Add the test that would have caught it. Not more tests — one specific interaction: render a list, modify a row's local state, remove an earlier row, and assert the modification is still on the correct passenger.

Audit for the same pattern. The team searched for `map((.*, i)` and `key={i}` and found nine more lists. Three of them contained rows with local state and could reorder; the other six were static and safe. They fixed the three and left the six with a comment recording why they were acceptable.
workedExamples.conclusion: One line of code, eight months, and a passenger who did not receive assistance they had booked. Four things generalise. **The defect was invisible to the test suite by construction**, because the fixture never performed the interaction that triggers it — which is a reminder that test *coverage* and test *scenarios* are different measures, an idea Section 10 develops. **'Unreproducible' meant 'we did not reproduce the right interaction'**, not 'it did not happen'. **Local state amplified the severity**: the same key defect over purely prop-driven rows would have been a flicker rather than a corruption. And **the audit distinguished nine instances into three dangerous and six harmless**, which is the right outcome — the goal is not to eliminate index keys everywhere, but to know which ones can reorder and which hold state.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What does a `key` claim, and what does React do when the claim is wrong?
A list defect appears 'only sometimes' and cannot be reproduced with test data. What single interaction would you add to the reproduction attempt, and what mechanism are you testing for?
Contrast resetting a form with a key change against resetting it with an effect. Give one completeness argument and one timing argument.

learningExperiences.title: Effects as synchronization, and the stale closure

contentBlocks.content:
## The definition that answers everything

`useEffect` does not mean "run after render". It does not mean `componentDidMount`. It means:

> **Keep this external system in sync with this React state, and undo that when it no longer applies.**

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const sub = gateFeed.subscribe(flightId, onUpdate);
  return () => sub.unsubscribe();          // undo exactly what the effect did
}, [flightId]);
```

The cleanup exists because the effect will run again when `flightId` changes, and the subscription to the old flight must end.

**If you cannot write the cleanup, the effect is probably not doing synchronization.** That single test resolves most questions about whether something belongs in an effect.

## Three consequences

- **Do not derive state from props in an effect.** Compute it during render. An effect that sets state from props causes a second render and one frame where the screen shows the wrong value.
- **Do not respond to events in an effect.** A POST on button click belongs in the click handler, not in an effect watching a flag. The handler knows *why* it ran; an effect watching a flag has to infer it.
- **Include every value the effect reads in the dependency array.** Removing a dependency to stop a loop hides the problem and captures stale values. The real fix is a stable identity — `useCallback`, a ref, or moving the value out.

Effects run twice in development Strict Mode on purpose. This surfaces missing cleanups. **If double-running breaks your effect, the effect has a defect.**

## Stale closures: Section 1, in React clothing

Section 1 established that a closure captures the **binding** — the storage location — not the value. React adds one fact that turns this into a common defect:

> **Every render creates new bindings.** A function defined in one render captures that render's values, permanently, because a render's `const` bindings never change.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);   // ✗ always 0 + 1
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);                                                       // captured the first render
```

The interval was created during the first render and closed over that render's `count`, which is `0` and will never be anything else. The counter goes to 1 and stops.

```tsx
setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000);                // ✓ functional update
```

The functional form receives the current value rather than a captured one. **Use it whenever the next state depends on the previous state.**

The symptom shape from Section 1 applies directly: **consistently stale means a captured binding; occasionally stale means ordering or a race; wrong rather than late means the data itself.**

interactionSequence.prompt: For each case, decide whether an effect is the right tool and give your reason: **(a)** computing a filtered passenger list from props and a search term; **(b)** sending an analytics event when an agent clicks 'Issue boarding pass'; **(c)** subscribing to a gate-status feed for the currently selected flight; **(d)** clearing the seat form when the selected flight changes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **(a) No.** Compute it during render. An effect that sets derived state causes a second render and one frame showing the unfiltered list. There is also no cleanup you could write, which is the tell. **(b) No.** This responds to an event, so it belongs in the click handler. An effect watching an `issued` flag cannot distinguish a click from any other route to that flag being set — a restored draft, a websocket update, a retry — and will fire for all of them. **(c) Yes.** This is genuine synchronization with an external system, and the cleanup is obvious: unsubscribe from the previous flight when `flightId` changes or the component unmounts. Note that the cleanup must unsubscribe from the *previous* flight, not the current one, which is the detail people get wrong. **(d) No.** Use a `key` change, as the previous experience argued: it is complete by construction and avoids the stale intermediate frame. A strong answer applies the cleanup test explicitly as the discriminator rather than recalling four separate rules.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your classifications?

interactionSequence.prompt: A counter driven by an interval increments to 1 and then stops. The interval is inside `useEffect(..., [])` and calls `setCount(count + 1)`. What is happening?
options: The interval is being cleared prematurely by the cleanup function
The callback captured `count` from the first render, so it computes `0 + 1` on every tick
React is batching the updates, so only the first one is applied
The dependency array should include `setCount`

optionFeedback.feedback: With an empty dependency array the cleanup runs only on unmount, so the interval keeps firing. The problem is what the callback reads, not whether it runs.
Correct. Every render creates a new `count` binding; this callback closed over the first render's, which is `0` forever. Use `setCount(c => c + 1)` so the updater receives the current value.
Batching groups updates within an event; it does not discard them. Each tick genuinely calls `setCount(1)`, and setting state to the value it already has is a no-op.
`setCount` is guaranteed stable, so including it changes nothing. Adding `count` as a dependency would work by recreating the interval each second, but that is a worse fix than the updater form.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Trace it precisely: tick one calls `setCount(0 + 1)`, so `count` becomes 1. Tick two calls `setCount(0 + 1)` again, because the callback still reads the first render's binding — and setting state to 1 when it is already 1 changes nothing, so React does not even re-render. The counter is frozen. This is Section 1's binding rule producing a React symptom, and recognising it as the same mechanism is the point of meeting it twice.
hints: Which render's `count` does this callback read, and does that binding ever change?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: explain the cleanup test to a colleague. Why does 'can you write a cleanup that reverses exactly what this effect did?' reliably identify effects that should not be effects?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong explanation connects the test to the definition rather than treating it as a heuristic. An effect synchronizes an external system with React state, and synchronization is inherently reversible — you subscribed, so you can unsubscribe; you opened, so you can close; you started an observer, so you can disconnect it. If nothing can be reversed, nothing external was synchronized, and the work is either a derivation (which belongs in render, where it needs no undoing because it produces a value rather than an effect) or a response to an event (which belongs in the handler, because it happened once and is not a state to be maintained). A very good answer notes that this also explains Strict Mode's double invocation: if the effect and its cleanup are genuinely inverse, running them twice is indistinguishable from running them once.

steps: Diagnose the second symptom first, because it is structural. The effect subscribes and returns no cleanup. Each time `flightId` changes, a new subscription is created and the old one is never removed.

Confirm the consequence. After an agent views twenty flights in a shift, twenty subscriptions are live. All twenty fire on every update, all twenty call `setStatus`, and the last one to fire wins — which is why the banner sometimes shows an earlier flight's status. **Both reported symptoms come from the same missing cleanup.**

Apply the cleanup test to confirm this is a genuine effect. Can you write something that reverses exactly what was done? Yes — unsubscribe. So it belongs in an effect, and it simply needs its other half.

Now find the second defect, which the cleanup does not fix. `setSeenCount(seenCount + 1)` reads `seenCount` from the render in which the callback was created. The subscription is created once per `flightId`, so the count freezes at 1 for each flight regardless of how many updates arrive.

Fix it with a functional update, so the updater receives the current value rather than a captured one:

```tsx
setSeenCount(c => c + 1);
```

Examine `agentId`. The callback reads it, but it is not in the dependency array, so if an agent hands over to a colleague mid-session the log records the wrong person. Adding `agentId` to the dependencies is correct — it will resubscribe, which is acceptable here — but note that resubscribing to fix a logging value is a smell. A ref holding the current agent would avoid it.

Verify with Strict Mode. In development the effect now runs, cleans up, and runs again. Because the cleanup genuinely reverses the effect, this is indistinguishable from running once — which is the test Strict Mode exists to apply.
workedExamples.conclusion: One component, three defects, two mechanisms. **The missing cleanup produced both reported symptoms** — the leak and the wrong-flight status — which is worth noticing, because a bug report describing two unrelated-sounding problems often has one cause. **The frozen counter was a stale closure**, invisible until the leak was fixed, since with twenty overlapping subscriptions nobody could tell what the count meant anyway. And **the `agentId` question shows the limits of the dependency array**: adding a value that only needs to be *read* forces the effect to re-run, so a ref is the right tool when you need the current value without resubscribing. Section 5 formalises the habit this example demonstrates — fix one thing, re-measure, and expect the next defect to become visible only after the first is gone.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the synchronization definition of `useEffect`, and give the one-question test it implies for deciding whether something belongs in an effect.
Name two kinds of work that are commonly put in effects and should not be, and say where each belongs instead.
Section 1 taught that closures capture bindings. State how that rule produces stale values specifically in React, and name the fix used when the next state depends on the previous.

An effect reads a value that changes often, but re-running the effect when it changes would be expensive. What tool gives you the current value without adding it to the dependency array, and what is the trade-off?

learningExperiences.title: Designing a component API

contentBlocks.content:
## Two questions decide most of it

**What does the caller need to say, and what should the component decide for itself?**

## Props express meaning, not appearance

`<Badge status="delayed" />` beats `<Badge colour="amber" />`.

The second version forces every caller to know the colour convention. That means the mapping from meaning to appearance lives at forty call sites instead of one, so a design change becomes a codebase-wide edit — and any caller that gets it wrong produces a badge that is quietly misleading rather than obviously broken.

## Composition beats configuration

When a component accumulates boolean props — `showFooter`, `hideIcon`, `compact`, `withDivider` — it has become a small framework. Each new flag multiplies the states it must support, and most combinations are never used or tested.

Accept children instead:

```tsx
<SeatPanel>
  <SeatPanel.Header>26A</SeatPanel.Header>
  <SeatPanel.Body>{…}</SeatPanel.Body>
</SeatPanel>
```

Variation now lives at the call site, where it is visible, without expanding the component's API surface.

contentBlocks.title: A prop that will come back in Section 4
contentBlocks.content:
One appearance prop deserves special mention now, because it looks reasonable and is not: a layout `variant` such as `<Card variant="compact" />`, chosen by the parent from the viewport width.

The component's real constraint is **the space it was given**, not the size of the screen. The same card in a 300 px sidebar on a 1440 px display receives the wide-viewport variant and overflows.

Section 4 shows the platform's answer — a container query — which removes the prop entirely and lets the component adapt wherever it is placed. For now, note the general shape: **a prop that exists because the component cannot see its own context is a prop that should not exist.**

interactionSequence.prompt: A `FlightStatusChip` takes `colour`, `icon`, `bold`, `small`, `uppercase`, and `borderStyle`. It is used in 40 places. Operations changes which colour means 'delayed'. What happens?
options: One change in the theme file, because colour values are centralised there
Forty call sites must be reviewed, because each caller decided the colour; a `status` prop would have kept the mapping in one place
Nothing changes, since colour is a visual concern independent of meaning
The component must be duplicated to support both conventions during the transition

optionFeedback.feedback: The theme centralises colour *values*, not the decision about which value carries which meaning. That decision currently lives at every call site, and the theme cannot see it.
Correct. And note the failure mode of a missed call site: it does not break, it renders a chip in the old colour, which now means something different. A misleading status is worse than a broken one.
The colour is carrying the meaning here — it is how an agent identifies a delayed flight at a glance — so it is precisely not independent of it.
Duplication multiplies the problem and leaves two components to keep in step. The component is not wrong; its API is asking callers the wrong question.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The test to apply when designing a prop: **does the caller know this, or does the component know this?** A caller knows which flight it is showing, so `status` is a fair question to ask. A caller does not reliably know the design system's colour semantics, so `colour` is not. Every prop that asks a caller something the component should own distributes a decision across the codebase, and distributed decisions drift.
hints: Where does the mapping from meaning to colour currently live?

interactionSequence.prompt: Think about a component in your own codebase with the most props. How many are booleans? Roughly how many of the possible combinations are actually used, and how many are tested? You do not need exact numbers — the ratio is the point.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Six boolean props permit 64 combinations. Teams typically use six to ten of them and test two or three. The remaining fifty-odd are not features — they are untested states that the component nonetheless claims to support, and that someone will eventually reach by accident. That count is the most persuasive thing you can bring to a discussion about refactoring the component, because it converts 'this feels complicated' into a number. The composition version has no equivalent count, because variation lives at the call site where it is visible in the diff rather than hidden behind a flag.

workedExamples.problem:
A `BoardingPanel` used across the check-in console has grown to eleven props. Convert it to a composed API and count what changes.

```tsx
<BoardingPanel
  passenger={p}
  showHeader
  showFooter
  hideAvatar
  compact
  withDivider
  footerAction="reissue"
  headerTitle="Boarding"
  colour="amber"
  bordered
  dense
/>
```
steps: Separate the props into two groups. **Data**: `passenger`. **Presentation and structure**: the other ten. Only the first is something a caller genuinely knows and the component does not.

Count the surface. Seven of the ten are booleans, permitting 2⁷ = 128 structural combinations, multiplied by the enumerated values of `footerAction` and `colour`. In practice the codebase uses about six shapes.

Identify the appearance props that should be meaning props. `colour="amber"` asks the caller to know the design system's semantics; replace it with something the caller actually knows, or let the component derive it from `passenger.status`.
Identify the structural props. `showHeader`, `showFooter`, `hideAvatar`, `withDivider`, and `headerTitle` all describe *what the panel contains*. That is exactly what children express better.

Design the composed API, exposing named sub-components so the structure is explicit at the call site:

```tsx
<BoardingPanel passenger={p}>
  <BoardingPanel.Header>Boarding</BoardingPanel.Header>
  <BoardingPanel.Body />
  <BoardingPanel.Footer>
    <ReissueButton passengerRef={p.ref} />
  </BoardingPanel.Footer>
</BoardingPanel>
```

Notice what became possible that was not before. `footerAction="reissue"` was an enumeration the component had to know about; now the footer accepts any element, so a new action requires no change to `BoardingPanel` at all.

Handle the remaining density props. `compact` and `dense` are genuine display density, which is a legitimate meaning-level prop — keep one, delete the duplicate, and note that two props meaning the same thing is itself a signal the API grew without review.
Count the result. Eleven props become two: `passenger` and `density`. The 128 structural combinations become zero, because structure is now expressed directly rather than encoded in flags.

Check the migration cost honestly. Every existing call site must change, and the composed version is more verbose at each one. That verbosity is the trade: the structure is visible in the diff rather than hidden behind a flag whose effect a reviewer has to remember.
workedExamples.conclusion: Eleven props became two, and 128 untested structural combinations became zero. Three points generalise. **Boolean props that describe what a component contains are children in disguise** — the conversion is mechanical once you notice it. **An enumerated action prop is a sign the component is doing the caller's job**: replacing `footerAction="reissue"` with a footer slot means the component never needs updating when a new action appears. And **the trade is real**: composition is more verbose at each call site, and that verbosity is precisely what makes the structure reviewable. A prop named `compact` tells a reviewer nothing about what will render; a `<Header>` element tells them exactly.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the rule about what props should express, and the test for deciding whether a given prop is fair to ask of a caller.
A component has six boolean props. How many structural combinations does it claim to support, and what number would you bring to a discussion about refactoring it?
What is a headless component, and why do headless libraries survive design system changes?

transferExercises.context: Restaurant kitchen display system — a different domain from the airline examples used in this section.
transferExercises.scenario: A kitchen display shows incoming orders as tickets. Tickets are reordered continuously by priority as prep times change, and expedited orders jump to the front. Each ticket has a per-item 'started' toggle held in local component state, so a chef can mark individual items as underway. The list is rendered with `orders.map((o, i) => <Ticket key={i} order={o} />)`. The `Ticket` component takes nine props including `compact`, `showTimer`, `hideAllergens`, `urgent`, and `colour`. The team's test suite renders a fixed list of six tickets and passes completely.
transferExercises.task: Produce a diagnosis and a redesign. First, explain precisely what goes wrong with the index keys in this specific system, being concrete about what a chef would observe and why it is dangerous here. Second, explain why the test suite passes despite the defect, and specify the single interaction you would add to catch it. Third, redesign the `Ticket` API: identify which props are appearance props that should express meaning, which are structural props that should become children, and state how many combinations the current API claims to support. Finally, explain why `hideAllergens` is a prop that should not exist in any form, using the reasoning from this section.
successCriteria: Explains that continuous reordering shifts indices, so React matches component instances to tickets by position and preserves the 'started' toggles against the wrong order
Identifies concretely that a chef would see items marked as started on an order where they have not been started, or the reverse, with no visual indication of the error
Notes that the local-state-plus-wrong-key combination is what makes this a corruption rather than a flicker
Explains that the fixed six-ticket fixture never reorders, so the defect is not merely untested but untriggerable by the suite as written
Specifies a test that modifies a ticket's local state, then reorders or removes an earlier ticket, and asserts the state is still on the correct order
Prescribes a stable key derived from the order's own identifier
Classifies `colour` and `urgent` as appearance props to be replaced by a meaning prop such as order priority or status, with the mapping owned by the component
Classifies `showTimer`, `hideAllergens`, and similar structural flags as content that belongs in children or slots
Quantifies the current API surface, recognising that the boolean props alone permit dozens of combinations that are neither used nor tested

Argues that `hideAllergens` should not exist because allergen information is safety-critical and a component API should not offer callers a way to suppress it — the component, not the caller, should own that decision

learningExperiences.title: Context is injection, not storage

contentBlocks.content:
## What context is for

Context is **dependency injection**. It answers: how does a deeply nested component receive the thing it needs — a theme, the current user, a store handle — without threading it through every intermediate component?

It is not a state manager. Section 6 gives state a proper home; context's job is delivery, not storage.

## What it costs

**Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes**, regardless of which part of the value it actually uses. Context propagates by the identity of the whole value, and it has no mechanism for partial subscription.

Two consequences follow directly.

**Split contexts by change frequency.** A `UserContext` that also carries a sidebar-open flag re-renders every consumer whenever the sidebar toggles — including components that only ever read the user's name.

**Memoize the value.** Writing `value={{ user, logout }}` creates a new object on every render of the provider, so every consumer re-renders every time the provider does, even when `user` and `logout` are unchanged.

```tsx
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, logout }), [user, logout]);
```

That second point is Section 1's reference-equality rule appearing again: the object's *contents* are identical and its *identity* is new, and identity is what context compares.

interactionSequence.prompt: A provider supplies `value={{ agent, terminal, sidebarOpen }}` without memoization. A component deep in the tree consumes only `agent.name`. The sidebar is toggled. What happens to that component?
options: Nothing, because it does not read `sidebarOpen`
It re-renders, because context compares the identity of the whole value and that identity changed
It re-renders only if it is wrapped in `memo`
It re-renders, but only after the sidebar animation completes

optionFeedback.feedback: Context has no partial subscription. It cannot know which fields a consumer reads, so any change to the provided value's identity notifies every consumer.

Correct, and note there are two independent reasons here. The value object is recreated on every provider render, *and* `sidebarOpen` genuinely changed. Memoizing fixes the first; splitting the context fixes the second.
`memo` compares props from a parent. It does not intercept context updates — a memoized component still re-renders when a context it consumes changes.
The re-render happens when state changes, not when an animation ends. Animation timing is unrelated to React's update scheduling.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The important detail is that memoization alone would not have saved you here. Even with `useMemo`, `sidebarOpen` changing produces a new value, so every consumer still re-renders. **Memoizing addresses unnecessary identity changes; splitting addresses genuine changes to data that most consumers do not care about.** You usually need both, and knowing which one a given problem calls for is the difference between a fix and a partial fix.
hints: What does context compare to decide whether to notify consumers?

interactionSequence.prompt: Which of these is context genuinely well suited to?
options: Holding a form's field values so any component can read them
Providing a stable handle — a store instance, a client object, a theme token set — that rarely or never changes identity
Sharing a frequently updating value such as scroll position across the tree
Replacing a state management library entirely

optionFeedback.feedback: Field values change on every keystroke, so every consumer re-renders on every keystroke. Section 8 shows the correct approach: a form library with per-field subscriptions.

Correct, and this is exactly the pattern Section 6 uses for per-instance stores. The context value never changes identity, so consumers never re-render from it; the actual updates flow through the store's own selector subscriptions.
A high-frequency value in context re-renders every consumer at that frequency, which is the worst possible use. Keep such values in a store with selective subscription, or outside React entirely.

Context delivers values; it does not manage them. It has no selective subscription, no devtools, and no update batching beyond React's own — which is why it complements a state library rather than replacing one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The pattern in option (b) is worth holding onto, because it resolves the apparent contradiction between 'context re-renders every consumer' and 'context is the right way to distribute a store'. Carry a **stable handle** and the re-render cost never materialises, because the identity never changes. Section 6 builds directly on this when creating per-instance stores.
hints: Which of these values changes identity rarely?

steps: Confirm the mechanism. Toggling the sidebar updates `sidebarOpen`, which re-renders `AppProvider`, which creates a new value object, which notifies every consumer of `AppContext`.

Establish that there are two separate faults, because fixing one alone will not solve the problem. **Fault one**: the value object is recreated on every provider render regardless of whether anything changed. **Fault two**: values with completely different change frequencies share one context.
Fix fault one with memoization, and note that this alone is insufficient — `sidebarOpen` really did change, so the memo produces a new value and every consumer still re-renders.
Fix fault two by grouping values by how often they change. `agent` and `terminal` change perhaps twice a shift. `theme` changes rarely. `sidebarOpen` changes constantly.

Apply a second refinement inside `SidebarProvider`: separate the **value** from the **setter**. The setter is stable, so components that only toggle the sidebar — a button, a keyboard shortcut handler — should not re-render when the sidebar's state changes.

```tsx
<SidebarStateContext.Provider value={sidebarOpen}>
  <SidebarActionsContext.Provider value={actions}>   {/* memoized, stable */}
    {children}
  </SidebarActionsContext.Provider>
</SidebarStateContext.Provider>
```
Re-measure. Toggling the sidebar now re-renders only the components that actually read `sidebarOpen` — the layout wrapper and a handful of others. The 200+ becomes a handful.
Verify that nothing regressed for the session data. Components reading `agent` re-render only when the agent changes, which is what you wanted all along.

Consider whether some of this state belongs in context at all. `sidebarOpen` is used by one layout subtree; Section 6 would ask whether it should simply be local state there, which would remove the context entirely.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two hundred renders reduced to a handful, using three techniques that address three different causes. **Memoization** stops identity changing when nothing changed. **Splitting by change frequency** stops consumers hearing about changes they do not care about. **Separating state from actions** stops components that only *trigger* changes from re-rendering when those changes happen. The final step is the one to carry forward: before optimising a context, ask whether the value belongs in context at all. A value read by one subtree is local state, and Section 6 makes that question systematic.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What is context for, and what does it cost? Name the two fixes and say which problem each one addresses.
Why does carrying a stable store handle in context avoid the usual criticism of context, while carrying form field values does not?

learningExperiences.title: Key terms, common errors, and summary

terms.definition: The phase in which React compares the newly rendered description of the UI with the previous one to determine what changed.
The phase in which React applies reconciliation's differences to the real DOM and then runs effects. This is where layout, style recalculation, and paint occur.
The live occurrence of a component in the tree, holding its own state and effects. Keys determine which instance is matched to which item across renders.
Deliberately changing a component's key so React discards the instance and its state, mounting a fresh one. Cleaner than an effect that clears fields individually.
The function returned from an effect, which must reverse exactly what the effect did. Its absence on a subscribing or listening effect is a defect.
Passing a function to a state setter, such as `setCount(c => c + 1)`, so the updater receives the current value rather than one captured from an earlier render.
React's deliberate double-running of effects in development, which surfaces missing cleanups. If double-running breaks an effect, the effect has a defect.
A component exposing named sub-components, such as `Panel.Header`, so structure is expressed by composition rather than by boolean props.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
1. **Index keys on a list that can reorder, insert, or filter.** State becomes attached to the wrong item, silently.
2. **Believing a re-render means a DOM update**, which sends performance work in the wrong direction.
3. **Forgetting that a parent re-render re-renders children** regardless of their props.
4. **Calculating state from props inside an effect** instead of during render, causing an extra render and a stale frame.
5. **Doing an event's work inside an effect** that watches a flag, which fires for every route to that flag.
6. **Removing a dependency to stop a loop** instead of stabilising the identity.
7. **Effects with no cleanup** that subscribe, listen, or open something — the subscriptions accumulate.
8. **Reading captured state inside an interval or timeout** instead of using a functional update.
9. **Appearance props** such as `colour` and `variant` where meaning props belong.
10. **Collecting boolean props** until the component becomes a small untested framework.
11. **One context holding values with very different change frequencies.**
12. **Unmemoized context values**, which re-render every consumer on every provider render.
13. **Reaching for `memo` before asking why the renders are happening** — the structural fix is usually better and usually simpler.

## Summary

- Render, reconcile, and commit are separate. **A re-render is not a DOM update**, and only four things cause one — including, importantly, a parent re-rendering.
- **Keys are claims about identity.** Index keys corrupt state when a list reorders, and the defect is invisible to fixtures that never reorder. Changing a key on purpose is the cleanest reset.
- **Effects synchronize with external systems and undo themselves.** If you cannot write the cleanup, it is probably not an effect. Not for derived state; not for event responses.
- **Every render creates new bindings**, so functions defined in a render capture that render's values. Functional updates defeat the resulting stale closures.
- **Props express meaning, composition beats configuration, custom hooks are the reuse unit**, and headless components survive redesigns.
- **Context is injection, not storage.** Split by change frequency, memoize the value, and separate state from actions. Best of all, carry a stable handle.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: which of the four mechanisms in this section — the render model, keys, effects, or component API design — do you expect to encounter first in real code, and what would the symptom look like from a user's point of view rather than from the code's?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The user-facing framing is the valuable half of this exercise, because bug reports arrive in that language and never in the code's. Worth noting how differently the four present. **Key defects** present as data that is subtly wrong — a setting on the wrong record — with nothing broken on screen, which is why they are reported vaguely and closed as unreproducible. **Effect defects** present as staleness, duplication, or a page that gets slower the longer it is open. **Render-model misunderstandings** present as sluggishness rather than incorrectness, and are reported as 'the app feels slow'. **API design problems** are rarely reported by users at all; they present as development velocity dropping and as inconsistency creeping across screens. That last one is worth remembering, because it means nobody will file a ticket — you have to notice it yourself.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Recall the six summary claims of this section without looking: the three phases, the four triggers, what keys claim, what effects are for, what every render creates, and what context is.

learningExperiences.title: Practical activity: break it, then fix it

contentBlocks.content:
## Reproduce the defects deliberately

Every item below asks you to **create the defect first, observe it, and only then fix it.** That order matters more here than anywhere else in the course, because these defects are defined by how they present. Knowing that index keys are wrong is worth little; recognising the mid-list-only symptom in a vague bug report is worth a great deal.

You will need React DevTools installed, with the Profiler available and 'Highlight updates when components render' switched on.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: You are building a small list-and-detail screen of the kind that exists in every business application — a list of records, each row with some local state, a detail panel, and a shared context. Every defect you create here is one you will meet in real code, usually reported in language that does not mention the mechanism at all.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Produce each of this section's defects on purpose, observe its symptom from a user's point of view, then fix it and confirm the fix with the profiler.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Any React setup — Vite, Create React App, or a sandbox
React DevTools browser extension, with the Profiler tab available
'Highlight updates when components render' enabled in DevTools settings
instructions: **1. Build the base.** A list of at least eight items, each row containing a text input whose value is local state in the row component, plus a delete button. Key the rows by index.

**2. Corrupt it.** Type into the input on row 6, then delete row 2. Record exactly what happens to the text you typed and which row it is now on. Write the symptom as a *user* would report it — do not mention keys.
**3. Fix and confirm.** Switch to a stable key and repeat step 2. Then write the one test that would have caught this, and say why a test using a fixed list could not.

**4. Reset two ways.** Add a detail panel with four form fields that must clear when the selected record changes. Implement it with an effect that clears each field, then with a `key` change. For the effect version, watch carefully for a frame showing the new record alongside the old field values. Record which version showed it.

**5. Leak a subscription.** Write an effect that subscribes to a timer or mock feed keyed on the selected record, with no cleanup. Change the selection six times and count the live subscriptions. Add the cleanup and count again.

**6. Freeze a counter.** Write an interval inside `useEffect(..., [])` that calls `setCount(count + 1)`. Observe it stopping at 1. Explain in one sentence which render's `count` it is reading, then fix it with a functional update.

**7. Measure the blast radius.** Put a text input's state at the top of your tree, above the list. Type one character with the Profiler recording. Record how many components rendered and how many DOM mutations the commit produced. Move the state down into the input's own subtree and repeat both measurements.

**8. Split a context.** Create one context holding a rarely changing value and a rapidly changing one. Log renders of a consumer that reads only the rarely changing value, and toggle the other. Then memoize the value and re-measure; then split into two contexts and re-measure again. **Record three numbers**, and say which of the two fixes was responsible for which improvement.

**9. Collapse an API.** Take any component of yours with four or more boolean props. Count the combinations it claims to support, then convert the structural ones to children. Count the props removed and note anything that became possible that was not before.
reflectionPrompts: In step 2 you wrote the symptom in a user's words. If that sentence arrived as a bug report, how long do you think it would take you to reach the cause — and what in the wording would be the clue?
Step 8 asked for three numbers. Did memoization alone fix the problem? If not, what does that tell you about diagnosing context re-renders in real code?
Step 7 asked for both a render count and a DOM mutation count. Were they similar or very different, and what would you conclude about where to spend optimisation effort?
Which of these defects do you think you have already shipped at some point without knowing? What would have made you notice?

selfAssessmentCriteria: Step 2 records the symptom in user-facing language, without reference to keys or React internals
Step 3 specifies a test involving a reordering or removal interaction, and explains why a static fixture cannot trigger the defect
Step 4 records whether the stale intermediate frame was observed, rather than assuming it
Step 5 records a subscription count before and after adding the cleanup
Step 6 includes a one-sentence explanation naming which render's binding is being read
Step 7 records both a render count and a DOM mutation count, before and after moving the state
Step 8 records three separate measurements and attributes each improvement to the correct fix
Step 9 records a combination count and a count of props removed

retrievalPractice.prompt: You have twenty minutes and a report that a screen 'feels slow'. Using only this section's material, what do you measure first and what would each possible result tell you?

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Check your understanding

Answer without scrolling back. Retrieval that feels effortful is the retrieval that lasts.

Three true/false questions, then three short-answer questions.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** If a component re-renders, the DOM has been updated.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Render produces a description of the UI; reconciliation compares it with the previous one; only differences reach the DOM. A component can re-render forty times with identical output and cause zero DOM work.
Correct. Keeping render cost and commit cost separate is what lets you pick the right fix later: volume, computation, or blast radius are three different problems with three different solutions.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The practical consequence is that a large render count in the profiler is information, not a verdict. Ask what those renders cost in self time, and whether a commit followed. Section 9 turns this into a formal classification step.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** Index keys are acceptable as long as the list is not sorted.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Insertion, deletion, and filtering all shift indices, not just sorting. Only append-only, never-filtered lists are genuinely safe, and that constraint rarely survives a product cycle.

Correct. The risk is any operation that changes an item's position. Note also that the severity depends on whether rows hold local state — with state, it is corruption; without, it is at worst a flicker.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Remember the diagnostic signature: **mid-list changes only.** Removing the last item works fine, which is exactly why casual testing misses it and why the reports come back as 'only sometimes'.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** Removing a dependency from an effect's dependency array is a valid way to stop an infinite loop.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It silences the loop while capturing stale values, so you trade a visible defect for an invisible one. The loop was telling you that an identity is unstable.
Correct. Stabilise the identity instead — memoize the object or function, move the value outside the component, or use a ref if you need the current value without re-running the effect.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: An infinite effect loop is nearly always a dependency whose identity changes every render: an object literal, an array literal, or an inline function. The loop is a symptom of an unstable reference — which is Section 1's reference-equality rule producing yet another React-shaped consequence.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Give the synchronization definition of `useEffect`. Explain what it tells you about cleanups, and name two cases where an effect is the wrong tool, saying where that work belongs instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** An effect keeps an external system in sync with React state and undoes that when it no longer applies. Because synchronization is inherently reversible, the cleanup must reverse exactly what the effect did — subscribe and unsubscribe, open and close, observe and disconnect. That gives you a decisive test: if you cannot write such a cleanup, the work is probably not synchronization. Two wrong uses: **deriving state from props or other state**, which belongs in render, because an effect causes a second render and one frame displaying the wrong value; and **responding to an event**, which belongs in the event handler, because an effect watching a flag cannot distinguish a click from any other route to that flag being set. A third acceptable answer is **resetting state when a prop changes**, which is better handled with a key change. **Accept** paraphrases of the definition provided the reversibility point is made. **Reject** 'it runs after render', which describes the timing and explains none of the decisions.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A context consumer re-renders when the only field it reads has not changed. Explain the mechanism, give the two fixes, and say which problem each fix addresses.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** Context propagates by the identity of the whole provided value and has no mechanism for partial subscription, so it cannot know which fields a consumer reads. Any change to the value's identity notifies every consumer. Two fixes, addressing two different causes. **Memoizing the provided value** stops the identity changing when nothing actually changed — without it, an object literal such as `value={{ user, logout }}` is a new object on every provider render. **Splitting contexts by change frequency** stops consumers being notified about genuine changes to data they do not use. You usually need both: memoization alone does not help when a frequently changing field really did change, because the memo correctly produces a new value. A strong answer adds the third refinement — separating state from actions, so components that only trigger changes do not re-render when those changes occur — or notes that carrying a stable handle avoids the whole problem. **Reject** answers naming only memoization, since that is the incomplete fix people most often ship.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A component takes `colour`, `icon`, `bold`, `compact`, and `withDivider`. Explain what is wrong with this API, using both a maintenance argument and an argument about what a caller can reasonably be asked to know. Then describe what you would replace it with.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** The maintenance argument: five props, four of them boolean or appearance-level, permit far more combinations than are ever used or tested — sixteen structural combinations from the booleans alone, multiplied by the colour and icon values. The component claims to support states nobody has verified, and each new flag doubles the count. The caller argument: `colour` asks every call site to know the design system's semantics, so the mapping from meaning to appearance lives at forty places instead of one. When the mapping changes, every site must be reviewed, and a missed one renders a chip in the old colour, which now means something different — misleading rather than broken. The replacement: a single meaning prop such as `status`, letting the component own the colour and icon mapping, and children or named slots replacing the structural flags so composition expresses what the component contains. **Accept** answers that make either argument well and gesture at the other. **Reject** answers that object only on grounds of tidiness or prop count without identifying the distributed decision or the untested combinations.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

retrievalPractice.prompt: Section 1 taught that closures capture bindings and that change is detected by reference. Name one React defect from this section caused by each of those two facts.
From memory, list the four mechanisms in this section that explain most confusing React behaviour, and give the user-facing symptom of each.

transferExercises.context: Music streaming playlist editor — a different domain from both the airline examples and the kitchen display transfer above.
transferExercises.scenario: A playlist editor lets a user reorder tracks by dragging, remove tracks, and expand any track to edit a personal note stored as local state in the track row. A single `PlayerContext` provides the current user, the playback theme, the currently playing track, and the playback position, which updates roughly four times a second. Track rows are keyed by index. The editor also has a search field whose state lives in the top-level page component, above the playlist. Users report three things: notes occasionally appear on the wrong track; typing in the search field is laggy on long playlists; and the browser tab becomes slower the longer the editor is left open.
transferExercises.task: Diagnose all three reports. For each: name the mechanism, state the specific evidence you would gather with React DevTools to confirm it before changing any code, and describe the fix. Then answer two further questions. First, for the laggy search field, explain what you would measure to decide between moving the state, using composition, and using memoization — and say which you would try first and why. Second, explain why the `PlayerContext` as designed is a problem even for components that never read the playback position, and give the full sequence of fixes with the specific problem each one addresses.
successCriteria: Identifies the misplaced notes as index keys on a reorderable list, with local state in the row making it a corruption rather than a flicker
Names the confirming evidence as reproducing with a drag or a mid-list removal while a note is being edited, and inspecting the component tree to see instances matched by position
Identifies the laggy search as blast radius — state at the top of the tree re-rendering the entire playlist on every keystroke — and distinguishes render cost from DOM cost
Names the confirming evidence as a Profiler recording of one keystroke showing the render count and self time, plus whether the commit produced DOM mutations
Identifies the progressive slowdown as an effect without a cleanup, most plausibly a playback or position subscription accumulating as the current track changes
Names the confirming evidence as counting live subscriptions or observing the effect re-running without a corresponding cleanup, and notes that Strict Mode would surface it in development

For the search field, proposes moving the state down as the first attempt, justified by it removing the cause rather than suppressing the symptom, with composition as the fallback when the state genuinely must live high and memoization last

Explains that the `PlayerContext` re-renders every consumer roughly four times a second because playback position changes the identity of the whole provided value, regardless of which fields a consumer reads

Gives the full fix sequence: memoize the provided value, split contexts by change frequency so playback position is separate from user and theme, and separate state from actions so components that only trigger playback changes do not re-render
Notes that memoization alone is insufficient here, because the playback position genuinely changes and correctly produces a new value each time

sections.title: CSS and Motion: Letting the Platform Do the Work
sections.description: One habit costs more performance for less benefit than any other in this course: solving in JavaScript what the browser already solves in CSS. This section gives you a decision rule for when to reach for the platform and when JavaScript is genuinely needed, then applies it to three areas — layout response (where container queries remove the variant prop Section 3 argued against), cascade structure (layers, tokens, logical properties), and motion (which tools to use, and why a reduced-motion response is not a switch). Examples come from a museum's public collections website.

learningObjectives.description: Apply the CSS-or-JavaScript decision rule to hover, focus, sticky positioning, and data-driven styling, and justify each assignment.
Explain why a platform implementation is frequently more correct, not only faster, by naming an input mode a JavaScript reimplementation commonly misses.
Replace a viewport-driven layout variant prop with a container query, removing the prop entirely and verifying the component in more than one context.
Resolve a specificity conflict by declaring cascade layer order rather than escalating specificity or using `!important`.
Implement theming with custom properties and confirm with the profiler that switching causes zero React renders.
Adopt logical properties by default and state the cost asymmetry between doing so now and retrofitting them later.
Choose the correct motion tool in order of preference, and justify installing an animation library only by React's node-removal behaviour rather than by animation in general.
Design a reduced-motion response that removes travel while preserving the signal that something changed.

motivationHooks.prompt: A museum's collections grid used three `useState` hooks per card — for hover, focus, and a reveal — across sixty visible cards. That is 180 hooks, and 38 to 44 milliseconds of scripting every time a pointer crossed the grid. Nobody had measured it, because it did not look like a performance problem; it looked like ordinary React code. It was also invisible to the site's accessibility audit, because the audit checked whether elements had labels, not whether a keyboard user could ever reach them. Both defects were removed by deleting code, not by writing more.

Write this down before reading on. A card should show a shadow on hover. A developer implements it with `useState` and `onMouseEnter`/`onMouseLeave`. It works perfectly in every manual test. **Name one real user for whom this implementation is completely broken** — not slow, not awkward, but unable to see the shadow at all. You do not need to know CSS to answer this; you need to know who uses a mouse and who does not.

This section finishes an argument Section 3 started. There, a `variant` prop chosen from viewport width was shown to break in a sidebar, because it asked the wrong question. Container queries here are the fix — they let the component answer the right question itself, and the prop disappears. The same 'ask the platform first' instinct then extends to motion: before Section 9 teaches you to measure performance, this section removes an entire category of performance problem by never creating it.

The user is anyone navigating by keyboard. `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave` are pointer events — they never fire from Tab, from a screen reader's virtual cursor, or from switch-access hardware. So a keyboard user does not see the shadow late or clumsily; they never see it, and if the shadow reveals content rather than merely decorating the card, that content simply does not exist for them. `:hover, :focus-within` in two lines of CSS covers both groups. Hold onto the shape of this answer — 'the platform version is not just faster, it is more correct' — because it recurs through the whole section.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about styling and motion in a React application.

**If the browser can express a behaviour declaratively, let it.** The test is concrete: ask what information the behaviour needs that the browser does not already have. Hover, focus, sticky positioning, and layout response to available space all fail that test — the browser already has everything it needs, and JavaScript reimplementations of them cost renders and commonly break for keyboard users.

**Container queries answer a question media queries cannot.** A component's real constraint is the space it was given, not the width of the screen, and a `variant` prop chosen from viewport width breaks the moment someone places the component somewhere new. This closes Section 3's argument about props expressing meaning rather than presentation.

**Cascade layers replace the specificity arms race.** Layer order beats specificity outright, so a single-class utility can override a deeply nested component rule with no `!important` anywhere.

**Custom properties are runtime values.** Changing one re-themes the application with zero React renders, which is Section 1's reference-equality rule appearing in CSS: the DOM updates without React's tree ever being asked to compare anything.

**Logical properties cost nothing today and save a great deal later.** In a left-to-right interface they behave exactly like physical properties; the saving only appears the day right-to-left support is needed, and by then it is too late to have made the decision cheaply.

**Motion explains change; it does not decorate it.** Prefer transitions, then keyframes, then the Web Animations API, then a library — and the one genuinely React-specific reason for a library is that React removes a node before CSS can animate its exit.

**Reduced motion means removing travel, not removing feedback.** A blunt global switch stops harm today; a considered per-animation pass restores communication afterwards. Both matter, in that order.
keyTakeaways: Test: what does this need that the browser doesn't already have? If nothing, use CSS.
The platform version is frequently more correct, not only faster — it is what covers keyboard, touch, and assistive technology by default.
Container queries let a component answer 'how much space do I have' itself, removing variant props from component APIs.
@layer beats specificity; declare an order once instead of escalating forever.
Custom properties re-theme with zero React renders.
Adopt logical properties now — the cost is zero today and large on retrofit.
Animate transform and opacity; they can run on the compositor without recalculating layout.
The only React-specific justification for an animation library is animating an element's removal.
Reduced motion: remove the travel, keep the state-change signal.
