learningExperiences.title: Case study: 38 percent, and two findings nobody was looking for

contentBlocks.content:
## Return to the opening story, in full

The section opened with a traffic collapse and two findings from the migration that fixed it. Read the complete account now, including a judgement call about when server rendering was — and was not — the right choice at all.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the full account: the publisher's subscriber account area was deliberately left as plain client-side rendering during the migration, even though every other major route was moved to some form of server rendering. Using this section's material, argue for why this was the correct choice rather than an inconsistency.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Server rendering's benefits in this scenario are discoverability by search crawlers and fast first-paint content for anonymous visitors arriving from search or social links — neither of which applies to a subscriber account area, since it requires authentication to view at all and therefore has zero search-discoverability value, and since its users are already logged-in, returning visitors rather than first-time arrivals whose very first paint matters most. It is the direct analogue of every internal, authenticated console this course has used as an example throughout — the same reasoning this section's summary applies generally: an authenticated tool with no public-facing discoverability need gains essentially none of server rendering's benefits while still paying its genuine costs in complexity. Leaving it as CSR is not an inconsistency; it is the same per-route reasoning correctly applied to a route with different requirements from its neighbours.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this argument?

interactionSequence.prompt: After finding both the module-level store leak and the serialised credential, the team debates two responses. **A:** fix both specific instances found, since both are now known and resolved. **B:** additionally audit the entire codebase for every other module-level mutable value and every other place a full object is passed as a prop to a client component. Compare, using the widening-scope reasoning from Section 8 and Section 10's case studies.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: B is the stronger response, for the same reason it was in both of those earlier case studies: a defect of a given class, once found, is evidence the underlying category of mistake exists in the codebase's habits, not proof that this one instance was an isolated event. Both the module-level-store pattern and the whole-object-as-prop pattern are the kind of thing a codebase either avoids systematically or repeats casually across many otherwise-unrelated components — there is no strong reason to believe either instance found here was uniquely isolated, and every earlier case study in this course where a team stopped at the reported instance alone later found siblings they had missed. A is not wrong to fix what is known immediately; it is incomplete if it stops there rather than treating the finding as a prompt to look for the same mistake elsewhere.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this comparison?

workedExamples.problem: **Case study — 38 percent, and two findings nobody was looking for.** Reconstruct the full migration at the publisher, from the traffic collapse through both incidental security findings.
steps: **The starting point.** A client-rendered React application, article content fetched inside `useEffect` for every article page — a pattern that had worked without complaint for the internal tools the team had previously built, none of which needed search discoverability at all.

**The symptom.** Organic search traffic fell 38 percent within two months of the client-rendered relaunch. Investigation began with search-console reports showing pages indexed with no body content — matching this section's core misconception almost exactly.

**Confirming the cause.** Viewing raw page source, rather than the browser's live element inspector, showed exactly what this section predicts: a shell with navigation and layout, and an empty content region where the article body should have been, since the fetch inside `useEffect` had not yet run at the point the server's HTML was generated and sent.

**The migration.** Article pages moved to static generation with on-demand regeneration on edit; the homepage and section fronts to incremental regeneration on a short interval; a live blog format, newly introduced for major breaking-news events, to streaming server-side rendering; the subscriber account area deliberately left as client-side rendering, for the reasons argued in this experience's first interaction.

**The measured result.** Time to readable text on a mid-range Android test device, on a throttled connection: 6.8 seconds down to 1.4. Organic search traffic recovered over the following quarter and modestly exceeded its pre-collapse baseline, attributed partly to social previews now correctly showing headlines and images for the first time.

**Finding one, incidental to the migration itself.** While testing the newly server-rendered article pages under simulated concurrent load — a step the team had not previously needed, since client rendering has no equivalent shared-process concern — a Redux store created at module level was found leaking a logged-in editor's unpublished draft into a different, concurrent anonymous reader's response.

**Finding two, found during the same load-testing pass.** An internal recommendations-service response, including an unused `apiCredentials` field, had been passed in full as a prop from a Server Component to a client component that only ever rendered two of its fields — serialising the credential into every single article page's public HTML.

**The response.** Both specific instances were fixed immediately — the store rebuilt with per-request creation, the prop narrowed to only the fields actually used. Following the widening-scope reasoning from this experience's second interaction, the team also audited the full codebase specifically for these two patterns and found one further instance of each, in components unrelated to the ones originally reported, neither of which had yet caused any known incident.
workedExamples.conclusion: A traffic problem, diagnosed and fixed using Section 3's effect-timing rule, led directly to two serious security findings that nobody had been looking for — both surfaced only because server rendering's concurrency model exposed assumptions that had been safe, and invisible, under client rendering for years. The transferable lesson connects three separate parts of this course: **moving code to a new execution environment does not just risk new bugs in new code — it can expose old, previously safe assumptions as newly dangerous, in code that has not changed at all**, which is exactly why this section spent most of its time on what changes for habits from earlier sections, rather than teaching a large body of genuinely new material.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why did the two security findings in the case study surface only during the server-rendering migration, rather than at any point during the two prior years of client-side rendering?

learningExperiences.title: Key terms, common errors, and summary

terms.definition: Client-side rendering, server-side rendering per request, static generation at build time, and incremental regeneration refreshed periodically — chosen per route.
Attaching React's event handlers and internal state to server-rendered HTML rather than recreating the DOM from scratch.
A difference between the client's first render and the server's HTML, caused by anything the server could not have known — a clock, randomness, or a browser-only global.
A component that runs only on the server, ships no JavaScript to the client, cannot use state or effects, and can await data directly.
The directive marking where code begins shipping to the browser. Everything imported below it is included in the client bundle.
A server function invocable from client code, compiling to a real, public HTTP endpoint that requires its own independent authorization.
Sending HTML progressively as segments become ready, so a page's static shell can render immediately while slower content streams in afterward.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
1. **One rendering strategy for an entire site**, rather than a decision made per route.
2. **A non-deterministic first render** — a clock, randomness, or a browser-only global read during render — causing a hydration mismatch.
3. **Fetching content in `useEffect` and believing the page is genuinely server-rendered** as a result.
4. **A module-level store or cache**, safe under client rendering, silently becoming a cross-user leak on a server.
5. **Passing a whole object as a prop to a client component**, serialising every field — including unused, sensitive ones — into public page source.
6. **Treating a Server Action as private** because only one form currently happens to call it.
7. **Assuming server rendering automatically fixes interaction responsiveness** — it improves perceived load; responsiveness still depends on hydration cost.
8. **Adopting server rendering for an internal, authenticated tool** that gains none of its actual benefits.

## Summary

- **Rendering strategy is a per-route decision**, not a single project-wide setting.
- **Hydration asserts the client's first render reproduces the server's HTML.** Fix mismatches by determinism first, after-mount rendering second, suppression last.
- **Effects do not run during server rendering** — the single most common way "we have SSR" delivers no actual benefit.
- **A module-level store is a cross-user leak on a server.** Section 1's rule, unchanged, in a new environment with a more severe consequence.
- **Props to a client component are serialised into the page.** Pass only what is used, never a whole object.
- **A Server Action is a public endpoint** and needs the same authorization discipline as any other.
- **SSR is a trade.** An authenticated internal tool usually gains nothing from it.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: of the four earlier-section rules this section reapplied — effects, module evaluation, state tiers, and client-as-boundary — which one's new consequence here surprised you most, and why?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A common and defensible answer is the module-evaluation rule, precisely because its Section 1 form (a plain in-memory Map, demonstrated in a deliberately abstract scratch example) can feel like a minor technical curiosity in isolation, whereas its consequence here — a named editor's actual unpublished draft appearing in a stranger's browser — makes the abstract mechanism concrete and its real-world stakes immediately obvious in a way the original teaching example, by design, kept understated.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Recall the seven summary claims of this section without looking.

learningExperiences.title: Practical activity: view source, leak it, then fix it

contentBlocks.content:
## View source, not the element inspector

Several steps below specifically require reading the browser's **View Page Source** output, not the Elements panel — the two show different things, and this section's whole diagnostic method depends on knowing which one reflects what the server actually sent.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: You are building a minimal article page in a server-rendering framework, then deliberately reproducing this section's three core defects — the empty-shell effect, the module-level leak, and the serialised secret — before fixing each.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Confirm what the server actually sends for two different fetching approaches, demonstrate a cross-request store leak and fix it, and demonstrate a prop-serialisation leak and fix it.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A server-rendering React framework (Next.js or an equivalent), set up with one simple article route
Ability to view raw page source in your browser, distinct from the element inspector
instructions: **1. Build a server-rendered article.** Fetch the article's content directly in a Server Component (or the framework's equivalent data-loading mechanism), and render it. View the raw page source and confirm the headline text is present in the actual HTML sent.
**2. Rebuild it fetching in `useEffect` instead.** View the raw page source again for this version. Record precisely what is and is not present, compared with step 1.

**3. Create a module-level store.** Export a plain mutable object or Map at module scope. Simulate two different "users" — two separate function calls or two separate simulated requests — both importing and using the same module. Demonstrate that a value written by one is visible to the other.
**4. Fix it.** Refactor to create a fresh store instance per request or per call, and re-run the same two-user simulation to confirm no leakage occurs.

**5. Serialise a secret, then fix it.** Create a Server Component that fetches an object containing at least one field your client component never displays. Pass the whole object as a prop to a client component. View the raw page source and locate the unused field's value in the HTML. Then narrow the prop to only the fields actually used, and confirm it is no longer present.
reflectionPrompts: In step 2, exactly what was present in the raw source, and what was missing? Was the result what you expected before running it?
In step 3, how many lines of code did it take to create a real, working demonstration of a cross-user leak? Does that number change how seriously you take this specific pattern?
In step 5, was the leaked field's value genuinely visible in the raw page source, in plain readable text, with no special tools required to find it?
Which of these three defects do you think would be hardest to notice in a real code review, and why?

selfAssessmentCriteria: Step 1 and step 2 both include an actual raw-source comparison, not a description of what would happen
Step 3 demonstrates an actual value leaking between two simulated users, not a hypothetical description
Step 4 confirms the leak is resolved with the same simulation re-run
Step 5 locates the specific leaked field's value directly in raw page source before the fix, and confirms its absence after

retrievalPractice.prompt: A colleague says a page 'is server-rendered' because the framework's documentation says so. What single check would you run to verify the actual content is present, not just the framework's capability?

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Check your understanding

Answer without scrolling back.

Three true/false questions, then three short-answer questions.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** Server rendering is strictly better than client rendering and should be the default for every React application.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It adds infrastructure, a second runtime, and genuine framework commitment. An authenticated internal tool with no discoverability need gains essentially none of its benefits while paying all of its costs.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most of the earlier sections' worked examples — the fare console, the meter telemetry, the crew scheduler — are correctly client-rendered for exactly this reason.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** Fetching data in `useEffect` still produces server-rendered content, since the component runs on the server too.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Effects run only after mount, in the browser — the server's rendering pass never reaches an effect, so any content fetched inside one is entirely absent from what the server actually sends.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: View raw page source, not the element inspector, to see exactly what the server sent — this is the single most reliable way to confirm or refute this claim about any real page.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false.** A store created at module level transfers safely from a client-rendered application to a server-rendered one, since the code itself has not changed.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The code is unchanged, but the execution environment is not — a server process shares one context across every request it handles, so the store becomes shared across users rather than private to one, exactly as Section 1 predicted for any module-level mutable value.
Correct.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This section's case study is a concrete instance of exactly this: two years of safe operation under one environment, becoming a real data leak under another, with the code itself never touched.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A React site uses a server-rendering framework, yet search engines index an empty shell for every page. Give the most likely cause, and describe the specific check that would confirm it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** The most likely cause is that page content is fetched inside `useEffect`, which never runs as part of the server's rendering pass, so the actual HTML the server sends contains only a shell with no content — the framework's server-rendering capability is genuinely active, but the component is opting back out of its benefit by deferring content to a lifecycle stage that pass never reaches. The confirming check is to view the page's raw HTML source directly, rather than inspecting the live DOM through the browser's element inspector — the element inspector shows the page *after* hydration and any effects have already run and populated it, which is exactly the misleading comparison that lets this misunderstanding persist undetected. **Accept** any answer correctly naming the effect-timing cause and the raw-source-versus-live-DOM distinction as the confirming check. **Reject** answers proposing server slowness or crawler incompatibility as the primary cause.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** An API credential appears in a public page's HTML source. Explain the most likely mechanism, and the fix.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** A Server Component very likely fetched a response containing the credential — perhaps as one field among several needed only for internal server-side purposes — and passed the entire response object as a prop to a client component, rather than passing only the specific fields that component actually displays. Every prop crossing from a Server Component to a client component is serialised directly into the page's HTML, regardless of which fields the receiving component actually reads, so the unused credential field ends up in publicly readable page source exactly like every other field in the object. The fix is to pass only the specific fields genuinely required by the client component — explicitly naming them, rather than spreading or forwarding the whole object — and to keep genuinely sensitive values, including credentials, in server-only code paths that never construct a props object containing them in the first place. **Accept** any answer correctly identifying whole-object prop passing as the mechanism and field-level narrowing as the fix. **Reject** answers proposing only to rename the environment variable, which does not address the actual serialisation mechanism.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A team says a Server Action does not need its own authorization check because only one internal admin form calls it. Respond, and explicitly name the earlier section this argument echoes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: **Model answer.** A Server Action compiles to a real, addressable HTTP endpoint regardless of how conveniently it is invoked from client-side code, so it remains directly callable by anything capable of constructing a matching request — entirely bypassing the admin form and any assumptions its user interface happens to encode. "Only our form calls this" describes what the current interface does, not what the server is actually willing to accept from any other caller, so the action needs its own independent, server-side authorization check regardless. This is precisely Section 10's hidden-UI argument — that conditional rendering or a route guard enforces nothing on its own — restated for a Server Action's calling convention specifically. **Accept** any answer that correctly identifies the endpoint-regardless-of-invocation-style point and explicitly connects it to Section 10's hidden-UI or route-guard material. **Reject** answers that do not draw the explicit connection to that earlier section's argument.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your answer?

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name two of this course's earlier misconceptions that reappear in this section under a new name or in a new environment, and state the shared underlying rule for each.
From memory, name this section's main topic and the four earlier-section rules it reapplied, with one concrete consequence of each in the server-rendering environment.

transferExercises.context: Migrating an existing client-rendered ticketing application to a server-rendering framework — a different domain from the news-publisher examples used throughout this section.
transferExercises.scenario: A ticketing application currently has: a Redux store created at module level (`export const useEventStore = create(...)`), event data fetched inside `useEffect` on each event's detail page, a theme preference read directly from `localStorage` during render, and an admin "cancel event" action currently gated only by a client-side role check with no corresponding server-side check. The team plans to move the application to a server-rendering framework to improve event-page discoverability in search results.
transferExercises.task: For each of the four described patterns, predict the specific defect it will produce once the application is server-rendered, using this section's material rather than general caution. State which of the four defects is a rendering or correctness problem and which is a security problem, and explain the distinction. Then propose the fix for each, and identify which single one of the four you would prioritise fixing first if the team could only address one before the migration ships, with justification.
successCriteria: Predicts the module-level Redux store will leak state across concurrent users' requests, connecting the prediction explicitly to Section 1's module-evaluation rule
Predicts the useEffect-fetched event data will produce an empty shell in server-rendered output, defeating the stated goal of improving search discoverability entirely
Predicts the localStorage theme read will cause a hydration mismatch, since localStorage does not exist on the server, and proposes rendering after mount or an equivalent deterministic fallback

Correctly classifies the module-level store as a security problem (cross-user data leak) and the useEffect fetch as a correctness or business problem (the migration's stated goal fails), distinguishing the two rather than treating all four as equivalent severity

Identifies that the cancel-event action's client-only permission check remains exactly as exploitable after the migration as before, unrelated to server rendering itself, and connects this to Section 10 rather than treating it as a server-rendering-specific concern

Prioritises either the module-level store (highest-severity security issue) or the useEffect fetch (defeats the entire stated purpose of the migration) with a reasoned justification for the choice, rather than an arbitrary selection
